When a meaning on both ends is stated, having set aside the meaning in the middle, one knows, 'There is a meaning in the middle.' This same method applies to the sequence of the Pāḷi and so on. As for the sequence of connection, when a sutta is begun starting with virtue and the six super-knowledges appear at the end, one knows, 'The sutta has proceeded according to the connection and according to the division.' When a sutta is begun by way of views, even if the truths appear later, one knows, 'It has not proceeded according to the connection.' When a sutta is begun by way of quarrels and disputes, even if the principles of cordiality appear later, one knows, 'It has not proceeded according to the connection.' When a sutta is begun by way of the thirty-two kinds of animal talk, even if the ten topics of discussion appear later, one knows, 'It has not proceeded according to the connection.'

10. Bhaddajisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bhaddaji Sutta

170. Dasame abhibhūti abhibhavitvā ṭhito jeṭṭhako. Anabhibhūtoti aññehi anabhibhūto. Aññadatthūti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Dassanavasena daso, sabbaṃ passatīti adhippāyo. Vasavattīti sabbaṃ janaṃ vase vatteti. Yathā passatoti iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ vā hotu aniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ vā[M 3.0061], yenākārena taṃ passantassa. Anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti anantarāyeva arahattaṃ [V 3.0062] uppajjati. Yathā suṇatoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Atha vā yaṃ cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nirantarameva vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, taṃ tassa arahattaṃ cakkhuviññāṇānantaraṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – idaṃ dassanānaṃ agganti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo.

170. In the tenth sutta, 'abhibhū' means the foremost one who stands having overcome. 'Anabhibhūto' means unconquered by others. 'Aññadatthu' is a particle in the sense of certainty. 'Dasso' (seer) is by way of seeing; the intention is that he sees all. 'Vasavattī' means he makes all people follow his will. 'As one sees': for one who sees it, whether the object be desirable or undesirable, in whatever way. 'Immediately, the destruction of the taints occurs' means that immediately the fruit of Arahantship arises. 'As one hears': here too, this is the method. Alternatively, having seen a form with the eye, and having immediately established insight, one attains the fruit of Arahantship; that fruit of Arahantship of that person is called 'immediately following eye-consciousness.' Referring to that, it was said: 'This is the foremost of sights.' In the second phrase too, this is the method.

Yathā sukhitassāti yena maggasukhena sukhitassa. Anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti samanantarameva arahattaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ sukhānaṃ agganti idaṃ maggasukhaṃ sukhānaṃ uttamaṃ. Yathā saññissāti idhāpi maggasaññāva adhippetā. Yathā bhūtassāti yasmiṃ bhave yasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhitassa. Anantarāti [P 3.0302] anantarāyena arahattaṃ uppajjati. idaṃ bhavānaṃ agganti ayaṃ pacchimo attabhāvo bhavānaṃ aggaṃ nāma. Atha vā yathā bhūtassāti yehi khandhehi maggakkhaṇe bhūtassa vijjamānassa. Anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti maggānantarameva phalaṃ uppajjati. Idaṃ bhavānaṃ agganti idaṃ maggakkhaṇe khandhapañcakaṃ bhavānaṃ aggaṃ nāmāti.

'As one who is happy' means one who is happy with the happiness of the path. 'Immediately, the destruction of the taints occurs' means that immediately the fruit of Arahantship arises. 'This is the foremost of happinesses' means this happiness of the path is supreme among happinesses. 'As one who perceives': here too, perception associated with the path is intended. 'As one who has become': for one who is established in whatever existence, in whatever individual existence. 'Immediately' means the fruit of Arahantship arises without obstacle. 'This is the foremost of existences' means this final individual existence is called the foremost among existences. Alternatively, 'as one who has become': for one who has become manifest with those aggregates at the moment of the path. 'Immediately, the destruction of the taints occurs' means that immediately after the path, the fruit arises. 'This is the foremost of existences' means this pentad of aggregates at the moment of the path is called the foremost among existences.

Āghātavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on Resentment.

(18) 3. Upāsakavaggo

(18) 3. The Chapter on Lay Followers

1-3. Sārajjasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Commentary on the Sārajja Sutta, etc.

171-173. Tatiyassa paṭhamadutiyatatiyesu agāriyappaṭipatti kathitā. Sotāpannasakadāgāminopi hontu, vaṭṭantiyeva.

In the first, second, and third suttas of the third chapter, the practice of householders is taught. Let them be stream-enterers or once-returners, it is indeed proper.

4. Verasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vera Sutta

174. Catutthe bhayānīti cittutrāsabhayāni. Verānīti akusalaverānipi puggalaverānipi[V 3.0063]. Cetasikanti cittanissitaṃ. Dukkhanti kāyapasādavatthukaṃ dukkhaṃ. Domanassanti domanassavedanaṃ. Imasmiṃ sutte viratipahānaṃ kathitaṃ.

174. In the fourth sutta, 'fears' means terrors of the mind. 'Enmities' means both unwholesome enmities and personal enmities. 'Mental' means dependent on the mind. 'Suffering' means suffering that has the sensitive body-matter as its base. 'Displeasure' means the feeling of displeasure. In this sutta, abandoning by way of abstinence is taught.

5. Caṇḍālasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Caṇḍāla Sutta

175. Pañcame [M 3.0062] upāsakapatikuṭṭhoti upāsakapacchimako. Kotūhalamaṅgalikoti “iminā idaṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pavattattā kotūhalasaṅkhātena diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalena samannāgato. Maṅgalaṃ pacceti no kammanti maṅgalaṃ oloketi, kammaṃ na oloketi. Ito ca bahiddhāti imamhā sāsanā bahiddhā. Pubbakāraṃ karotīti dānādikaṃ kusalakiccaṃ paṭhamataraṃ karoti.

175. In the fifth, `upāsakapaṭikuṭṭho` means the lowest of lay supporters. `Kotūhalamaṅgaliko` means one who, because it occurs thus, “By this, this will be,” is endowed with auspicious signs that are seen, heard, or cognized, which are known as ‘curiosity’. `Maṅgalaṃ pacceti no kammaṃ` means he looks to auspicious signs; he does not look to kamma. `Ito ca bahiddhā` means outside of this Dispensation. `Pubbakāraṃ karoti` means he first does a wholesome duty such as giving.

6. Pītisuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Pīti Sutta

176. Chaṭṭhe [P 3.0303] kinti mayanti kena nāma upāyena mayaṃ. Pavivekaṃ pītinti paṭhamadutiyajjhānāni nissāya uppajjanakapītiṃ. Kāmūpasaṃhitanti kāmanissitaṃ duvidhe kāme ārabbha uppajjanakaṃ. Akusalūpasaṃhitanti “migasūkarādayo vijjhissāmī”ti saraṃ khipitvā tasmiṃ viraddhe “viraddhaṃ mayā”ti evaṃ akusale nissāya uppajjanakaṃ. Tādisesu pana ṭhānesu avirajjhantassa “suṭṭhu me viddhaṃ, suṭṭhu me pahaṭa”nti uppajjanakaṃ akusalūpasaṃhitaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ nāma. Dānādiupakaraṇānaṃ asampattiyā uppajjamānaṃ pana kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassanti veditabbaṃ.

176. In the sixth, `kinti mayaṃ` means: by what means shall we? `Pavivekaṃ pītiṃ` means: the joy that arises in dependence on the first and second jhānas, etc. `Kāmūpasaṃhitaṃ` means: that which is dependent on sensual pleasure, arising with the twofold sensual pleasures as its object. `Akusalūpasaṃhitaṃ` means: that which arises in dependence on the unwholesome, as when, having shot an arrow with the thought, “I will shoot deer, pigs, etc.,” and having missed, one thinks, “I have missed.” Furthermore, in such cases, for one who does not miss, the happiness and joy that arises thinking, “I have shot well, I have struck well,” is called happiness and joy connected with the unwholesome. Furthermore, the suffering and displeasure that arises from the lack of requisites for giving, etc., should be known as suffering and displeasure connected with the wholesome.

7. Vaṇijjāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Vaṇijjā Sutta

177. Sattame vaṇijjāti vāṇijakammāni. Upāsakenāti tisaraṇagatena. Satthavaṇijjāti āvudhabhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā tassa vikkayo. Sattavaṇijjāti manussavikkayo. Maṃsavaṇijjāti sūkaramigādayo posetvā tesaṃ vikkayo. Majjavaṇijjāti yaṃkiñci majjaṃ kāretvā tassa vikkayo. Visavaṇijjāti visaṃ kāretvā tassa vikkayo. Iti sabbampi imaṃ vaṇijjaṃ neva attanā kātuṃ, na pare samādapetvā kāretuṃ vaṭṭati.

177. In the seventh, `vaṇijjā` means trading activities. `Upāsakena` means by a lay follower who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels. `Satthavaṇijjā` is trade in weapons: having caused weapons to be made and selling them. `Sattavaṇijjā` is trade in beings: the selling of human beings. `Maṃsavaṇijjā` is trade in meat: rearing pigs, deer, etc., and selling them. `Majjavaṇijjā` is trade in intoxicants: making any kind of intoxicant and selling it. `Visavaṇijjā` is trade in poison: making poison and selling it. Thus, it is not proper to do any of this trading oneself, nor to have it done by inciting others.

8. Rājasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Rājasutta

178. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0064] pabbājentīti raṭṭhamhā pabbājenti. Yathāpaccayaṃ vā karontīti yathādhippāyaṃ yathājjhāsayaṃ karonti. Tatheva pāpakammaṃ pavedentīti yathā tena kataṃ, taṃ tatheva aññesaṃ ārocenti kathenti.

178. In the eighth, `pabbājenti` means they banish from the country. `Yathāpaccayaṃ vā karonti` means they act according to their wish and inclination. `Tatheva pāpakammaṃ pavedenti` means they announce and relate to others the evil deed exactly as it was done by that person.

9. Gihisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Gihisutta

179. Navame [M 3.0063][P 3.0304] saṃvutakammantanti pihitakammantaṃ. Ābhicetasikānanti uttamacittanissitānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti paccakkheyeva dhamme pavattikkhaṇe sukhavihārānaṃ. Ariyakantehīti ariyānaṃ kantehi maggaphalasīlehi.

179. In the ninth, `saṃvutakammantaṃ` means one whose actions are closed off. `Ābhicetasikānaṃ` means of those who are dependent on the supreme mind. `Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ` means of pleasant abidings in this very life, at the moment of occurrence. `Ariyakantehi` means with the virtues associated with the path and fruit, which are beloved by the noble ones.

Ariyadhammaṃ samādāyāti ettha ariyadhammoti pañca sīlāni kathitāni. Merayaṃ vāruṇinti catubbidhaṃ merayaṃ pañcavidhañca suraṃ. Dhammañcānuvitakkayeti navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ anussativaseneva vitakkeyya. Abyāpajjhaṃ hitaṃ cittanti niddukkhaṃ mettādibrahmavihāracittaṃ. Devalokāya bhāvayeti brahmalokatthāya bhāveyya. Puññatthassa jigīsatoti puññena atthikassa puññaṃ gavesantassa. Santesūti buddhapaccekabuddhatathāgatasāvakesu. Vipulā hoti dakkhiṇāti evaṃ dinnadānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti. Anupubbenāti sīlapūraṇādinā anukkamena. Sesaṃ tikanipāte vuttatthameva.

In the passage `ariyadhammaṃ samādāya`, here `ariyadhammo` is said to be the five precepts. `Merayaṃ vāruṇiṃ` refers to the four kinds of fermented liquor and the five kinds of distilled liquor. `Dhammañcānuvitakkaye` means one should reflect on the ninefold supramundane Dhamma by way of recollection. `Abyāpajjhaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ` means a mind free from suffering, associated with the divine abodes beginning with loving-kindness. `Devalokāya bhāvaye` means one should develop it for the sake of the Brahma world. `Puññatthassa jigīsato` means for one who is in need of merit, who seeks merit. `Santesu` means among the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Tathāgata. `Vipulā hoti dakkhiṇā` means a gift given thus is of great fruit. `Anupubbena` means in sequence, beginning with the fulfillment of virtue. The rest has the meaning already stated in the Tikanipāta.

10. Gavesīsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Gavesī Sutta

180. Dasame sitaṃ pātvākāsīti mahāmaggeneva gacchanto taṃ sālavanaṃ oloketvā “atthi nu kho imasmiṃ ṭhāne kiñci sukāraṇaṃ uppannapubba”nti addasa kassapabuddhakāle gavesinā upāsakena kataṃ sukāraṇaṃ. Athassa etadahosi – “idaṃ sukāraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa apākaṭaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, handa naṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa pākaṭaṃ karomī”ti maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ padese ṭhitova sitapātukammaṃ [P 3.0305] akāsi, aggaggadante dassetvā mandahasitaṃ hasi[V 3.0065]. Yathā hi lokiyamanussā udaraṃ paharantā “kahaṃ kaha”nti hasanti, na evaṃ buddhā. Buddhānaṃ pana hasitaṃ haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāramattameva hoti.

180. In the tenth, `sitaṃ pātvākāsi` means that while traveling along the great road, he looked at that grove of sal trees and, while considering, “I wonder if any good cause has ever arisen in this place?” he saw the good cause that was performed by the lay follower Gavesī during the time of the Buddha Kassapa. Then this thought occurred to him: “This good cause is not manifest to the community of bhikkhus; it is concealed. Let me now make it manifest to the community of bhikkhus.” Stepping off the path, he stood in a certain spot and performed the act of manifesting a smile; showing the tips of his teeth, he smiled a gentle smile. For just as worldly people laugh “ha ha,” striking their chests, the Buddhas do not laugh in such a way. Rather, the smiling of the Buddhas is merely the appearance of joy and delight.

Hasitañca nāmetaṃ terasahi somanassasahagatacittehi hoti. Tattha lokiyamahājano akusalato catūhi, kāmāvacarakusalato catūhīti aṭṭhahi cittehi hasati, sekhā akusalato diṭṭhigatasampayuttāni dve apanetvā chahi cittehi hasanti, khīṇāsavā catūhi sahetukakiriyacittehi, ekena ahetukakiriyacittenāti pañcahi cittehi [M 3.0064] hasanti. Tesupi balavārammaṇe āpāthamāgate dvīhi ñāṇasampayuttacittehi hasanti, dubbalārammaṇe duhetukacittadvayena ca ahetukacittena cāti tīhi cittehi hasanti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātusomanassasahagatacittaṃ bhagavato pahaṭṭhākāramattahasitaṃ uppādeti.

And this thing called smiling occurs with thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy. Among them, ordinary worldly people laugh with eight types of consciousness: four unwholesome and four sense-sphere wholesome. Learners, having excluded the two unwholesome types associated with wrong view, laugh with six types of consciousness. Those whose taints are destroyed laugh with five types of consciousness: four rooted functional types of consciousness and one rootless functional type of consciousness. Among these too, when a strong object comes into range, they laugh with two types of consciousness associated with knowledge; when a weak object comes into range, they laugh with three types of consciousness: the two two-rooted types of consciousness and the one rootless type of consciousness. In this instance, however, the rootless functional mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy produces the Blessed One's smile, which is merely the appearance of delight.

Taṃ panetaṃ hasitaṃ evaṃ appamattakampi therassa pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Kathaṃ? Tathārūpe hi kāle tathāgatassa catūhi dāṭhāhi cātuddīpikamahāmeghamukhato samosaritā vijjulatā viya virocamānā mahātālakkhandhappamāṇā rasmivaṭṭiyo uṭṭhahitvā tikkhattuṃ siravaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dāṭhaggesuyeva antaradhāyanti. Tena saññāṇena āyasmā ānando bhagavato pacchato gacchamānopi sitapātubhāvaṃ jānāti.

Furthermore, this smile, slight as it was, became manifest to the Elder. How? For at such a time, from the four canine teeth of the Tathāgata, shining like a streak of lightning flashing from the mouth of a great rain cloud that pervades the four continents, pairs of rays the size of great palm-tree trunks arose, circumambulated the excellent head three times to the right, and disappeared right at the tips of the canine teeth. By that sign, the Venerable Ānanda, even while walking behind the Blessed One, knew of the manifestation of the smile.

Iddhanti samiddhaṃ. Phītanti atisamiddhaṃ sabbapāliphullaṃ viya. Ākiṇṇamanussanti janasamākulaṃ. Sīlesu aparipūrakārīti pañcasu sīlesu asamattakārī. Paṭidesitānīti [P 3.0306] upāsakabhāvaṃ paṭidesitāni. Samādapitānīti saraṇesu patiṭṭhāpitānīti attho. Iccetaṃ samasamanti iti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ sabbākārato samabhāveneva samaṃ, na ekadesena. Natthi kiñci atirekanti mayhaṃ imehi kiñci atirekaṃ natthi. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Atirekāyāti visesakāraṇatthāya paṭipajjāmīti attho. Sīlesu paripūrakāriṃ dhārethāti pañcasu sīlesu samattakārīti jānātha. Ettāvatā tena pañca sīlāni samādinnāni nāma honti. Kimaṅga pana na mayanti mayaṃ pana keneva kāraṇena paripūrakārino na bhavissāma. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

'Prosperous' means accomplished. 'Thriving' means exceedingly accomplished, like a tree in full bloom. 'Crowded with people' means thronged with people. 'One who does not fulfill the precepts' means one who does not accomplish the five precepts. 'Were declared' means their state as lay followers was declared. 'Were established' means they were established in the refuges; this is the meaning. 'Thus, this is equal' means this reason is equal in every respect, not just in some part. 'There is nothing superior' means 'For me, there is no practice that surpasses these.' `Handa` is a particle in the sense of resolve. 'For the sake of superiority' means 'I will practice for the sake of a special cause'; this is the meaning. 'You should regard him as one who fulfills the precepts' means you should know that he is one who accomplishes the five precepts. To this extent, the five precepts are said to have been undertaken by him. 'Why then not we?' means 'For what reason, then, should we not become fulfillers?' The rest here is self-evident.

Upāsakavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Lay Followers, the Third.

(19) 4. Araññavaggo

(19) 4. The Forest Chapter

1. Āraññikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Forest Dwellers

181. Catutthassa [V 3.0066] paṭhame mandattā momūhattāti neva samādānaṃ jānāti, na ānisaṃsaṃ. Attano pana mandattā momūhattā aññāṇeneva āraññako [M 3.0065] hoti. Pāpiccho icchāpakatoti “araññe me viharantassa ‘ayaṃ āraññako’ti catupaccayasakkāraṃ karissanti, ‘ayaṃ bhikkhu lajjī pavivitto’tiādīhi ca guṇehi sambhāvessantī”ti evaṃ pāpikāya icchāya ṭhatvā tāya eva icchāya abhibhūto hutvā āraññako hoti. Ummādavasena araññaṃ pavisitvā viharanto pana ummādā cittakkhepā āraññako nāma hoti. Vaṇṇitanti [P 3.0307] idaṃ āraññakaṅgaṃ nāma buddhehi ca buddhasāvakehi ca vaṇṇitaṃ pasatthanti āraññako hoti. Idamatthitanti imāya kalyāṇāya paṭipattiyā attho etassāti idamatthī, idamatthino bhāvo idamatthitā. Taṃ idamatthitaṃyeva nissāya, na aññaṃ kiñci lokāmisanti attho. Sesamettha ito paresu ca uttānatthameva.

181. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, mandattā momūhattā ('due to dullness and delusion') means he knows neither the undertaking nor its benefits. But due to his own dullness and delusion, he becomes a forest-dweller simply out of ignorance. Pāpiccho icchāpakato ('with evil desires, overcome by wishes') means: thinking, “While I am dwelling in the forest, they will provide me with the honor of the four requisites, saying, ‘This is a forest-dweller,’ and they will praise me with virtues such as, ‘This monk is conscientious and secluded,’” thus, abiding in such an evil desire and being overcome by that very desire, he becomes a forest-dweller. As for one who enters the forest by way of madness and dwells there, he is called a forest-dweller on account of madness and mental distraction. Vaṇṇitaṃ ('praised') means: thinking, 'This ascetic practice of forest-dwelling is praised and commended by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha,' he becomes a forest-dweller. Idamatthitaṃ ('the state of having this purpose') means: for him, there is a purpose in this good practice, thus he is one 'having this purpose' (idamatthī); the state of one 'having this purpose' is idamatthitā. Relying on that very state of having a purpose, and not on any other worldly allurement—this is the meaning. The rest, both here and in the discourses that follow, has a clear meaning.

Araññavaggo catuttho.

The Forest Chapter, the Fourth.

(20) 5. Brāhmaṇavaggo

(20) 5. The Brahmin Chapter

1. Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Soṇa Discourse

191. Pañcamassa paṭhame brāhmaṇadhammāti brāhmaṇasabhāvā. Sunakhesūti kukkuresu. Neva kiṇanti na vikkiṇantīti na gaṇhantā kiṇanti, na dadantā vikkiṇanti. Sampiyeneva saṃvāsaṃ saṃbandhāya sampavattentīti piyo piyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paveṇiyā bandhanatthaṃ saṃvāsaṃ pavattayanti[V 3.0067]. Udarāvadehakanti udaraṃ avadihitvā upacinitvā pūretvā. Avasesaṃ ādāya pakkamantīti yaṃ bhuñjituṃ na sakkonti, taṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā gahetvā gacchanti. Imasmiṃ sutte vaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

191. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, brāhmaṇadhammā ('brahmin principles') means the nature of a brahmin. Sunakhesu ('among dogs') means among dogs. Neva kiṇanti na vikkiṇanti ('they neither buy nor sell') means: it is not that those who take are buying, nor that those who give are selling. Sampiyeneva saṃvāsaṃ saṃbandhāya sampavattenti ('they enter into association only out of affection for the sake of connection') means: a beloved one, having approached another beloved one, brings about association for the purpose of binding the lineage. Udarāvadehakaṃ ('stuffing the belly') means having put into, accumulated in, and filled the belly. Avasesaṃ ādāya pakkamanti ('they depart taking the remainder') means: whatever they are unable to eat, they make into a bundle, take it, and go. In this discourse, only the round of existence is taught.

2. Doṇabrāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Doṇa Discourse

192. Dutiye tvampi noti tvampi nu. Pavattāroti pavattayitāro. Yesanti yesaṃ santakaṃ. Mantapadanti [P 3.0308] vedasaṅkhātaṃ mantameva. Gītanti aṭṭhakādīhi dasahi porāṇakabrāhmaṇehi sarasampattivasena sajjhāyitaṃ. Pavuttanti aññesaṃ vuttaṃ, vācitanti attho. Samīhitanti samupabyūḷhaṃ rāsikataṃ, piṇḍaṃ [M 3.0066] katvā ṭhapitanti attho. Tadanugāyantīti etarahi brāhmaṇā taṃ tehi pubbehi gītaṃ anugāyanti anusajjhāyanti. Tadanubhāsantīti taṃ anubhāsanti. Idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Bhāsitamanubhāsantīti tehi bhāsitaṃ anubhāsanti. Sajjhāyitamanusajjhāyantīti tehi sajjhāyitaṃ anusajjhāyanti. Vācitamanuvācentīti tehi aññesaṃ vācitaṃ anuvācenti. Seyyathidanti te katameti attho. Aṭṭhakotiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni. Te kira dibbena cakkhunā oloketvā parūpaghātaṃ akatvā kassapasammāsambuddhassa bhagavato pāvacanena saha saṃsandetvā mante ganthesuṃ. Aparāpare pana brāhmaṇā pāṇātipātādīni pakkhipitvā tayo vede bhinditvā buddhavacanena saddhiṃ viruddhe akaṃsu. Tyāssu’meti ettha assūti nipātamattaṃ, te brāhmaṇā ime pañca brāhmaṇe paññāpentīti attho.

192. In the second discourse, tvampi no means tvampi nu ('do you also...?'). Pavattāro means originators. Yesaṃ means 'belonging to them.' Mantapadanti refers to the mantra itself, known as the Veda. Gītaṃ ('sung') refers to that which was chanted by the ten ancient brahmins, beginning with Aṭṭhaka, by means of perfection of sound. Pavuttaṃ ('spoken') means spoken to others, that is, taught; this is the meaning. Samīhitaṃ ('compiled') means gathered together, made into a collection, made into a mass and kept; this is the meaning. Tadanugāyanti ('they sing in imitation') means: nowadays, the brahmins sing in imitation of that which was sung by those of the past; they chant in imitation. Tadanubhāsanti ('they speak in imitation') means they speak in imitation of it. This is a synonym for the previous term. Bhāsitamanubhāsanti ('they speak in imitation of what was spoken') means they speak in imitation of what was spoken by them. Sajjhāyitamanusajjhāyanti ('they chant in imitation of what was chanted') means they chant in imitation of what was chanted by them. Vācitamanuvācenti ('they teach in imitation of what was taught') means they teach in imitation of what was taught by them to others. Seyyathidaṃ ('namely') means 'which are they?'; this is the meaning. Aṭṭhaka and so on are their names. It is said that they, having looked with the divine eye and not causing harm to others, composed the mantras after comparing them with the teaching of the Blessed One, Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One. But later brahmins, having inserted things like the killing of living beings, corrupted the three Vedas and made them contradictory to the word of the Buddha. In the phrase tyāssu’me, assu is merely a particle; the meaning is that those brahmins designate these five brahmins.

Mante adhīyamānoti vede sajjhāyanto gaṇhanto. Ācariyadhananti ācariyadakkhiṇaṃ ācariyabhāgaṃ. Na issatthenāti na yodhājīvakammena uppādeti. Na rājaporisenāti na rājupaṭṭhākabhāvena. Kevalaṃ bhikkhācariyāyāti suddhāya bhikkhācariyāya eva. Kapālaṃ [P 3.0309] anatimaññamānoti taṃ bhikkhābhājanaṃ anatimaññamāno. So hi puṇṇapattaṃ ādāya sīsaṃ nhāto kuladvāresu ṭhatvā “ahaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni komārabrahmacariyaṃ cariṃ, mantāpi me gahitā, ācariyassa ācariyadhanaṃ dassāmi, dhanaṃ me dethā”ti yācati. Taṃ sutvā manussā yathāsatti yathābalaṃ aṭṭhapi soḷasapi satampi sahassampi denti. Evaṃ sakalagāmaṃ caritvā laddhadhanaṃ ācariyassa niyyādeti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ kho doṇa brāhmaṇo brahmasamo hotīti evaṃ brahmavihārehi samannāgatattā brāhmaṇo brahmasamo nāma hoti.

Mante adhīyamāno ('studying the sacred texts') means chanting and learning the Vedas. Ācariyadhanaṃ ('teacher's wealth') means the teacher's offering, the teacher's share. Na issatthena ('not by archery') means he does not generate it through the work of living as a warrior. Na rājaporisena ('not by royal service') means not through being a king's attendant. Kevalaṃ bhikkhācariyāya ('only by the practice of alms-gathering') means only by the pure practice of going for alms. Kapālaṃ anatimaññamāno ('not despising the bowl') means not looking down upon the alms bowl. For he, having taken a full bowl and bathed his head, stands at the doors of families and begs, saying, “I have practiced the celibate life from youth for forty-eight years, and I have learned the sacred texts. I will give the teacher's wealth to my teacher; give me wealth.” Hearing this, people give according to their ability and strength—eight, sixteen, a hundred, or even a thousand. Having wandered through the entire village in this way, he hands over the wealth he has received to his teacher. This was said in reference to that. Evaṃ kho, doṇa, brāhmaṇo brahmasamo hoti ('Thus, Doṇa, a brahmin is equal to Brahmā') means: thus, because of being endowed with the divine abodes, a brahmin is called 'one who is equal to Brahmā'.

Neva [V 3.0068] kayena na vikkayenāti neva attanā kayaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, na parena vikkayaṃ katvā dinnaṃ. Udakūpassaṭṭhanti udakena upassaṭṭhaṃ pariccattaṃ. So hi yasmiṃ kule vayappattā dārikā atthi, gantvā tassa dvāre tiṭṭhati. “Kasmā ṭhitosī”ti vutte “ahaṃ aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni komārabrahmacariyaṃ cariṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ tumhākaṃ demi, tumhe mayhaṃ dārikaṃ dethā”ti vadati. Te dārikaṃ ānetvā tassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā denti. So taṃ udakūpassaṭṭhaṃ bhariyaṃ gaṇhitvā gacchati. Atimīḷhajoti atimīḷhe [M 3.0067] mahāgūtharāsimhi jāto. Tassa sāti tassa esā. Na davatthāti na kīḷanatthā. Na ratatthāti na kāmaratiatthā. Methunaṃ [P 3.0310] uppādetvāti dhītaraṃ vā puttaṃ vā uppādetvā “idāni paveṇi ghaṭīyissatī”ti nikkhamitvā pabbajati. Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokanti brahmalokameva sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Devasamo hotīti dibbavihārehi samannāgatattā devasamo nāma hoti.

Neva kayena na vikkayena ('neither by purchase nor by sale') means he neither takes a wife by purchasing her himself, nor accepts one given after being sold by another. Udakūpassaṭṭhaṃ ('relinquished with water') means given up by means of water. For if there is a girl of marriageable age in a certain family, he goes and stands at their door. When asked, “Why are you standing here?” he says, “I have practiced the celibate life from youth for forty-eight years. I give all of that to you; you give me your daughter.” They bring the girl, and letting water fall on his hand, they give her to him. He takes that wife, relinquished with water, and departs. Atimīḷhajo ('born in extreme filth') means born in a great heap of excrement. Tassa sā ('she is his') means she belongs to him. Na davatthā ('not for sport') means not for the sake of amusement. Na ratatthā ('not for pleasure') means not for the sake of sensual delight. Methunaṃ uppādetvā ('having produced a union') means: after begetting a daughter or a son, thinking, “Now the lineage will be connected,” he leaves home and goes forth into homelessness. Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ ('a good destination, a heavenly world') refers only to the Brahmā world. Devasamo hoti ('he is equal to a deva') means: because of being endowed with the divine abodes, he is called 'one who is equal to a deva'.

Tameva puttassādaṃ nikāmayamānoti yvāssa dhītaraṃ vā puttaṃ vā jātaṃ disvā puttapemaṃ puttassādo uppajjati, taṃ patthayamāno icchamāno. Kuṭumbaṃ ajjhāvasatīti kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā kuṭumbamajjhe vasati. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

“Desiring only that delight in a child” means: upon seeing a daughter or a son who has been born, whatever affection for a child and delight in a child arises, he aspires for and desires it. “He dwells amidst the household” means: having established a household, he dwells in the midst of the household. The remainder here is indeed clear.

3. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta.

193. Tatiye pagevāti paṭhamaññeva. Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitenāti kāmarāgaggahitena. Kāmarāgaparetenāti kāmarāgānugatena. Nissaraṇanti tividhaṃ kāmarāgassa nissaraṇaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, tadaṅganissaraṇaṃ, samucchedanissaraṇanti. Tattha asubhe paṭhamajjhānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ nāma, vipassanā tadaṅganissaraṇaṃ nāma, arahattamaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ tividhampi nappajānātīti attho. Attatthampītiādīsu arahattasaṅkhāto attano attho attattho nāma, paccayadāyakānaṃ attho parattho nāma, sveva duvidho ubhayattho nāma. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo.

193. In the third, 'just as before' means 'from the very first'. 'Overcome by sensual passion' means 'seized by sensual passion'. 'Engrossed in sensual passion' means 'followed by sensual passion'. Regarding 'escape', the escape from sensual passion is threefold: escape by suppression, escape by substitution, and escape by cutting off. Among these, the first jhāna on the impure is called escape by suppression; the path of Arahantship is called escape by cutting off. The meaning is that one does not know that escape, which is of three kinds. In 'one's own welfare', etc., one's own welfare, designated as the fruit of Arahantship, is called 'one's own welfare'; the welfare of the donors of requisites is called 'the welfare of others'; that very two-fold welfare is called 'the welfare of both'. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

Ayaṃ pana viseso – byāpādassa nissaraṇantiādīsu hi dveva nissaraṇāni vikkhambhananissaraṇañca samucchedanissaraṇañca. Tattha byāpādassa tāva mettāya paṭhamajjhānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ nāma, anāgāmimaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhassa ālokasaññā vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ[V 3.0069], arahattamaggo [P 3.0311] samucchedanissaraṇaṃ. Uddhaccakukkuccassa yo koci samatho vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, uddhaccassa panettha arahattamaggo, kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ. Vicikicchāya dhammavavatthānaṃ vikkhambhananissaraṇaṃ, paṭhamamaggo samucchedanissaraṇaṃ.

This, however, is the distinction: for 'the escape from ill will' and so on, there are only two escapes: escape by suppression and escape by cutting off. Among these, for ill will, the first jhāna on loving-kindness is called escape by suppression; the path of non-returning is escape by cutting off. For sloth and torpor, the perception of light is escape by suppression; the path of Arahantship is escape by cutting off. For restlessness and remorse, any serenity is escape by suppression; furthermore, among these, for restlessness, the path of Arahantship is escape by cutting off; for remorse, the path of non-returning is escape by cutting off. For doubt, the determination of phenomena is escape by suppression; the first path is escape by cutting off.

Yā panettha seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, udapatto saṃsaṭṭho lākhāya vātiādikā upamā vuttā, tāsu udapattoti udakabharitā pāti. Saṃsaṭṭhoti [M 3.0068] vaṇṇabhedakaraṇavasena saṃsaṭṭho. Ukkudhitoti kudhito. Ussadakajātoti usumakajāto. Sevālapaṇakapariyonaddhoti tilabījakādibhedena sevālena vā nīlamaṇḍūkapiṭṭhivaṇṇena vā udakapiṭṭhiṃ chādetvā nibbattena paṇakena pariyonaddho. Vāteritoti vātena erito kampito. Āviloti appasanno. Luḷitoti asannisinno. Kalalībhūtoti kaddamībhūto. Andhakāre nikkhittoti koṭṭhakantarādibhede anālokaṭṭhāne ṭhapito. Imasmiṃ sutte bhagavā tīhi bhavehi desanaṃ nivaṭṭetvā arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhapesi, brāhmaṇo pana saraṇamatte patiṭṭhitoti.

Regarding the simile given here, “Just as, brahmin, a bowl of water mixed with lac dye…”, and so on: among these, 'a bowl of water' means a bowl filled with water. 'Mixed' means mixed by means of causing a change of color. 'Boiling' means seething. 'Having produced steam' means having vapor produced. 'Overspread with algae and moss' means overspread with algae of various kinds such as the 'sesame seed' type, or with moss that has arisen, covering the water's surface, having the color of a dark green frog's back. 'Stirred by the wind' means shaken by the wind. 'Turbid' means not clear. 'Agitated' means not well-settled. 'Become muddy' means become like mud. 'Placed in darkness' means placed in a location without light, such as between granaries. In this sutta, the Blessed One, having delivered the teaching with the three kinds of existence, concluded it with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The brahmin, however, was established merely in the refuges.

4. Kāraṇapālīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Kāraṇapālī Sutta

194. Catutthe kāraṇapālīti pāloti tassa nāmaṃ, rājakulānaṃ pana kammante kāretīti kāraṇapālī nāma jāto. Kammantaṃ [P 3.0312] kāretīti pātova uṭṭhāya dvāraṭṭālakapākāre akate kāreti, jiṇṇe paṭijaggāpeti. Piṅgiyāniṃ brāhmaṇanti evaṃnāmakaṃ anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhitaṃ ariyasāvakaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ. So kira pātova uṭṭhāya gandhamālādīni gāhāpetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā nagaraṃ āgacchati, idaṃ brāhmaṇassa devasikaṃ vattanti. Taṃ so evaṃ vattaṃ katvā āgacchantaṃ addasa. Etadavocāti “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo paññavā ñāṇuttaro, kahaṃ nu kho pātova gantvā āgacchatī”ti cintetvā anukkamena santikaṃ āgataṃ sañjānitvā “handa kuto nū”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

194. In the fourth sutta, Kāraṇapālī: 'Pālī' is his name. But because he causes work to be done for the royal families, he came to be known as Kāraṇapālī. 'He causes work to be done' means that, rising early in the morning, he causes gates, watchtowers, and ramparts that are not yet made to be made, and he has the dilapidated ones repaired. 'The brahmin Piṅgiyāni' refers to a brahmin of that name who is a noble disciple established in the fruit of non-returning. It is said that he would rise early, have perfumes, garlands, and so forth taken, go to the Teacher, pay homage, make offerings with the perfumes and garlands, and then return to the city. This was the brahmin's daily practice. So he [Kāraṇapālī] saw him [Piṅgiyāni] coming after having performed this duty. 'He said this' means that, having thought, 'This brahmin is wise and has superior knowledge. Where could he be going so early and returning from?', and having recognized him as he gradually approached, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Well now, from where...?'

Tattha divā divassāti divasassāpi divā, majjhanhikakāleti attho. Paṇḍito maññeti bhavaṃ piṅgiyānī samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṇḍitoti maññati, udāhu noti ayamettha attho. Ko cāhaṃ, bhoti, bho, samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyajānane ahaṃ ko nāma? Ko ca samaṇassa [V 3.0070] gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jānissāmīti kuto cāhaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jānissāmi, kena nāma kāraṇena jānissāmīti evaṃ sabbathāpi attano ajānanabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sopi nūnassa tādisovāti yo samaṇassa gotamassa paññāveyyattiyaṃ jāneyya, sopi nūna dasa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ patto tādiso [M 3.0069] buddhoyeva bhaveyya. Sineruṃ vā hi pathaviṃ vā ākāsaṃ vā pametukāmena tappamāṇo daṇḍo [P 3.0313] vā rajju vā laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, samaṇassa gotamassa paññaṃ jānantenapi tassa ñāṇasadisameva sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Ādaravasena panettha āmeḍitaṃ kataṃ. Uḷārāyāti uttamāya seṭṭhāya. Ko cāhaṃ, bhoti, bho, ahaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa pasaṃsane ko nāma. Ko ca samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pasaṃsissāmīti kena kāraṇena pasaṃsissāmi.

Therein, 'by day of the day' means in the daytime of the day; the meaning is 'at midday'. 'You think him wise' means: 'Does the venerable Piṅgiyāni consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or not?'—this is the meaning here. 'And who am I, good sir?' means: 'Good sir, in knowing the keenness of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom, who am I? And how could I know the keenness of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom?'—meaning, 'For what reason could I know the keenness of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom?' Thus, in every way, he shows his own inability to know. 'Surely, he would be one like him' means: 'Whoever could know the keenness of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom, surely that person too, having fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience, would be a Buddha just like him.' Indeed, for one who wishes to measure Sineru, or the earth, or the sky, it is necessary to obtain a rod or a rope of that same measure. He shows that, similarly, one who would know the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama must obtain the wisdom of omniscience that is just like his knowledge. Here, the repetition is made out of respect. 'Of the sublime' means of the supreme, of the best. 'And who am I, good sir?' means: 'Good sir, in praising the ascetic Gotama, who am I? And how shall I praise the ascetic Gotama?'—meaning, 'For what reason would I be able to praise him?'

Pasatthappasatthoti sabbaguṇānaṃ upari carehi sabbalokapasatthehi attano guṇeheva pasattho, na tassa aññehi pasaṃsanakiccaṃ atthi. Yathā hi campakapupphaṃ vā nīluppalaṃ vā padumaṃ vā lohitacandanaṃ vā attano vaṇṇagandhasiriyāva pāsādikañceva sugandhañca, na tassa āgantukehi vaṇṇagandhehi thomanakiccaṃ atthi. Yathā ca maṇiratanaṃ vā candamaṇḍalaṃ vā attano ālokeneva obhāsati, na tassa aññena obhāsanakiccaṃ atthi, evaṃ samaṇo gotamo sabbalokapasatthehi attano guṇeheva pasattho thomito, sabbalokassa seṭṭhataṃ pāpito. Na tassa aññena pasaṃsanakiccaṃ atthi.

'Praised by the praised' means he is praised by his own virtues, which are praised by the entire world; for him, there is no need for praise from others. For just as a campaka flower, a blue lotus, a lotus, or red sandalwood is pleasing and fragrant by its own color, scent, and beauty, and there is no need to extol it with adventitious colors and scents; and just as a jewel or the moon-disc shines with its own light, and there is no need for it to be illuminated by another; so too is the ascetic Gotama praised and extolled by his own virtues, which are praised by the entire world. He has been brought to a state of being esteemed by the entire world. For him, there is no need for praise from another.

Pasatthehi vā pasatthotipi pasatthappasattho. Ke pana pasatthā nāma? Rājā pasenadi kosalo kāsikosalavāsikehi pasattho, bimbisāro aṅgamagadhavāsīhi, vesālikā licchavī vajjitaṭṭhavāsīhi pasatthā, pāveyyakā mallā kosinārakā mallā aññepi te te khattiyā tehi tehi jānapadehi pasatthā, caṅkiādayo brāhmaṇā brāhmaṇagaṇehi, anāthapiṇḍikādayo upāsakā upāsakagaṇehi, visākhāādikā upāsikā anekasatāhi upāsikāhi, sakuludāyiādayo paribbājakā anekehi paribbājakasatehi, uppalavaṇṇattheriādikā mahāsāvikā anekehi bhikkhunisatehi, sāriputtattherādayo mahātherā [P 3.0314] anekasatehi bhikkhūhi, sakkādayo devā anekasahassehi devehi, mahābrahmādayo brahmāno anekasahassehi brahmehi pasatthā. Te sabbepi dasabalaṃ thomenti vaṇṇenti pasaṃsantīti bhagavā “pasatthappasattho”ti vuccati. Atthavasanti atthānisaṃsaṃ.

Alternatively, 'praised by the praised' means he is praised by those who are themselves praised. Who, then, are these praised ones? King Pasenadi of Kosala is praised by the inhabitants of Kasi and Kosala; King Bimbisāra is praised by the inhabitants of Anga and Magadha; the Mallas of Pāvā and the Mallas of Kusinārā, and other such nobles are praised by those in their respective countries. Brahmins such as Caṅkī are praised by groups of brahmins; male lay disciples such as Anāthapiṇḍika are praised by groups of male lay disciples; female lay disciples such as Visākhā are praised by many hundreds of female lay disciples; wanderers such as Sakuludāyī are praised by many hundreds of wanderers; great female disciples such as the Therī Uppalavaṇṇā are praised by many hundreds of nuns; great elders such as the Thera Sāriputta are praised by many hundreds of monks; gods such as Sakka are praised by many thousands of gods; great brahmās such as Mahābrahmā are praised by many thousands of brahmās. All of these praised ones extol, commend, and praise the Possessor of the Ten Powers. Therefore, the Blessed One is called 'praised by the praised'. 'For the sake of the meaning' means for the sake of the benefit and advantage.

Athassa [V 3.0071][M 3.0070] so attano pasādakāraṇaṃ ācikkhanto seyyathāpi, bho, purisotiādimāha. Tattha aggarasaparitittoti bhojanarasesu pāyāso sneharasesu gosappi, kasāvarasesu khuddakamadhu aneḷakaṃ, madhurarasesu sakkarāti evamādayo aggarasā nāma. Tesu yena kenaci parititto ākaṇṭhappamāṇaṃ bhuñjitvā ṭhito. Aññesaṃ hīnānanti aggarasehi aññesaṃ hīnarasānaṃ. Suttasoti suttato, suttabhāvenāti attho. Sesupi eseva nayo. Tato tatoti suttādīsu tato tato. Aññesaṃ puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇāppavādānanti ye aññesaṃ puthūnaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ laddhisaṅkhātappavādā, tesaṃ. Na pihetīti na pattheti, te kathiyamāne sotumpi na icchati. Jighacchādubbalyaparetoti jighacchāya ceva dubbalabhāvena ca anugato. Madhupiṇḍikanti sālipiṭṭhaṃ bhajjitvā catumadhurena yojetvā kataṃ baddhasattupiṇḍikaṃ, madhurapūvameva vā. Adhigaccheyyāti [P 3.0315] labheyya. Asecanakanti madhurabhāvakaraṇatthāya aññena rasena anāsittakaṃ ojavantaṃ paṇītarasaṃ.

Then, explaining the reason for his own confidence, he spoke the words beginning with, 'Just as, good sir, a man...'. Therein, 'sated with the finest flavors': among food flavors, milk-rice; among fatty flavors, cow's ghee; among astringent flavors, flawless small-bee honey; and among sweet flavors, sugar—these and the like are called the finest flavors. Being sated with any one of these, having eaten his fill up to his throat, he is satisfied. 'Of other, inferior ones' means of other, inferior flavors compared to the finest flavors. 'From the Sutta' means by way of the Sutta, in the state of being a Sutta. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. 'From this and that' means from this and that among the Suttas and so on. 'Of the various doctrines of other ascetics and brahmins' means of those variously spoken words of other numerous ascetics and brahmins, which are known as their views. 'He does not long for' means he does not desire; he does not even wish to hear them being spoken of. 'Afflicted by hunger and weakness' means overcome by hunger and the state of weakness. 'A honey-cake' means a dense cake-ball made by roasting fine rice flour and combining it with the four sweet things; or simply a very sweet cake. 'He might obtain' means he might receive. 'Without admixture' means not sprinkled with another flavor for the purpose of making it sweet; it is possessed of nutritive essence and has a sublime flavor.

Haricandanassāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇacandanassa. Lohitacandanassāti rattavaṇṇacandanassa. Surabhigandhanti sugandhaṃ. Darathādayo vaṭṭadarathā, vaṭṭakilamathā, vaṭṭapariḷāhā eva. Udānaṃ udānesīti udāhāraṃ udāhari. Yathā hi yaṃ telaṃ mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ avasekoti vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati, taṃ oghoti vuccati. Evamevaṃ yaṃ pītivacanaṃ hadayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, adhikaṃ hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahi nikkhamati, taṃ udānanti vuccati. Evarūpaṃ pītimayavacanaṃ nicchāresīti attho.

'Of haricandana' means of sandalwood of golden color. 'Of lohitacandana' means of sandalwood of red color. 'Of fragrant scent' means having a good scent. 'Distress and so on' are indeed the distress of the round of rebirth, the weariness of the round of rebirth, and the burning of the round of rebirth. 'He uttered an udāna' means he uttered an utterance. Just as whatever oil a measuring pot cannot hold, it flows out and goes away—that is called 'avaseka'. And whatever water a lake cannot hold, it overflows and goes away—that is called 'ogha'. Even so, whatever speech born of joy the heart cannot hold, becoming excessive and not remaining inside, it comes out—that is called an 'udāna'. The meaning is: he uttered such a speech born of joy.

5. Piṅgiyānīsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Piṅgiyānī Sutta

195. Pañcame nīlāti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇātiādi tasseva vibhāgadassanaṃ. Tattha na tesaṃ pakativaṇṇo nīlo, nīlavilepanavilittattā panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nīlavatthāti paṭadukūlakoseyyādīnipi tesaṃ nīlāneva honti. Nīlālaṅkārāti nīlamaṇīhi nīlapupphehi alaṅkatā, tesaṃ hatthālaṅkāra-assālaṅkāra-rathālaṅkāra-sāṇivitānakañcukāpi sabbe nīlāyeva honti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

195. In the fifth [sutta], the word 'nīla' is all-encompassing. 'Nīlavaṇṇa' and so forth shows the specific divisions of that very term. In this context, their natural color is not blue; rather, this is said because they were anointed with blue paste. 'Nīlavattha' means their garments—such as cloth, fine cloth, and silk—are also blue. 'Nīlālaṅkāra' means they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers; all their elephant ornaments, horse ornaments, chariot ornaments, canopies, curtains, and tunics are also blue. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Padumaṃ [M 3.0071] yathāti yathā satapattaṃ rattapadumaṃ. Kokanadanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Pātoti pageva suriyuggamanakāle[V 3.0072]. Siyāti bhaveyya. Avītagandhanti [P 3.0316] avigatagandhaṃ. Aṅgīrasanti bhagavato aṅgamaṅgehi rasmiyo niccharanti, tasmā aṅgīrasoti vuccati. Tapantamādiccamivantalikkheti dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu ālokakaraṇavasena antalikkhe tapantaṃ ādiccaṃ viya virocamānaṃ. Aṅgīrasaṃ passāti attānameva vā mahājanaṃ vā sandhāya evaṃ vadati.

'Padumaṃ yathā' means: just as a red lotus with many petals. 'Kokanada' is a synonym for that very term. 'Pāto' means early, at the time of sunrise. 'Siyā' means it would be. 'Avītagandhaṃ' means not devoid of fragrance. 'Aṅgīrasaṃ' means: rays emanate from the major and minor limbs of the Blessed One; therefore, he is called Aṅgīrasa. 'Tapantamādiccamivantalikkhe' means: shining like the sun blazing in the sky by means of illuminating the four great continents with their retinue of two thousand lesser islands. 'Aṅgīrasaṃ passa' (Behold Aṅgīrasa): he speaks thus, referring either to himself or to the great populace.

6. Mahāsupinasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sutta of the Great Dreams

196. Chaṭṭhe mahāsupināti mahantehi purisehi passitabbato mahantānañca atthānaṃ nimittabhāvato mahāsupinā. Pāturahesunti pākaṭā ahesuṃ. Tattha supinaṃ passanto catūhi kāraṇehi passati dhātukkhobhato vā anubhūtapubbato vā devatopasaṃhārato vā pubbanimittato vāti.

196. In the sixth [sutta], 'great dreams' (mahāsupinā) are so called because they are to be seen by great men and because they are portents of great benefits. 'They appeared' means they became manifest. In this context, one who sees a dream sees it for four reasons: from a disturbance of the elements, from a previous experience, from the presentation by a deity, or from a premonition.

Tattha pittādīnaṃ khobhakaraṇapaccayappayogena khubhitadhātuko dhātukkhobhato supinaṃ passati. Passanto ca nānāvidhaṃ supinaṃ passati pabbatā patanto viya, ākāsena gacchanto viya, vāḷamigahatthicorādīhi anubaddho viya ca. Anubhūtapubbato passanto pubbe anubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ passati. Devatopasaṃhārato passantassa devatā atthakāmatāya vā anatthakāmatāya vā atthāya vā anatthāya vā nānāvidhāni ārammaṇāni upasaṃharanti. So tāsaṃ devatānaṃ ānubhāvena tāni ārammaṇāni passati. Pubbanimittato passanto puññāpuññavasena uppajjitukāmassa atthassa vā anatthassa vā pubbanimittabhūtaṃ supinaṃ passati bodhisattamātā viya puttapaṭilābhanimittaṃ, kosalarājā viya soḷasa supine, ayameva bhagavā bodhisattabhūto ime pañca mahāsupine viya cāti.

Among these, due to a disturbance of the elements, one whose elements are disturbed by the application of causes that agitate bile and so forth sees a dream. And in seeing, one sees various kinds of dreams: as if falling from a mountain, as if going through the sky, and as if being pursued by wild beasts, elephants, thieves, and others. Seeing from a previous experience, one sees an object that has been experienced before. When one sees a dream from the presentation by a deity, the deities, out of a desire for one's benefit or harm, present various objects for one's benefit or harm. Through the power of those deities, one sees those objects. Seeing from a premonition, one sees a dream that is a premonition of a benefit or non-benefit about to arise due to merit or demerit, just as the Bodhisatta's mother saw a premonition of obtaining a son, as King Kosala saw the sixteen dreams, and as this very Blessed One, being the Bodhisatta, saw these five great dreams.

Tattha yaṃ dhātukkhobhato anubhūtapubbato ca supine passati, na taṃ saccaṃ hoti. Yaṃ devatopasaṃhārato passati, taṃ saccaṃ vā hoti alikaṃ vā. Kuddhā hi devatā upāyena [P 3.0317] vināsetukāmā viparītampi katvā dassenti. Yaṃ pana pubbanimittato passati, taṃ ekantaṃ saccameva [M 3.0072] hoti. Etesaṃ catunnaṃ mūlakāraṇānaṃ saṃsaggabhedatopi supinabhedo hotiyeva.

Therein, whatever one sees in a dream due to a disturbance of the elements or a previous experience, that is not true. Whatever one sees due to the presentation by a deity, that may be true or false. For angry deities, desiring to destroy by some means, may create and show even the opposite. But whatever one sees from a premonition, that is certainly and only true. From the variation in the combination of these four root causes, there is indeed a variation in dreams.

Taṃ panetaṃ catubbidhampi supinaṃ sekhaputhujjanāva passanti appahīnavipallāsattā, asekhā na [V 3.0073] passanti pahīnavipallāsattā. Kiṃ panetaṃ passanto sutto passati paṭibuddho, udāhu neva sutto na paṭibuddhoti? Kiñcettha yadi tāva sutto passati, abhidhammavirodho āpajjati. Bhavaṅgacittena hi supati, taṃ rūpanimittādiārammaṇaṃ rāgādisampayuttaṃ vā na hoti. Supinaṃ passantassa ca īdisāni cittāni uppajjanti. Atha paṭibuddho passati, vinayavirodho āpajjati. Yañhi paṭibuddho passati, taṃ sabbohārikacittena passati. Sabbohārikacittena ca kate vītikkame anāpatti nāma natthi. Supinaṃ passantena pana katepi vītikkame ekantaṃ anāpatti eva. Atha neva sutto na paṭibuddho passati, na nāma passati. Evañca sati supinassa abhāvo ca āpajjati? Na abhāvo. Kasmā? Yasmā kapimiddhapareto passati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “kapimiddhapareto kho, mahārāja, supinaṃ passatī”ti.

Furthermore, these four kinds of dreams are seen only by trainees and worldlings, because they have not abandoned perversions; non-trainees do not see them, because they have abandoned perversions. But does one who sees a dream see it while asleep, while awake, or while neither asleep nor awake? In this matter, if one sees it while asleep, a contradiction with the Abhidhamma arises. For one sleeps with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta), and that consciousness does not have form-signs and so on as its object, nor is it associated with greed and so on. But for one who sees a dream, such minds do arise. If one sees it while awake, a contradiction with the Vinaya arises. For whatever one sees while awake, one sees with a mind engaged in worldly transaction (sabbohārikacitta). And when a transgression is committed with a mind engaged in worldly transaction, there is no such thing as 'no offense'. But when a transgression is committed by one seeing a dream, it is certainly 'no offense'. If one sees it while neither asleep nor awake, one does not see at all. And if this were so, would the non-existence of dreams result? It would not result in non-existence. Why? Because one who is overcome by 'monkey-sleep' (kapimiddha) sees. For this was said: 'Indeed, great king, one overcome by monkey-sleep sees a dream.'

Kapimiddhaparetoti makkaṭaniddāya yutto. Yathā hi makkaṭassa niddā lahuparivattā hoti, evaṃ yā niddā punappunaṃ kusalādicittavokiṇṇattā lahuparivattā, yassā pavattiyaṃ punappunaṃ bhavaṅgato uttaraṇaṃ hoti, tāya yutto supinaṃ passati. Tenāyaṃ supino kusalopi hoti akusalopi abyākatopi. Tattha supinante cetiyavandanadhammassavanadhammadesanādīni [P 3.0318] karontassa kusalo, pāṇātipātādīni karontassa akusalo, dvīhi antehi mutto āvajjanatadārammaṇakkhaṇe abyākatoti veditabbo. Svāyaṃ dubbalavatthukattā cetanāya paṭisandhiṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asamattho. Pavatte pana aññehi kusalākusalehi upatthambhito vipākaṃ deti. Kiñcāpi vipākaṃ deti, atha kho avisaye uppannattā abbohārikāva supinantacetanā. So panesa supino kālavasenapi divā tāva diṭṭho na sameti, tathā paṭhamayāme majjhimayāme pacchimayāme ca. Balavapaccūse pana asitapītakhāyite sammā pariṇāmaṃ gate kāyasmiṃ ojāya patiṭṭhitāya aruṇe uggacchamāneva diṭṭho [M 3.0073] supino sameti. Iṭṭhanimittaṃ supinaṃ passanto iṭṭhaṃ paṭilabhati, aniṭṭhanimittaṃ passanto aniṭṭhaṃ.

'One overcome by monkey-sleep' means one endowed with the sleep of a monkey. For just as a monkey's sleep is quickly changing, so too is the sleep that is quickly changing, being repeatedly interspersed with wholesome thoughts and so on, in the course of which there is frequent rising from the life-continuum. One endowed with such sleep sees a dream. Therefore, this dream can be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Herein, for one who performs acts in a dream such as venerating a cetiya, listening to the Dhamma, or teaching the Dhamma, it is wholesome. For one who performs acts such as taking life, it is unwholesome. Free from these two extremes, it should be understood as indeterminate at the moments of adverting and registering. This volition, having a weak basis, is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking. In the course of existence, however, being supported by other wholesome and unwholesome states, it gives a result. Although it gives a result, the volition in a dream, having arisen in an improper sphere, is merely non-transactional. Furthermore, this dream, by the power of time, does not come true if seen during the day, nor likewise if seen in the first, middle, or last watch of the night. But a dream seen at powerful dawn, when what has been eaten, drunk, and consumed has been well digested, when nutriment is established in the body, and just as the dawn is rising, comes true. One who sees a dream with a desired sign obtains a desired result; one who sees a dream with an undesired sign obtains an undesired result.

Ime pana pañca mahāsupine neva lokiyamahājano passati, na mahārājāno, na cakkavattirājāno, na aggasāvakā, na paccekabuddhā, na sammāsambuddhā, eko sabbaññubodhisattoyeva passati. Amhākaṃ pana bodhisatto kadā ime supine passīti? “Sve buddho bhavissāmī”ti cātuddasiyaṃ pakkhassa rattivibhāyanakāle passi. Terasiyantipi vadantiyeva. So ime supine disvā uṭṭhāya pallaṅkaṃ ābhuñjitvā nisinno cintesi – “sace mayā [V 3.0074] kapilavatthunagare ime supinā diṭṭhā assu, pitu mahārājassa katheyyaṃ. Sace pana me mātā jīveyya, tassā katheyyaṃ. Imasmiṃ kho pana ṭhāne imesaṃ paṭiggāhako nāma natthi, ahameva paṭigaṇhissāmī”ti. Tato “idaṃ imassa [P 3.0319] pubbanimittaṃ idaṃ imassā”ti sayameva supine paṭiggaṇhitvā uruvelagāme sujātāya dinnaṃ pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha bodhiṃ patvā anukkamena jetavane viharanto attano makulabuddhakāle diṭṭhe pañca mahāsupine vitthāretuṃ bhikkhū āmantetvā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Furthermore, these five great dreams are not seen by the great people of the world, nor by great kings, nor by wheel-turning monarchs, nor by chief disciples, nor by Paccekabuddhas, nor by Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas—only the one Omniscient Bodhisatta sees them. But when did our Bodhisatta see these dreams? He saw them on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, at the time of the night's dawning, on the occasion of thinking, "Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha." Some also say it was on the thirteenth day. Having seen these dreams, he arose, sat cross-legged, and reflected: "If I had seen these dreams in the city of Kapilavatthu, I would have told my father, the great king. And if my mother were alive, I would have told her. But in this place, there is no one to receive them, so I myself shall interpret them." Then, having interpreted the dreams himself, thinking, "This is the prior sign of this result," he consumed the milk-rice offered by Sujātā in the village of Uruvelā, ascended to the seat of enlightenment, attained awakening, and in due course, while dwelling in Jetavana, he addressed the monks and began this discourse to explain in detail the five great dreams he had seen at the time of his budding as a Buddha.

Tattha mahāpathavīti cakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūretvā ṭhitā mahāpathavī. Mahāsayanaṃ ahosīti sirisayanaṃ ahosi. Ohitoti ṭhapito. So pana na udakasmiṃyeva ṭhapito ahosi, atha kho pācīnasamuddassa uparūparibhāgena gantvā pācīnacakkavāḷamatthake ṭhapito ahosīti veditabbo. Pacchime samudde dakkhiṇe samuddeti etesupi eseva nayo. Tiriyā nāma tiṇajātīti dabbatiṇaṃ vuccati. Nābhiyā uggantvā nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosīti naṅgalamattena rattadaṇḍena nābhito uggantvā passantassa passantasseva vidatthimattaṃ ratanamattaṃ byāmamattaṃ yaṭṭhimattaṃ gāvutamattaṃ aḍḍhayojanamattaṃ yojanamattanti evaṃ uggantvā uggantvā anekayojanasahassaṃ nabhaṃ āhacca ṭhitā ahosi. Pādehi ussakkitvāti agganakhato paṭṭhāya pādehi abhiruhitvā. Nānāvaṇṇāti eko nīlavaṇṇo, eko pītavaṇṇo, eko lohitavaṇṇo, eko paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇoti evaṃ nānāvaṇṇā. Setāti paṇḍarā parisuddhā. Mahato mīḷhapabbatassāti tiyojanubbedhassa gūthapabbatassa. Uparūpari [P 3.0320] caṅkamatīti matthakamatthake caṅkamati[M 3.0074]. Dīghāyukabuddhā pana tiyojanike mīḷhapabbate anupavisitvā nisinnā viya honti.

Herein, 'the great earth' refers to the great earth that stands filling the Cakkavāḷa-sphere. 'It was a great couch' means it was a glorious couch. 'Placed' means established. It should be understood that it was not placed only upon the water; rather, having gone over the upper part of the eastern ocean, it was placed on the summit of the eastern Cakkavāḷa mountain. The same principle applies to the western and southern oceans. 'A species of grass called Tiriyā' refers to dabba-grass. 'Having risen from the navel, it stood striking the sky' means that with a red stalk the length of a plow-handle, it rose from the navel, and as one watched, it grew to the length of a span, a cubit, a fathom, a rod, a gāvuta, half a yojana, and a yojana—thus it rose and rose, striking the sky for many thousands of yojanas. 'Climbing up with his feet' means climbing up with the feet, starting from the tips of the toes. 'Of various colors' means one was yellow, and one was the color of a pale palāsa leaf—thus of various colors. 'White' means pure white. 'Of a great dung mountain' refers to a dung mountain three yojanas high. 'He walks up and down on top' means he walked the ambulatory path on the very summit. Long-lived Buddhas, however, are as if seated, having entered the three-yojana-high dung mountain.

Evaṃ ettakena ṭhānena pubbanimittāni dassetvā idāni saha pubbanimittehi paṭilābhaṃ dassetuṃ yampi, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sabbaguṇadāyakattā buddhānaṃ arahattamaggo anuttarā sammāsambodhi nāma. Tasmā yaṃ so cakkavāḷamahāpathaviṃ sirisayanabhūtaṃ addasa, taṃ buddhabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ himavantapabbatarājānaṃ bimbohanaṃ addasa, taṃ sabbaññutaññāṇabimbohanassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ cattāro hatthapāde cakkavāḷamatthake ṭhite addasa, taṃ dhammacakkassa appaṭivattiyabhāve pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ attānaṃ uttānakaṃ nipannaṃ addasa, taṃ tīsu bhavesu avakujjānaṃ sattānaṃ uttānamukhabhāvassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ akkhīni ummīletvā passanto [V 3.0075] viya ahosi, taṃ dibbacakkhupaṭilābhassa pubbanimittaṃ. Yaṃ yāva bhavaggā ekālokaṃ ahosi, taṃ anāvaraṇañāṇassa pubbanimittaṃ. Sesaṃ pāḷivaseneva veditabbanti.

Thus, having shown the prior signs with this much, now, in order to show the attainment together with the prior signs, he spoke the words beginning with "Yampi, bhikkhave..." Herein, because it gives all virtuous qualities, the Arahant-path of the Buddhas is called the Unsurpassed Perfect Self-Awakening. Therefore, that he saw the great earth of the Cakkavāḷa become a glorious couch, that was a prior sign of his becoming a Buddha. That he saw Himavanta, the king of mountains, become a pillow, that was a prior sign of the pillow that is omniscient knowledge. That he saw his four limbs—hands and feet—standing on the summit of the Cakkavāḷa mountain, that was a prior sign of the irreversible nature of the Wheel of Dhamma. That he saw himself lying supine, that was a prior sign of beings in the three existences, who were face down, being turned upright. That he was as if opening his eyes and seeing, that was a prior sign of the attainment of the divine eye. That there was a single light up to the peak of existence, that was a prior sign of unobstructed knowledge. The remainder should be known by way of the Pāḷi itself.

7. Vassasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vassasutta

197. Sattame nemittāti nimittapāṭhakā. Tejodhātu pakuppatīti mahāaggikkhandho uppajjati. Pāṇinā udakaṃ sampaṭicchitvāti uppannaṃ utusamuṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ tiyojanasatena hatthena paṭiggahetvā. Pamattā hontīti attano kīḷāya pamattā honti vippavuṭṭhasatino. Tesañhi sakāya ratiyā “ramāmā”ti citte uppanne akālepi [P 3.0321] devo vassati, tadabhāve na vassati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “na kālavassa”nti. Aṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva.

197. In the seventh discourse, 'nemittā' refers to those who are readers of signs. 'The fire element is disturbed' means a great mass of fire arises. 'Having received water with the hand' means having received with a hand spanning three hundred yojanas the rainwater that has arisen from the season. 'They are heedless' means they are heedless in their own play, their mindfulness lost. For when the thought, 'Let us delight,' arises in their minds due to their own enjoyment, the rain god rains even out of season, and in its absence, does not rain. Referring to that, this was said: 'He does not rain in season.' The eighth and ninth discourses are straightforward in meaning.

10. Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Nissāraṇīyasutta

200. Dasame nissāraṇīyāti nissaṭā visaññuttā. Dhātuyoti attasuññasabhāvā. Kāmaṃ manasikarototi kāmaṃ manasikarontassa, asubhajjhānato vuṭṭhāya agadaṃ gahetvā visaṃ vīmaṃsanto viya vīmaṃsanatthaṃ kāmābhimukhaṃ cittaṃ pesentassāti attho. Na pakkhandatīti nappavisati. Nappasīdatīti pasādaṃ nāpajjati. Na santiṭṭhatīti nappatiṭṭhahati. Na vimuccatīti na adhimuccati. Yathā pana kukkuṭapattaṃ vā nhārudaddulaṃ vā aggimhi pakkhittaṃ paṭilīyati patikuṭati pativaṭṭati na saṃpasārīyati, evaṃ paṭilīyati [M 3.0075] na saṃpasārīyati. Nekkhammaṃ kho panāti idha nekkhammaṃ nāma asubhesu paṭhamajjhānaṃ, tadassa manasikaroto cittaṃ pakkhandati. Tassa taṃ cittanti tassa taṃ asubhajjhānacittaṃ. Sugatanti gocare gatattā suṭṭhu gataṃ. Subhāvitanti ahānabhāgiyattā suṭṭhu bhāvitaṃ. Suvuṭṭhitanti kāmato vuṭṭhitaṃ. Suvimuttanti kāmehi suṭṭhu vimuttaṃ. Kāmapaccayā āsavā nāma kāmahetukā cattāro āsavā. Vighātāti dukkhā. Pariḷāhāti [P 3.0322] kāmarāgapariḷāhā. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vediyatīti so taṃ kāmavedanaṃ vighātapariḷāhavedanañca na vediyati. Idamakkhātaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇanti idaṃ asubhajjhānaṃ kāmehi nissaṭattā kāmānaṃ nissaraṇanti akkhātaṃ. Yo pana taṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tatiyamaggaṃ patvā anāgāmiphalena nibbānaṃ disvā “puna kāmā nāma natthī”ti jānāti. Tassa cittaṃ accantanissaraṇameva. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

200. In the tenth discourse, 'nissāraṇīya' means that which is freed, disengaged. 'Dhātuyo' refers to their nature being empty of self. 'One who attends to sensual pleasure' means: for a monk who, having emerged from the jhāna on the unattractive, sends his mind towards sensual pleasure for the purpose of examination, like one who takes an antidote to examine poison; this is the meaning. 'It does not rush in' means it does not enter. 'It does not become clear' means it does not attain serenity. 'It does not stand firm' means it does not become established. 'It is not intent upon' means it is not resolved. Just as a chicken feather or a sinew-knot, when thrown into a fire, shrinks, curls up, recoils, and does not spread out, so too does it shrink and not spread out. Here, in 'But renunciation...', 'renunciation' means the first jhāna on the unattractive. For one who attends to this, the mind rushes in. 'His mind' means his mind of the jhāna on the unattractive. 'Well-gone' means well-gone because it has gone to its object. 'Well-developed' means well-developed because it partakes of non-decline. 'Well-arisen' means well-arisen from sensual pleasure. 'Well-liberated' means well-liberated from sensual pleasures. The taints due to sensual pleasures are the four taints that have sensual pleasure as their cause. 'Distress' means suffering. 'Fever' means the fever of sensual passion. 'He does not experience that feeling' means he does not experience that feeling of sensual pleasure, nor the feeling of distress and fever. 'This is called the escape from sensual pleasures' means this jhāna on the unattractive, because it is an escape from sensual pleasures, is called the escape from sensual pleasures. But one who, having made that jhāna a basis, contemplating the formations, having reached the third path and seen Nibbāna with the fruit of non-returning, knows: 'Again, there are no such things as sensual pleasures.' His mind is the ultimate escape. In the remaining passages, this is the method.

Ayaṃ [V 3.0076] pana viseso – dutiyavāre mettājhānāni byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ nāma. Tatiyavāre karuṇājhānāni vihiṃsāya nissaraṇaṃ nāma. Catutthavāre arūpajjhānāni rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāma. Accantanissaraṇañcettha arahattaphalaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Pañcamavāre sakkāyaṃ manasikarototi suddhasaṅkhāre pariggaṇhitvā arahattaṃ pattassa sukkhavipassakassa phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya vīmaṃsanatthaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhābhimukhaṃ cittaṃ pesentassa. Idamakkhātaṃ sakkāyassa nissaraṇanti idaṃ arahattamaggena ca phalena ca nibbānaṃ disvā ṭhitassa bhikkhuno “puna sakkāyo natthī”ti uppannaṃ arahattaphalasamāpatticittaṃ sakkāyassa nissaraṇanti akkhātaṃ. Idāni evaṃ sakkāyanissaraṇaṃ nirodhaṃ patvā ṭhitassa khīṇāsavassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento tassa kāmanandīpi nānusetītiādimāha. Tattha nānusetīti na nibbattati. Ananusayāti anibbattiyā. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

This, however, is the distinction: in the second section, the jhānas of loving-kindness are called the escape from ill will. In the third section, the jhānas of compassion are called the escape from cruelty. In the fourth section, the formless jhānas are called the escape from forms. And here, the fruit of Arahantship should be connected as the ultimate escape. In the fifth section, 'one attends to personality' means: for a dry-insight meditator who has attained Arahantship by comprehending the mere formations, when, having arisen from the attainment of fruition, they send their mind towards the five aggregates subject to clinging for the purpose of examination. 'This is called the escape from personality' means: for a bhikkhu who stands having seen Nibbāna by means of the Arahant path and fruit, the mind of the attainment of Arahant fruition that has arisen thus, 'Again, there is no personality,' is called the escape from personality. Now, speaking in praise of the one whose taints are destroyed, who stands having reached cessation which is the escape from personality, He said: 'Delight in sensual pleasure does not lie latent in him,' and so on. Therein, 'does not lie latent' means it does not arise. 'Without latent tendency' means due to non-arising. The rest here is straightforward in meaning.

Brāhmaṇavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on the Brahmin, the Fifth.

Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Fourth Fifty is Concluded.

5. Pañcamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

5. The Fifth Fifty

(21) 1. Kimilavaggo

(21) 1. The Kimila Section

1. Kimilasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Kimila Sutta.

201. Pañcamassa [V 3.0077][M 3.0076][P 3.0323] paṭhame kimilāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Niculavaneti mucalindavane. Etadavocāti ayaṃ kira thero tasmiṃyeva nagare seṭṭhiputto satthu santike pabbajitvā pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ paṭilabhi. So attanā nivutthaṃ khandhasantānaṃ anussaranto kassapadasabalassa sāsanosakkanakāle pabbajitvā catūsu parisāsu sāsane agāravaṃ karontīsu nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ āruyha tattha samaṇadhammaṃ katvā attano nivutthabhāvaṃ addasa. So “satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchissāmī”ti etaṃ “ko nu kho, bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

201. In the first sutta of the fifth vagga, in the city named Kimilā. Niculavana: that is, the Mucalinda Grove. ‘He said this’: it seems this elder, the son of a merchant in that very city, went forth in the presence of the Teacher and attained the knowledge of past lives. Recalling the continuity of aggregates in which he had dwelt, he saw that during the decline of the Dispensation of Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One, when the four assemblies were behaving disrespectfully toward the teaching, he built a ladder, climbed a mountain, practiced the recluse’s life there, and perceived his own state of dwelling. Thinking, ‘I will approach the Teacher and ask him about that reason,’ he spoke these words beginning with, ‘What indeed, venerable sir?’

Satthari agāravā viharanti appatissāti satthari gāravañceva jeṭṭhakabhāvañca anupaṭṭhapetvā viharanti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Tattha cetiyaṅgaṇādīsu chattaṃ dhāretvā upāhanā āruyha vicaranto nānappakārañca niratthakakathaṃ kathento satthari agāravo viharati nāma. Dhammassavanagge pana nisīditvā niddāyanto ceva nānappakārañca niratthakakathaṃ kathento dhamme agāravo viharati nāma. Saṅghamajjhe bāhāvikkhepakaṃ nānattakathaṃ kathento theranavamajjhimesu ca cittīkāraṃ akaronto saṅghe agāravo viharati nāma. Sikkhaṃ aparipūrento sikkhāya agāravo viharati nāma. Aññamaññaṃ kalahabhaṇḍanādīni karonto aññamaññaṃ agāravo viharati nāma. Dutiyaṃ uttānatthameva.

‘Those who dwell disrespectfully toward the Teacher are without deference’: they dwell without establishing reverence and seniority toward the Teacher. The same method applies to the rest. Here, one who carries an umbrella in the courtyard of a shrine, wears sandals, wanders about, and engages in various kinds of meaningless talk, is said to dwell disrespectfully toward the Teacher. Furthermore, one who sits in the hall for hearing the Dhamma, falls asleep, and engages in various kinds of meaningless talk is said to dwell disrespectfully toward the Dhamma. One who gestures with their arms in the midst of the Saṅgha, engages in various kinds of talk, and fails to show respect to elders, newly ordained monks, and those in between is said to dwell disrespectfully toward the Saṅgha. One who does not fulfill the training is said to dwell disrespectfully toward the training. One who engages in quarrels and disputes with one another is said to dwell disrespectfully toward one another. The second sutta is clear in meaning.

3. Assājānīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Assājānīya Sutta.

203-204. Tatiye [V 3.0078] ajjavenāti ujubhāvena avaṅkagamanena. Javenāti [P 3.0324] padajavena. Maddavenāti sarīramudutāya. Khantiyāti adhivāsanakkhantiyā. Soraccenāti sucisīlatāya. Bhikkhuvāre ajjavanti ñāṇassa ujukagamanaṃ. Javoti sūraṃ hutvā ñāṇassa gamanabhāvo. Maddavanti [M 3.0077] sīlamaddavaṃ. Khantīti adhivāsanakkhantiyeva. Soraccaṃ sucisīlatāyeva. Catutthe pañca balāni missakāni kathitāni.

In the third sutta, ‘by straightforwardness’ means by uprightness, by not going crookedly. ‘By speed’ means by speed of foot. ‘By gentleness’ means by softness of body. ‘By patience’ means by the patience of endurance. ‘By meekness’ means by pure virtue. In the section on monks, ‘straightforwardness’ refers to the direct movement of knowledge. ‘Speed’ means the state of knowledge’s movement, being heroic. ‘Gentleness’ means the gentleness of virtue. ‘Patience’ is indeed the patience of endurance. ‘Meekness’ is indeed pure virtue. In the fourth sutta, the five strengths are described as mixed.

5. Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta

205. Pañcame cetokhilāti cittassa thaddhabhāvā, kacavarabhāvā, khāṇukabhāvā. Satthari kaṅkhatīti satthu sarīre vā guṇe vā kaṅkhati. Sarīre kaṅkhamāno “dvattiṃsavarapurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāma sarīraṃ atthi nu kho natthī”ti kaṅkhati, guṇe kaṅkhamāno “atītānāgatapaccuppannajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ atthi nu kho natthī”ti kaṅkhati. Vicikicchatīti vicinanto kicchati, dukkhaṃ āpajjati, vinicchetuṃ na sakkoti. Nādhimuccatīti evametanti adhimokkhaṃ na paṭilabhati. Na sampasīdatīti guṇesu otaritvā nibbicikicchabhāvena pasīdituṃ anāvilo bhavituṃ na sakkoti. Ātappāyāti kilesasantāpakavīriyakaraṇatthāya. Anuyogāyāti punappunaṃ yogāya. Sātaccāyāti satatakiriyāya. Padhānāyāti padahanatthāya. Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhiloti ayaṃ satthari vicikicchāsaṅkhāto [P 3.0325] paṭhamo cittassa thaddhabhāvo evametassa bhikkhuno appahīno hoti.

205. In the fifth sutta, ‘mental barrenness’ refers to the mind’s rigidity, its being like refuse, and its being like a stump. ‘Doubting the Teacher’ means one doubts the Teacher’s body or qualities. Doubting the body, one wonders, ‘Does a body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man exist or not?’ Doubting the qualities, one wonders, ‘Does the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present exist or not?’ ‘Being perplexed’ means that while investigating, one struggles, falls into suffering, and is unable to decide. ‘Not being convinced’ means one does not attain the conviction that ‘it is thus.’ ‘Not being serene’ means one is unable to settle into the qualities with a doubt-free mind, to become serene, to become unperturbed. ‘For ardour’ means for the sake of making an effort that torments the defilements. ‘For application’ means for repeated practice. ‘For continuity’ means for constant action. ‘For striving’ means for the sake of exertion. ‘This is the first mental barrenness’: this first rigidity of mind, designated as doubt toward the Teacher, remains unabandoned in this monk.

Dhammeti pariyattidhamme ca paṭivedhadhamme ca. Pariyattidhamme kaṅkhamāno “tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassānīti vadanti, atthi nu kho etaṃ natthī”ti kaṅkhati. Paṭivedhadhamme kaṅkhamāno “vipassanānissando maggo nāma, magganissandaṃ phalaṃ nāma, sabbasaṅkhārapaṭinissaggo nibbānaṃ nāmāti vadanti, taṃ atthi nu kho natthī”ti kaṅkhati. Saṅghe kaṅkhatīti “ujuppaṭipanno”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vasena “evarūpaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipanno cattāro maggaṭṭhā cattāro phalaṭṭhāti aṭṭhannaṃ puggalānaṃ samūhabhūto saṅgho nāma atthi nu kho natthī”ti kaṅkhati. Sikkhāya kaṅkhamāno “adhisīlasikkhā nāma adhicittaadhipaññāsikkhā nāmāti vadanti, sā atthi nu kho [V 3.0079] natthī”ti kaṅkhati. Ayaṃ pañcamoti ayaṃ sabrahmacārīsu kopasaṅkhāto pañcamo cittassa thaddhabhāvo kacavarabhāvo khāṇukabhāvo.

‘The Dhamma’ refers to both the Dhamma of study and the Dhamma of penetration. Doubting the Dhamma of study, one wonders, ‘They say the Buddha’s words consist of the three baskets, eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma—does this exist or not?’ Doubting the Dhamma of penetration, one wonders, ‘They say the result of insight is the path, the result of the path is the fruit, and the relinquishment of all formations is called Nibbāna—does this exist or not?’ ‘Doubting the Saṅgha,’ by way of such phrases as ‘practicing uprightly,’ one wonders, ‘Does the Saṅgha—which is a group of eight individuals, the four on the path and the four established in the fruit, who have undertaken such a practice—exist or not?’ Doubting the training, one wonders, ‘They speak of the higher training in virtue, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom—does this exist or not?’ ‘This is the fifth’: this fifth rigidity of mind, its being like refuse, and its being like a stump, is designated as anger toward fellow practitioners.

6. Vinibandhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Vinibandha Sutta

206. Chaṭṭhe cetasovinibandhāti cittaṃ vinibandhitvā muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā viya gaṇhantīti cetasovinibandhā. Kāmeti vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepi. Kāyeti [M 3.0078] attano kāye. Rūpeti bahiddhārūpe. Yāvadatthanti yattakaṃ icchati, tattakaṃ. Udarāvadehakanti udarapūraṃ. Tañhi udaraṃ avadehanato udarāvadehakanti vuccati. Seyyasukhanti mañcapīṭhasukhaṃ, utusukhaṃ vā. Passasukhanti [P 3.0326] yathā samparivattakaṃ sayantassa dakkhiṇapassa vāmapassānaṃ sukhaṃ hoti, evaṃ uppannasukhaṃ. Middhasukhanti niddāsukhaṃ. Anuyuttoti yuttappayutto viharati. Paṇidhāyāti patthayitvā. Sīlenātiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Vatanti vatasamādānaṃ. Tapoti tapacaraṇaṃ. Brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Devo vā bhavissāmīti mahesakkhadevo vā bhavissāmi. Devaññataro vāti appesakkhadevesu vā aññataroti.

206. In the sixth sutta, ‘bonds of the mind’ are so called because they bind the mind, grasping it as if making a fist. ‘Sensual pleasures’ refers to both sensual objects and sensual defilements. ‘Body’ means one’s own body. ‘Form’ means external forms. ‘As much as one wants’ means as much as one desires, that much. ‘To one’s belly’s content’ means filling the belly. For it is called ‘to one’s belly’s content’ because it fills the belly. ‘The pleasure of lying down’ means the comfort of beds and chairs, or seasonal comfort. ‘The pleasure of the side’ means the comfort that arises for one who, while lying down, turns over, that of the right and left sides. ‘The pleasure of torpor’ means the pleasure of sleep. ‘Devoted’ means one dwells diligently engaged. ‘Having made an aspiration’ means having aspired. In phrases such as ‘by virtue,’ ‘virtue’ refers to the fourfold purification virtue. ‘Observance’ means the undertaking of an observance. ‘Asceticism’ means ascetic practice. ‘The holy life’ means abstinence from sexual activity. ‘I will become a god’ means ‘I will become a deity of great power.’ ‘Or some other god’ means ‘or one among the deities of lesser power.’

7-8. Yāgusuttādivaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Yāgu Sutta and Others

207-208. Sattame vātaṃ anulometīti vātaṃ anulometvā harati. Vatthiṃ sodhetīti dhamaniyo suddhā karoti. Āmāvasesaṃ pācetīti sace āmāvasesakaṃ hoti, taṃ pāceti. Aṭṭhame acakkhussanti na cakkhūnaṃ hitaṃ, cakkhuṃ visuddhaṃ na karoti.

In the seventh sutta, 'it makes the wind compliant' means: having made the wind compliant, it carries it away. 'It cleanses the bladder' means: it makes the channels pure. 'It digests the undigested remainder' means: if there is an undigested remainder, it digests it. In the eighth sutta, 'not for the eyes' means: it is not beneficial for the eyes; it does not make the eye pure.

9. Gītassarasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Gītassara Sutta

209. Navame āyatakenāti dīghena, paripuṇṇapadabyañjanakaṃ gāthāvattañca vināsetvā pavattena. Sarakuttimpi nikāmayamānassāti evaṃ gītassaro kātabboti sarakiriyaṃ patthayamānassa. Samādhissa bhaṅgo hotīti samathavipassanācittassa vināso hoti.

209. In the ninth sutta, 'with a drawn-out voice' means: with a long voice; by a manner of recitation that destroys both the speech that has complete words and syllables and the proper conduct for reciting verses. 'Of one desiring the artifice of the voice' means: of one who aspires to the practice of sound, thinking, 'Thus should the sound of singing be made.' 'There is a break in concentration' means: there is the destruction of the mind of serenity and insight.

10. Muṭṭhassatisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Muṭṭhassati Sutta

210. Dasame [V 3.0080] dukkhaṃ supatīti nānāvidhaṃ supinaṃ passanto dukkhaṃ supati. Dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhatīti paṭibujjhantopi uttasitvā salomahaṃso paṭibujjhati. Imasmiṃ sutte satisampajaññaṃ missakaṃ kathitaṃ.

210. In the tenth sutta, 'one sleeps miserably' means: seeing various dreams, one sleeps miserably. 'One awakens miserably' means: even when awakening, one awakens startled and with hair standing on end. In this sutta, mindfulness and clear comprehension are taught in a mixed way.

Kimilavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: Kimila
