(22) 2. Akkosakavaggo

(22) 2. The Chapter on the Reviler

1. Akkosakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta

211. Dutiyassa [M 3.0079][P 3.0327] paṭhame akkosakaparibhāsakoti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosako, bhayadassanena paribhāsako. Chinnaparipanthoti lokuttaraparipanthassa chinnattā chinnaparipantho. Rogātaṅkanti rogoyeva kicchajīvikāyāvahanato rogātaṅko nāma.

211. In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'a reviler and abuser' means: one who reviles with the ten grounds for reviling; one who abuses by showing danger. 'One whose obstacles are cut off' means: one whose obstacles are cut off because the supramundane obstacle is cut off. 'Disease and affliction' means: disease itself is called 'affliction' because it brings about a difficult livelihood.

2. Bhaṇḍanakārakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Bhaṇḍanakāraka Sutta

212. Dutiye adhikaraṇakārakoti catunnaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ aññatarassa kārako. Anadhigatanti pubbe appattavisesaṃ.

212. In the second sutta, 'a maker of legal issues' means: a maker of any of the four legal issues. 'Not attained' means: a special state not previously reached.

3. Sīlasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sīla Sutta

213. Tatiye dussīloti asīlo nissīlo. Sīlavipannoti vipannasīlo bhinnasaṃvaro. Pamādādhikaraṇanti pamādakāraṇā. Idañca suttaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ vasena āgataṃ, pabbajitānampi pana labbhateva[V 3.0081]. Gahaṭṭho hi yena yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti, yadi kasiyā, yadi vaṇijjāya, pāṇātipātādivasena pamatto taṃ taṃ yathākālaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, athassa mūlaṃ vinassati. Māghātakālepi pāṇātipātaṃ adinnādānādīni ca karonto daṇḍavasena mahatiṃ bhogajāniṃ nigacchati. Pabbajito dussīlo pamādakāraṇā sīlato buddhavacanato jhānato sattaariyadhanato ca jāniṃ nigacchati. Gahaṭṭhassa “asuko asukakule jāto dussīlo pāpadhammo pariccattaidhalokaparaloko salākabhattamattampi na detī”ti catuparisamajjhe pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati. Pabbajitassa “asuko nāsakkhi sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ buddhavacanaṃ [P 3.0328] gahetuṃ, vejjakammādīhi jīvati, chahi agāravehi samannāgato”ti evaṃ abbhuggacchati.

213. In the third sutta, 'immoral' means: without virtue, devoid of virtue. 'Of corrupt virtue' means: one with ruined virtue, one with broken restraint. 'On account of negligence' means: because of negligence. This sutta is presented by way of householders, but it is certainly applicable to monastics as well. For a householder, by whatever craft he makes a living, whether by farming or by trade, if he is negligent by way of killing living beings and so on, he is not able to accomplish his various tasks at the proper time, and the basis of his welfare is destroyed. Even at a time when killing is prohibited, by killing living beings, taking what is not given, and so on, he incurs a great loss of wealth by way of fines. An immoral monastic, because of negligence, incurs loss with regard to virtue, the Buddha's word, meditative absorption, and the seven noble treasures. For a householder, an evil reputation arises in the midst of the fourfold assembly: 'So-and-so, born in such-and-such a family, is immoral, of evil nature, has abandoned his welfare in this world and the next, and does not even give a ticket-meal.' For a monastic, an evil reputation arises thus: 'So-and-so was not able to guard his virtue or to grasp the Buddha's word; he lives by medical practice and so on, and is endowed with the six kinds of disrespect.'

Avisāradoti gahaṭṭho tāva “avassaṃ bahūnaṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha maṃ niggaṇhissanti vā, rājakulassa vā dassantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati. Maṅkubhūto ca patitakkhandho adhomukho [M 3.0080] aṅguṭṭhakena bhūmiṃ kasanto nisīdati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Pabbajitopi “bahū bhikkhū sannipatitā, avassaṃ koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha me uposathampi pavāraṇampi ṭhapetvā sāmaññā cāvetvā nikkaḍḍhissantī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Ekacco pana dussīlopi dappito viya carati, sopi ajjhāsayena maṅku hotiyeva.

'Lacking confidence' means: first, a householder approaches with fear, thinking, 'Surely, in a gathering of many people, someone will know of my deed, and then they will censure me or report me to the royal court.' Being shamefaced, with drooping shoulders, with face downcast, he sits scratching the ground with his big toe; he is not able to speak with confidence. A monastic, too, approaches with fear, thinking, 'Many monks are gathered; surely someone will know of my deed, and then, having suspended my Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, and having made me fall from the state of a monk, they will expel me.' He is not able to speak with confidence. A certain immoral person, however, may wander about as if proud, but even he is indeed shamefaced by disposition.

Sammūḷho kālaṃ karotīti tassa hi maraṇamañce nipannassa dussīlakammaṃ samādāya vattitaṭṭhānaṃ āpāthaṃ āgacchati. So ummīletvā idhalokaṃ passati, nimmīletvā paralokaṃ. Tassa cattāro apāyā upaṭṭhahanti, sattisatena sīse pahariyamāno viya hoti. So “vāretha vārethā”ti viravanto marati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sammūḷho kālaṃ karotī”ti. Pañcamapadaṃ uttānameva. Ānisaṃsakathā vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā.

'He dies bewildered' means: for him, lying on his deathbed, the place where he lived having undertaken immoral deeds comes into view. Opening his eyes, he sees this world; closing his eyes, he sees the next world. The four states of deprivation appear to him; it is as if he is being struck on the head with a hundred spears. He dies crying out, 'Ward it off! Ward it off!' Therefore it is said, 'He dies bewildered.' The fifth point is self-evident. The talk on benefits should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been said.

4. Bahubhāṇisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Bahubhāṇi Sutta

214. Catutthe bahubhāṇisminti paññāya aparicchinditvā bahuṃ bhaṇante. Mantabhāṇisminti [P 3.0329] mantā vuccati paññā, tāya paricchinditvā bhaṇante.

214. In the fourth discourse, 'one who speaks much' (bahubhāṇī) refers to one who speaks much without discerning with wisdom. 'One who speaks with discernment' (mantabhāṇī) refers to one who speaks after discerning with wisdom, for 'mantā' is said to be wisdom.

5. Paṭhamaakkhantisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the First Akkhanti Sutta

215. Pañcame [V 3.0082] verabahuloti puggalaverenapi akusalaverenapi bahuvero. Vajjabahuloti dosabahulo.

215. In the fifth discourse, 'full of enmity' (verabahulo) means one who has much enmity, both personal enmity and unwholesome enmity. 'Full of faults' (vajjabahulo) means one who has many defects.

6. Dutiyaakkhantisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Second Akkhanti Sutta

216. Chaṭṭhe luddoti dāruṇo kakkhaḷo. Vippaṭisārīti maṅkubhāvena samannāgato.

216. In the sixth discourse, 'cruel' (luddo) means harsh and rough. 'Remorseful' (vippaṭisārī) means endowed with a state of dejection.

7.Paṭhamaapāsādikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the First Apāsādika Sutta

217. Sattame apāsādiketi apāsādikehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgate. Pāsādiketi pasādāvahe parisuddhasamācāre. Aṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva.

217. In the seventh discourse, 'uninspiring of confidence' (apāsādike) means endowed with bodily actions and so forth that are uninspiring of confidence. 'Inspiring of confidence' (pāsādike) means inspiring confidence, with perfectly pure conduct. The eighth and ninth discourses are clear in meaning.

10. Madhurāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Madhurā Sutta

220. Dasame [M 3.0081] pañcime, bhikkhave, ādīnavā madhurāyanti ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cārikaṃ caramāno madhurānagaraṃ sampāpuṇitvā antonagaraṃ pavisituṃ ārabhi. Athekā micchādiṭṭhikā yakkhinī acelā hutvā dve hatthe pasāretvā jivhaṃ nillāletvā dasabalassa purato aṭṭhāsi. Satthā antonagaraṃ appavisitvā tatova nikkhamitvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Mahājano khādanīyabhojanīyañceva sakkārasammānañca ādāya vihāraṃ gantvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ adāsi. Satthā tassa nagarassa niggaṇhanatthāya imaṃ suttaṃ ārabhi. Tattha visamāti na samatalā. Bahurajāti vātapaharaṇakāle uddhatena rajakkhandhena pariyonaddhā viya hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

220. In the tenth discourse, regarding the phrase 'these five dangers of Madhurā, bhikkhus'—at one time the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, was traveling on a tour and arrived at the city of Madhurā. He began to enter the inner city. Then a female yakkha with wrong views, having become naked, stretched out her two hands, lolled out her tongue, and stood in front of the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, without entering the inner city, came out from there and went to the monastery. The great multitude, taking edibles and foods as well as honor and respect, went to the monastery and gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. The Teacher began this discourse in order to censure that city. There, 'uneven' (visamā) means not level. 'Full of dust' (bahurajā) means it is as if covered by a mass of dust stirred up when the wind blows. The rest is clear throughout.

Akkosakavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Abuse, the Second.

(23) 3. Dīghacārikavaggo

(23) 3. The Chapter on Long Journeying

1. Paṭhamadīghacārikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Dīghacārika Sutta

221. Tatiyassa [V 3.0083][P 3.0330] paṭhame anavatthacārikanti avavatthitacārikaṃ. Sutaṃ na pariyodapetīti yampissa sutaṃ atthi, taṃ pariyodapetuṃ na sakkoti. Sutenekaccena avisārado hotīti thokathokena sutena vijjamānenāpi ñāṇena somanassappatto na hoti. Samavatthacāreti samavatthitacāre. Dutiyaṃ uttānatthameva.

221. In the first discourse of the third chapter, 'unsettled in journeying' (anavatthacārikaṃ) means unestablished in journeying. 'Does not purify what is learned' (sutaṃ na pariyodapeti) means he is unable to purify whatever learning he has. 'Is not confident in some learning' (sutenekaccena avisārado hoti) means he does not attain joy through even the small knowledge he possesses. 'Settled in journeying' (samavatthacāre) means established in journeying. The second discourse is clear in meaning.

3-4. Atinivāsasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Explanation of the Atinivāsa Sutta and Other Discourses

223-224. Tatiye bahubhaṇḍoti bahuparikkhāro. Bahubhesajjoti sappinavanītādīnaṃ bahutāya bahubhesajjo. Byattoti byāsatto. Saṃsaṭṭhoti pañcavidhena saṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho hutvā. Ananulomikenāti sāsanassa ananucchavikena. Catutthe vaṇṇamaccharīti guṇamaccharī. Dhammamaccharīti pariyattimaccharī.

In the third discourse, 'many possessions' (bahubhaṇḍo) means much equipment. 'Many medicines' (bahubhesajjo) means having many medicines due to the abundance of ghee, fresh butter, and so forth. 'Competent' (byatto) means clever. 'Mingling' (saṃsaṭṭho) means being associated through five kinds of association. 'Inappropriate' (ananulomikena) means unsuitable for the Dispensation. In the fourth discourse, 'stingy with praise' (vaṇṇamaccharī) means stingy with virtues. 'Stingy with the Dhamma' (dhammamaccharī) means stingy with the scriptural learning.

5-6. Kulūpakasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Explanation of the Kulūpaka Sutta and Other Discourses

225-226. Pañcame [M 3.0082] anāmantacāre āpajjatīti “nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjeyyā”ti sikkhāpade (pārā. 294) vuttaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati. Raho nisajjāyātiādīnipi tesaṃ tesaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vasena veditabbāni. Chaṭṭhe ativelanti atikkantapamāṇakālaṃ. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

In the fifth discourse, 'one incurs the offense of wandering without leave' means one incurs the offense stated in the training rule: 'Should a bhikkhu who has been invited and has a meal, without asking leave of a bhikkhu who is present, go visiting among families either before or after the meal...' (Pārā. 294). The phrases 'sitting in private' and so forth should also be understood according to their respective training rules. In the sixth discourse, 'for too long' means exceeding the time limit. The seventh is clear in meaning.

8. Ussūrabhattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on Meals Eaten After Midday

228. Aṭṭhame [V 3.0084] ussūrabhatteti atidivāpacanabhatte. Na kālena paṭipūjentīti yāgukāle yāguṃ, khajjakakāle khajjakaṃ[P 3.0331], bhojanakāle bhojanaṃ apacantā yuttappayuttakālassa atināmitattā na kālena paṭipūjenti, attano citteneva denti nāma. Tato tepi tesu attano gehaṃ āgatesu tatheva karonti. Kulapaveṇiyā āgatā balipaṭiggāhikā devatāpi yuttappayuttakālena lābhaṃ labhamānāyeva rakkhanti gopayanti pīḷaṃ akatvā. Akāle labhamānā pana “ime amhesu anādarā”ti ārakkhaṃ na karonti.

228. In the eighth discourse, 'meal eaten after midday' means food cooked too late in the day. 'Not serving on time' means not preparing gruel at the time for gruel, snacks at the time for snacks, or the main meal at the time for the main meal. Because the appropriate and suitable time has been exceeded, they do not serve on time, but rather give according to their own inclination. Consequently, when those monastics come to their homes, they also do likewise. Even the deities who receive offerings, having come in the family tradition, protect and guard them without causing harm only if they receive their gain at the appropriate and suitable time. But if they receive it at the wrong time, they think, 'These people are disrespectful towards us,' and do not provide protection.

Samaṇabrāhmaṇāpi “etesaṃ gehe bhojanavelāya bhojanaṃ na hoti, ṭhitamajjhanhike dentī”ti maṅgalāmaṅgalesu kātabbaṃ na karonti. Vimukhā kammaṃ karontīti “pāto kiñci na labhāma, khudāya paṭipīḷitā kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkomā”ti kammaṃ vissajjetvā nisīdanti. Anojavantaṃ hotīti akāle bhuttaṃ ojaṃ harituṃ na sakkoti. Sukkapakkho vuttavipallāsena veditabbo.

Even ascetics and brahmins, thinking, 'In this household, food is not available at mealtime; they give it only at high noon,' do not perform for them what should be done on auspicious occasions. 'They turn away from work' means they abandon their tasks and sit idle, thinking, 'We get nothing in the morning; afflicted by hunger, we are unable to work.' 'It is not invigorating' means food eaten at the wrong time is unable to draw out nutritive essence. The bright fortnight should be understood as the opposite of what was said.

9. Paṭhamakaṇhasappasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the First Discourse on the Black Serpent

229. Navame sabhīrūti saniddo mahāniddaṃ niddāyati. Sappaṭibhayoti taṃ nissāya bhayaṃ uppajjati, tasmā sappaṭibhayo. Mittadubbhīti pānabhojanadāyakampi mittaṃ dubbhati hiṃsati. Mātugāmepi eseva nayo.

229. In the ninth discourse: `sabhīru` means one who is sleepy, who sleeps a great sleep. `Sappaṭibhaya` means that on account of that cobra, fear arises; therefore, one is with fear. `Mittadubbhī` means one who harms, who vexes a friend, even one who gives drink and food. In the case of a woman as well, this is the method.

10. Dutiyakaṇhasappasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Second Discourse on the Black Serpent

230. Dasame [M 3.0083] ghoravisoti kakkhaḷaviso. Dujjivhoti dvidhā bhinnajivho. Ghoravisatāti ghoravisatāya. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

230. In the tenth discourse: 'of deadly venom' means one with harsh venom. 'Double-tongued' means one with a tongue split in two. 'The state of having deadly venom' is because of having deadly venom. In the remaining two terms as well, the same method applies.

Dīghacārikavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Wandering Long, the Third.

(24) 4. Āvāsikavaggo

(24) 4. The Chapter on Residents

1. Āvāsikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on the Resident

231. Catutthassa [V 3.0085][P 3.0332] paṭhame na ākappasampannoti samaṇākappena sampanno. Abhāvanīyo hotīti vaḍḍhanīyo na hoti. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

231. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter: 'not endowed with proper conduct' means not endowed with the demeanor of an ascetic. 'Is not to be cultivated' means is not to be developed. The second is clear in meaning.

3. Sobhanasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Discourse on the Beautiful One

233. Tatiye paṭibaloti kāyabalena ca ñāṇabalena ca samannāgatattā paṭibalo.

233. In the third discourse: `paṭibala` means one is capable because of being endowed with both physical strength and the strength of knowledge.

4. Bahūpakārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on Great Help

234. Catutthe khaṇḍaphullanti patitaṭṭhānañca bhinnaṭṭhānañca. Paṭisaṅkharotīti paṭipākatikaṃ karoti. Ārocetīti idaṃ pavāritakulānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ.

234. In the fourth discourse: `khaṇḍaphulla` means the place that has fallen and the place that is broken. `Paṭisaṅkharoti` means one makes it back to its original state. This word `āroceti` is spoken by way of the families who have extended an invitation.

5. Anukampasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Discourse on Compassion

235. Pañcame adhisīlesūti pañcasu sīlesu. Dhammadassane nivesetīti catusaccadhammadassane patiṭṭhāpeti. Arahaggatanti sabbasakkārānaṃ arahe ratanattayeva gataṃ, tīsu vatthūsu garucittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapethāti attho. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

235. In the fifth discourse: `adhisīlesu` means in the five precepts. `Dhammadassane niveseti` means one establishes them in the seeing of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. `Arahaggataṃ` means concerning the Triple Gem, which is worthy of all offerings; the meaning is, 'You should establish reverence for the three objects.' The sixth is clear in meaning.

7. Dutiyaavaṇṇārahasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Second Discourse on One Not Deserving Blame

237. Sattame [M 3.0084] āvāsapaligedhīti āvāsaṃ balavagiddhivasena gilitvā viya ṭhito. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānamevāti.

237. In the seventh discourse: `āvāsapaligedhī` means one who stands as if having swallowed the dwelling by way of strong greed. All the rest is clear in meaning.

Āvāsikavaggo catuttho.

The Chapter on Residents, the Fourth.

(25) 5. Duccaritavaggo

(25) 5. The Chapter on Wrongdoing

1. Paṭhamaduccaritasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Discourse on Wrongdoing

241. Pañcamassa [V 3.0086][P 3.0333] paṭhame duccarite sucariteti idaṃ abhedato vuttaṃ, kāyaduccaritetiādi kāyadvārādīnaṃ vasena bhedato. Saddhammāti dasakusalakammapathadhammato. Asaddhammeti akusalakammapathasaṅkhāte assaddhamme.

241. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, 'misconduct' and 'good conduct' are stated undifferentiatedly, while 'bodily misconduct' and so on are differentiated according to the bodily door and so on. 'True Dhamma' means the Dhamma consisting of the ten wholesome courses of action. 'False Dhamma' means the non-Dhamma designated as the unwholesome courses of action.

9. Sivathikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Charnel Ground

249. Navame sivathikāyāti susāne. Ārodanāti ārodanaṭṭhānaṃ. Asucināti jigucchanīyena.

249. In the ninth discourse: `sivathikāya` means in a cemetery. `Ārodanā` means a place of lamentation. `Asucinā` means by that which is repulsive.

10. Puggalappasādasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on Confidence in a Person

250. Dasame puggalappasādeti ekapuggalasmiṃ uppannappasāde. Ante nisīdāpetīti bhikkhūnaṃ āsanapariyante nisīdāpeti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

250. In the tenth discourse, 'confidence in a person' means confidence that has arisen in a single individual. 'He makes him sit at the end' means he has him sit at the edge of the monks' seating. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Duccaritavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Wrongdoing, the Fifth.

The Fifth Fifty is concluded.

(26) 6. Upasampadāvaggo

(26) 6. The Chapter on Full Ordination

1-3. Upasampādetabbasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Explanation of the Discourses Beginning with 'One to be Fully Ordained'

251-253. Chaṭṭhassa [M 3.0085][V 3.0087] paṭhame upasampādetabbanti upajjhāyena hutvā upasampādetabbaṃ. Dutiye nissayo dātabboti ācariyena hutvā nissayo dātabbo. Tatiye sāmaṇero upaṭṭhāpetabboti upajjhāyena hutvā sāmaṇero gahetabbo. Iti imāni tīṇipi suttāni paṭhamabodhiyaṃ khīṇāsavavasena vuttāni. Catutthādīni anupadavaṇṇanāto uttānatthāneva.

In the first discourse of the sixth fifty, 'one should be fully ordained' means one should be given full ordination by a preceptor. In the second, 'dependence should be given' means dependence should be given by a teacher. In the third, 'a novice should be attended to' means a novice should be accepted by a preceptor. Thus, these three discourses were spoken at the time of the First Awakening with reference to those whose taints are destroyed. The fourth and following are clear in meaning from the word-by-word explanation.

1. Sammutipeyyālādivaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Repetition Series on Appointment, etc.

272. Bhattuddesakādīnaṃ [P 3.0334] vinicchayakathā samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 325) vuttanayena veditabbāti. Sammato na pesetabboti pakatiyā sammato “gaccha bhattāni uddisāhī”ti na pesetabbo.

272. The discussion on the determination of the alms-meal appointer, etc., should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā Vinaya Commentary (Cūḷavagga Commentary 325). 'One who is appointed should not be sent' means one who is appointed in the usual way should not be sent with the instruction, 'Go and announce the meal.'

273-285. Sāṭiyaggāhāpakoti vassikasāṭikāya gāhāpako. Pattaggāhāpakoti “yo ca tassā bhikkhuparisāya pattapariyanto, so tassa bhikkhuno padātabbo”ti ettha vuttapattaggāhāpako.

'The robe allotter' is one who allots the rainy-season robe. 'The bowl allotter' refers to the one mentioned here: 'Whatever is the bowl portion of that community of monks, that should be given to that monk.'

293-302. Ājīvakoti naggaparibbājako. Nigaṇṭhoti purimabhāgappaṭicchanno. Muṇḍasāvakoti nigaṇṭhasāvako. Jaṭilakoti tāpaso. Paribbājakoti channaparibbājako. Māgaṇḍikādayopi titthiyā eva. Etesaṃ pana sīlesu paripūrakāritāya abhāvena sukkapakkho na gahito. Sesamettha uttānamevāti.

'An Ājīvaka' is a naked wanderer. 'A Nigaṇṭha' is one who covers the forepart. 'A Muṇḍasāvaka' is a disciple of a Nigaṇṭha. 'A Jaṭila' is an ascetic. 'A Paribbājaka' is a clothed wanderer. Māgaṇḍika and others are also sectarians. However, because of the lack of complete fulfillment in their virtues, the bright side is not taken. The rest here is evident.

Chakkanipāta-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Book of the Sixes

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Āhuneyyavaggo

1. The Section on Those Worthy of Offerings

1. Paṭhamaāhuneyyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings

1. Chakkanipātassa [V 3.0089][M 3.0087][P 3.0335] paṭhame idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhūti, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Neva sumano hoti na dummanoti iṭṭhārammaṇe rāgasahagatena somanassena sumano vā aniṭṭhārammaṇe dosasahagatena domanassena dummano vā na hoti. Upekkhako viharati sato sampajānoti majjhattārammaṇe asamapekkhanena aññāṇupekkhāya upekkhakabhāvaṃ anāpajjitvā sato [V 3.0090] sampajāno hutvā ārammaṇe majjhatto viharati. Imasmiṃ sutte khīṇāsavassa satatavihāro kathito.

In the first [discourse] of the Book of the Sixes, 'here, monks, a monk' means, monks, a monk in this dispensation. 'He is neither pleased nor displeased' means he is not pleased with a desirable object through joy accompanied by greed, nor is he displeased with an undesirable object through displeasure accompanied by aversion. 'He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending' means that, not having fallen into a state of equanimity through the equanimity of ignorance by not properly regarding a neutral object, he dwells balanced towards the object, being mindful and clearly comprehending. In this discourse, the constant dwelling of one whose taints are destroyed is taught.

2. Dutiyaāhuneyyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Second Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings

2-4. Dutiye anekavihitaṃ iddhividhantiādīni visuddhimagge vuttāneva. Āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavanti āsavānaṃ khayena anāsavaṃ, na cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ viya abhāvenāti. Imasmiṃ sutte khīṇāsavassa abhiññā paṭipāṭiyā kathitā. Tatiyacatutthesu khīṇāsavo kathito.

2–4. In the second [discourse], the phrases ‘various kinds of psychic power’ and so forth are as stated in the Visuddhimagga. The phrase ‘taintless through the destruction of the taints’ means taintless through the destruction of the taints, not through their absence, as in the case of eye-consciousness and so forth. In this discourse, the sequence of the direct knowledges of one whose taints are destroyed is taught. In the third and fourth [discourses], one whose taints are destroyed is discussed.

5-7. Ājānīyasuttattayavaṇṇanā

5–7. Explanation of the Three Discourses on the Thoroughbreds

5-7. Pañcame aṅgehīti guṇaṅgehi. Khamoti adhivāsako. Rūpānanti rūpārammaṇānaṃ. Vaṇṇasampannoti [P 3.0336] sarīravaṇṇena sampanno. Chaṭṭhe balasampannoti kāyabalena sampanno. Sattame javasampannoti padajavena sampanno.

5–7. In the fifth [discourse], ‘with limbs’ means with limbs that are qualities. ‘Enduring’ means one who endures. ‘Of forms’ means of objects of form. ‘Perfect in appearance’ means endowed with beauty of body. In the sixth [discourse], ‘perfect in strength’ means endowed with strength of body. In the seventh [discourse], ‘perfect in speed’ means endowed with speed of foot.

8-9. Anuttariyasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–9. Explanation Beginning with the Discourse on the Unsurpassable

8-9. Aṭṭhame anuttariyānīti aññena uttaritarena rahitāni niruttarāni. Dassanānuttariyanti rūpadassanesu anuttaraṃ. Esa nayo sabbapadesu[M 3.0088]. Hatthiratanādīnañhi dassanaṃ na dassanānuttariyaṃ, niviṭṭhasaddhassa pana niviṭṭhapemavasena dasabalassa vā bhikkhusaṅghassa vā kasiṇaasubhanimittādīnaṃ vā aññatarassa dassanaṃ dassanānuttariyaṃ nāma. Khattiyādīnaṃ guṇakathāsavanaṃ na savanānuttariyaṃ, niviṭṭhasaddhassa pana niviṭṭhapemavasena tiṇṇaṃ vā ratanānaṃ guṇakathāsavanaṃ tepiṭakabuddhavacanasavanaṃ vā savanānuttariyaṃ nāma. Maṇiratanādīnaṃ lābho na lābhānuttariyaṃ, sattavidhaariyadhanalābho pana lābhānuttariyaṃ nāma. Hatthisippādisikkhanaṃ na sikkhānuttariyaṃ, sikkhāttayassa pūraṇaṃ pana sikkhānuttariyaṃ nāma. Khattiyādīnaṃ pāricariyā na pāricariyānuttariyaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ pana ratanānaṃ pāricariyā pāricariyānuttariyaṃ nāma. Khattiyādīnaṃ guṇānussaraṇaṃ na anussatānuttariyaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ pana ratanānaṃ guṇānussaraṇaṃ anussatānuttariyaṃ [V 3.0091] nāma. Iti imāni cha anuttariyāni lokiyalokuttarāni kathitāni. Navame buddhānussatīti buddhaguṇārammaṇā sati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

1. 8–9. In the eighth [discourse], ‘the unsurpassed’ means those things that are without a superior, lacking anything higher. ‘Unsurpassable seeing’ means the unsurpassed among sights. This principle applies in all instances. For example, seeing treasures such as elephants is not unsurpassable seeing, but for one with unwavering faith and affection, seeing the Ten-Powered One, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, or any object among such things as a kasiṇa-sign or an asubha-sign, is called unsurpassable seeing. Hearing praise of nobles and so forth is not unsurpassable hearing, but for one with unwavering faith and affection, hearing praise of the Three Jewels or hearing the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka is called unsurpassable hearing. Gaining treasures such as jewels is not unsurpassable gain, but gaining the seven kinds of noble wealth is called unsurpassable gain. Learning skills such as elephant-craft is not unsurpassable training, but fulfilling the threefold training is called unsurpassable training. Serving nobles and so forth is not unsurpassable service, but serving the Three Jewels is called unsurpassable service. Recalling the virtues of nobles and so forth is not unsurpassable recollection, but recalling the virtues of the Three Jewels is called unsurpassable recollection. Thus, these six unsurpassed things, both mundane and supramundane, have been taught. In the ninth [discourse], ‘mindfulness of the Buddha’ means mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object. This same principle applies to the remaining terms.

10. Mahānāmasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Mahānāma Sutta

10. Dasame mahānāmoti dasabalassa cūḷapitu putto eko sakyarājā. Yena [P 3.0337] bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti bhuttapātarāso hutvā dāsaparijanaparivuto gandhamālādīni gāhāpetvā yattha satthā, tattha agamāsi. Ariyaphalaṃ assa āgatanti āgataphalo. Sikkhāttayasāsanaṃ etena viññātanti viññātasāsano. Iti ayaṃ rājā “sotāpannassa nissayavihāraṃ pucchāmī”ti pucchanto evamāha.

1. In the tenth [discourse], Mahānāma is a certain Sakyan king, the son of the Ten-Powered One’s younger paternal uncle. As for the phrase, ‘He approached the Blessed One,’ it means: having eaten his morning meal, surrounded by an entourage of servants, and having caused perfumes, garlands, and so on to be taken, he went to where the Teacher was. ‘The noble fruit has come to him,’ thus he is called āgataphala (one to whom the fruit has come). ‘The teaching of the threefold training has been understood by him,’ thus he is called viññātasāsana (one who has understood the teaching). Thus this king, intending, ‘I shall ask about the dependent dwelling of a stream-enterer,’ and wishing to ask, spoke thus.

Nevassa rāgapariyuṭṭhitanti na uppajjamānena rāgena uṭṭhahitvā gahitaṃ. Ujugatanti buddhānussatikammaṭṭhāne ujukameva gataṃ. Tathāgataṃ ārabbhāti tathāgataguṇe ārabbha. Atthavedanti aṭṭhakathaṃ nissāya uppannaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ. Dhammavedanti pāḷiṃ nissāya uppannaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ. Dhammūpasañhitanti pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca nissāya uppannaṃ. Pamuditassāti duvidhena pāmojjena pamuditassa. Pīti jāyatīti pañcavidhā pīti nibbattati. Kāyo passambhatīti nāmakāyo ca karajakāyo ca darathapaṭippassaddhiyā paṭippassambhati. Sukhanti kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ. Samādhiyatīti ārammaṇe sammā ṭhapitaṃ hoti. Visamagatāya pajāyāti rāgadosamohavisamagatesu sattesu. Samappattoti samaṃ upasamaṃ patto hutvā. Sabyāpajjhāyāti sadukkhāya. Dhammasotaṃ [M 3.0089] samāpannoti vipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammasotaṃ samāpanno. Buddhānussatiṃ bhāvetīti buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ brūheti vaḍḍheti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Iti [P 3.0338] mahānāmo sotāpannassa nissayavihāraṃ pucchi. Satthāpissa tameva kathesi. Evaṃ imasmiṃ sutte sotāpannova kathitoti.

1. ‘Not obsessed by lust’ means not seized by arising lust. ‘Gone straight’ means gone straight indeed in the meditation subject of recollection of the Buddha. ‘Concerning the Tathāgata’ means having taken the virtues of the Tathāgata as an object. ‘Meaning-inspired joy’ means the joy and gladness that has arisen relying on the commentary. ‘Dhamma-inspired joy’ means the joy and gladness that has arisen relying on the Pāli text. ‘Connected with the Dhamma’ means that which has arisen relying on both the Pāli and the commentary. ‘For one who is gladdened’ means for one who is gladdened by the twofold gladness. ‘Joy arises’ means the fivefold joy is produced. ‘The body becomes tranquil’ means both the mental body and the physical body are calmed by the calming of distress. ‘Happiness’ means bodily and mental happiness. ‘Becomes concentrated’ means it becomes well-placed on the object. ‘Among a generation that has gone to the uneven’ means among beings who have gone to the uneven through lust, hatred, and delusion. ‘Having attained evenness’ means having reached calm. ‘With affliction’ means with suffering. ‘Having entered the stream of Dhamma’ means having entered the stream of Dhamma called insight. ‘He develops recollection of the Buddha’ means he cultivates and increases the meditation subject of recollection of the Buddha. In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere. Thus, Mahānāma asked about the dependent dwelling of a stream-enterer, and the Teacher also explained that very thing to him. Thus, in this sutta, only the stream-enterer is spoken of.

Āhuneyyavaggo paṭhamo.

1. The First Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings.

2. Sāraṇīyavaggo

2. The Chapter on Amiability

1. Paṭhamasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Discourse on Amiability

11. Dutiyassa [V 3.0092] paṭhame sāraṇīyāti saritabbayuttakā. Mettaṃ kāyakammanti mettena cittena kātabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Vacīkammamanokammesupi eseva nayo. Imāni ca pana bhikkhūnaṃ vasena āgatāni, gihīsupi labbhanti. Bhikkhūnañhi mettena cittena ābhisamācārikadhammapūraṇaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya bodhivandanatthāya saṅghanimantanatthāya gamanaṃ, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhe bhikkhū disvā paccuggamanaṃ, pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ, āsanapaññāpanaṃ, anugamananti evamādikaṃ mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma.

11. In the first sutta of the second chapter, sāraṇīyā means 'things that should be remembered.' 'Loving bodily action' is bodily action to be done with a mind associated with loving-kindness. This same method applies also to verbal and mental actions. Furthermore, these actions are presented in connection with monks, but they are also found among laypeople. For monks, the fulfillment of the duties of proper conduct with a mind associated with loving-kindness is called 'loving bodily action.' For laypeople, actions such as going for the purpose of venerating a cetiya, venerating the Bodhi tree, or inviting the Saṅgha; seeing monks who have entered the village for alms and going out to meet them, taking their bowls, preparing a seat, and accompanying them on their way—such actions are called 'loving bodily action.'

Bhikkhūnaṃ mettena cittena ācārapaṇṇattisikkhāpanaṃ, kammaṭṭhānakathanaṃ, dhammadesanā, tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ “cetiyavandanāya gacchāma, bodhivandanāya gacchāma, dhammassavanaṃ karissāma, dīpamālāpupphapūjaṃ karissāma, tīṇi sucaritāni samādāya vattissāma, salākabhattādīni dassāma, vassāvāsikaṃ dassāma, ajja saṅghassa cattāro paccaye dassāma, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā khādanīyādīni saṃvidahatha, āsanāni paññāpetha, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetha, saṅghaṃ paccuggantvā [P 3.0339] ānetha, paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā ussāhajātā veyyāvaccaṃ karothā”tiādivacanakāle mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma.

For monks, with a mind of loving-kindness, the laying down of training rules regarding conduct, the explaining of meditation subjects, the teaching of the Dhamma, and the word of the Buddha which is the Tipiṭaka—this is called 'loving verbal action.' For laypeople, at the time of saying such things as: ‘Let us go to venerate the cetiya; let us go to venerate the Bodhi tree; let us listen to the Dhamma; let us make offerings of lamps, garlands, and flowers; let us undertake and practice the three kinds of good conduct; let us give ticket-food and so on; let us give the rains-residence cloth; today let us give the four requisites to the Saṅgha; having invited the Saṅgha, prepare the edibles and so on; arrange the seats; set up the water; go out to meet the Saṅgha and bring them; having seated them on the prepared seats, with enthusiasm, perform the services’—this is called 'loving verbal action.'

Bhikkhūnaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīni ca katvā vivittāsane nisīditvā “imasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjhā”ti [M 3.0090] cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Gihīnaṃ “ayyā sukhī hontu averā abyāpajjhā”ti cintanaṃ mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

For monks, rising early in the morning, attending to the body, performing duties such as those in the cetiya courtyard, and then sitting in a secluded place and thinking, ‘May the monks in this monastery be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction’—this is called 'loving mental action.' For laypeople, thinking, ‘May the venerable sirs be happy, free from enmity, and free from affliction’—this is called 'loving mental action.'

Āvi ceva raho cāti sammukhā ca parammukhā ca. Tattha navakānaṃ cīvarakammādīsu sahāyabhāvagamanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma, therānaṃ pana pādadhovanadānādibhedaṃ sabbampi sāmīcikammaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. Ubhayehipi dunnikkhittānaṃ dārubhaṇḍādīnaṃ tesu avaññaṃ [V 3.0093] akatvā attanā dunnikkhittānaṃ viya paṭisāmanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma. “Devatthero tissatthero”ti evaṃ paggayha vacanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Vihāre asantaṃ pana paṭipucchantassa “kahaṃ amhākaṃ devatthero, kahaṃ amhākaṃ tissatthero, kadā nu kho āgamissatī”ti evaṃ mamāyanavacanaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma. Mettāsinehasiniddhāni pana nayanāni ummīletvā pasannena mukhena olokanaṃ sammukhā mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. “Devatthero tissatthero arogo hotu appābādho”ti samannāharaṇaṃ parammukhā mettaṃ manokammaṃ nāma.

‘Openly and in secret’ means both in their presence and in their absence. Among these, for junior monks, becoming a companion in tasks such as robe-making is called 'loving bodily action in their presence.' For senior monks, all respectful service of various kinds, such as giving water for washing the feet, is called 'loving bodily action in their presence.' For both groups, when wooden articles and so on have been badly placed, putting them away properly without contempt for those monks, as if one were putting away one's own badly placed things, is called 'loving bodily action in their absence.' Speaking in praise, saying, ‘Devatthera, Tissatthera,’ is called 'loving verbal action in their presence.' When asking about a monk who is not in the monastery, speech showing endearment, such as, ‘Where is our Devatthera? Where is our Tissatthera? When will he come?’ is called 'loving verbal action in their absence.' Opening the eyes, which are softened by the glue of loving-kindness and affection, and looking with a serene face is called 'loving mental action in their presence.' Directing the mind, thinking, ‘May Devatthera and Tissatthera be healthy and have few ailments,’ is called 'loving mental action in their absence.'

Lābhāti cīvarādayo laddhapaccayā. Dhammikāti [P 3.0340] kuhanādibhedaṃ micchājīvaṃ vajjetvā dhammena samena bhikkhācariyavattena uppannā. Antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampīti pacchimakoṭiyā pattapariyāpannaṃ pattassa antogataṃ dvattikaṭacchubhikkhāmattampi. Appaṭivibhattabhogīti ettha dve paṭivibhattāni nāma āmisapaṭivibhattaṃ pana puggalapaṭivibhattañca. Tattha “ettakaṃ dassāmi, ettakaṃ na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena paṭivibhajanaṃ āmisapaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. “Asukassa dassāmi, asukassa na dassāmī”ti evaṃ cittena vibhajanaṃ pana puggalapaṭivibhattaṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi akatvā yo appaṭivibhattaṃ bhuñjati, ayaṃ appaṭivibhattabhogī nāma. Sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogīti ettha sādhāraṇabhogino idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ labhati, taṃ taṃ neva lābhenalābhaṃ-nijigīsanatāmukhena gihīnaṃ deti, na attanā paribhuñjati, paṭiggaṇhanto ca “saṅghena sādhāraṇaṃ hotū”ti gahetvā ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ saṅghasantakaṃ viya passati.

Gains means requisites such as robes and so forth that have been obtained. 'Righteously' means that they are obtained through the practice of going for alms according to the Dhamma and with fairness, having avoided wrong livelihood of various kinds such as deceit. 'Even just what fits into the bowl' means, at the lowest limit, what is contained in the bowl, what has gone inside the bowl, even just the amount of two or three spoonfuls of alms-food. Herein, regarding 'one who partakes without dividing,' there are two kinds of division: division of material things and division of persons. Among these, dividing with the thought, 'I will give this much, I will not give that much,' is called division of material things. And dividing with the thought, 'I will give to this person, I will not give to that person,' is called division of persons. Whoever, without making both of these two divisions, partakes, is called 'one who partakes without dividing.' Herein, regarding 'one who partakes in common with virtuous fellow practitioners,' this is the characteristic of one who partakes in common: whatever excellent thing one obtains, one neither gives it to householders with the primary motive of desiring to overcome another's gain with one's own gain, nor does one partake of it oneself. And when accepting, having taken it with the thought 'Let it be in common with the Saṅgha,' one regards it as if it were the property of the Saṅgha, to be partaken of after striking the bell.

Imaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammaṃ ko pūreti, ko na pūreti? Dussīlo tāva na pūreti. Na hi tassa santakaṃ sīlavantā gaṇhanti. Parisuddhasīlo pana [M 3.0091] vattaṃ akhaṇḍento pūreti. Tatridaṃ vattaṃ – yo hi odissakaṃ katvā mātu vā pitu vā ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ vā deti, so dātabbaṃ deti. Sāraṇīyadhammo panassa na hoti, palibodhajagganaṃ nāma hoti. Sāraṇīyadhammo hi muttapalibodhassa vaṭṭati. Tena pana odissakaṃ [P 3.0341] dentena gilānagilānupaṭṭhākaāgantukagamikānañceva navapabbajitassa ca saṅghāṭipattaggahaṇaṃ ajānantassa dātabbaṃ. Etesaṃ datvā avasesaṃ therāsanato paṭṭhāya thokaṃ thokaṃ adatvā yo yattakaṃ gaṇhāti, tassa tattakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Avasiṭṭhe [V 3.0094] asati puna piṇḍāya caritvā therāsanato paṭṭhāya yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ, taṃ taṃ datvā sesaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ. “Sīlavantehī”ti vacanato dussīlassa adātumpi vaṭṭati.

Now, who fulfills this principle of amiability, and who does not? Firstly, an immoral one does not fulfill it. Indeed, the virtuous do not accept what belongs to him. But one of pure virtue fulfills it, not breaking the observance. Herein, this is the observance: Whoever, having designated something, gives it to his mother, or father, or teachers, preceptors, and so on, he gives what should be given. But for him, it is not the principle of amiability; it is called 'attending to an impediment.' Indeed, the principle of amiability is suitable for one who is free from impediments. But by that one giving a designated thing, it should be given to the sick, to the one attending the sick, to a visitor, to one departing, and to a newly ordained one who does not know how to take the outer robe and bowl. After giving to these, as for the remainder, starting from the seat of the elders, one should not give it out in small portions; whatever amount someone takes, that much should be given to them. If there is no remainder, having gone for alms again, starting from the seat of the elders, having given whatever is excellent, the rest should be consumed. Because of the statement 'with the virtuous,' it is also permissible not to give to an immoral person.

Ayaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammo susikkhitāya parisāya supūro hoti, susikkhitāya hi parisāya yo aññato labhati, so na gaṇhāti. Aññato alabhantopi pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhati, na atirekaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sāraṇīyadhammo evaṃ punappunaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ dentassāpi dvādasahi vassehi pūreti, na tato oraṃ. Sace hi dvādasame vasse sāraṇīyadhammapūrako piṇḍapātapūraṃ pattaṃ āsanasālāyaṃ ṭhapetvā nhāyituṃ gacchati, saṅghatthero ca “kasseso patto”ti vatvā “sāraṇīyadhammapūrakassā”ti vutte “āharatha na”nti sabbaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ vicāretvāva bhuñjitvā rittapattaṃ ṭhapeti. Atha kho so bhikkhu rittapattaṃ disvā “mayhaṃ asesetvāva paribhuñjiṃsū”ti domanassaṃ uppādeti, sāraṇīyadhammo bhijjati, puna dvādasa vassāni pūretabbo hoti. Titthiyaparivāsasadiso hesa, sakiṃ khaṇḍe jāte puna pūretabbova. Yo pana “lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata me, yassa me pattagataṃ anāpucchāva sabrahmacārī paribhuñjantī”ti somanassaṃ janeti, tassa puṇṇo nāma hoti.

Furthermore, this principle of amiability is easy to fulfill in a well-trained assembly. Indeed, in a well-trained assembly, one who receives from elsewhere does not take; and one who does not receive from elsewhere takes only a suitable amount, not in excess. Moreover, this principle of amiability is fulfilled in twelve years, and not less, even for one who repeatedly goes for alms in this way and gives whatever he obtains. For if, in the twelfth year, the monk fulfilling the principle of amiability places his bowl filled with alms-food in the dining hall and goes to bathe, and the elder of the Saṅgha, having asked, 'Whose bowl is this?' and having been told, 'It belongs to the one fulfilling the principle of amiability,' says, 'Bring it,' and then, having apportioned all the alms-food, partakes of it and leaves the bowl empty; and if that monk, upon seeing the empty bowl, gives rise to displeasure, thinking, 'They have partaken of it without leaving any for me,' the principle of amiability is broken. It must be fulfilled again for twelve years. For this is similar to the probation of the sectarians: once it is broken, it must be fulfilled again. But for one who generates joy, thinking, 'A gain it is for me! Well-gained it is for me, that my fellow practitioners partake of what is in my bowl without asking!'—for him, it is called 'fulfilled'.

Evaṃ pūritasāraṇīyadhammassa pana neva issā na macchariyaṃ hoti, manussānaṃ piyo hoti, amanussānaṃ [P 3.0342] piyo hoti, sulabhapaccayo. Pattagatamassa diyyamānampi na khīyati, bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ labhati, bhaye vā chātake vā patte devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjanti.

Furthermore, for one who has thus fulfilled the principle of amiability, there is neither envy nor stinginess. He is dear to human beings and dear to non-human beings, and his requisites are easy to obtain. What has gone into his bowl, even when being given away, is not exhausted. In a place where goods are to be distributed, he obtains the best portion. When he encounters danger or famine, deities become solicitous.

Tatrimāni [M 3.0092] vatthūni – senagirivāsī tissatthero kira mahāgirigāmaṃ upanissāya vasati, paññāsa mahātherā nāgadīpaṃ cetiyavandanatthāya gacchantā girigāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā nikkhamiṃsu. Thero pavisanto te disvā pucchi – “laddhaṃ, bhante”ti? Vicarimhā, āvusoti. So aladdhabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “bhante, yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hothā”ti. Mayaṃ, āvuso, paññāsa janā pattatemanamattampi na labhimhāti. Bhante, nevāsikā nāma paṭibalā honti, alabhantāpi bhikkhācāramaggasabhāgaṃ jānantīti. Therā āgamesuṃ. Thero gāmaṃ pāvisi. Dhurageheyeva mahāupāsikā khīrabhattaṃ sajjetvā theraṃ olokayamānā ṭhitā therassa dvāraṃ sampattasseva pattaṃ pūretvā adāsi. So taṃ ādāya therānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “gaṇhatha[V 3.0095], bhante”ti saṅghattheraṃ āha. Thero “amhehi ettakehi kiñci na laddhaṃ, ayaṃ sīghameva gahetvā āgato, kiṃ nu kho”ti sesānaṃ mukhaṃ olokesi. Thero olokanākāreneva ñatvā, “bhante, dhammena samena laddho, nikkukkuccā gaṇhathā”ti ādito paṭṭhāya sabbesaṃ yāvadatthaṃ datvā attanāpi yāvadatthaṃ bhuñji.

Herein are these stories: It is said that the elder Tissa, a resident of Senagiri, lived near Mahāgirigāma. Fifty great elders, while going to Nāgadīpa to pay homage to the shrine, went for alms in Girigāma but, having obtained nothing, they departed. The elder, upon entering, saw them and asked, 'Venerable sirs, was anything obtained?' 'We wandered, friend,' they replied. Knowing they had obtained nothing, he said, 'Venerable sirs, please wait here until I return.' They replied, 'Friend, we are fifty persons and did not obtain even enough to moisten a bowl.' He said, 'Venerable sirs, resident monks are capable; even when not receiving, they know the customary alms-round path.' The elders waited. The elder entered the village. At the very first house, a great laywoman had prepared milk-rice and was standing watching for the elder. As soon as the elder reached the door, she filled his bowl and gave it to him. Taking it, he went to the elders and said to the elder of the Saṅgha, 'Venerable sirs, please take this.' The elder of the Saṅgha looked at the faces of the others, thinking, 'So many of us have obtained nothing, yet this one has returned quickly with this. What can this be?' The elder Tissa, knowing by their very manner of looking, said, 'Venerable sirs, this was obtained righteously and fairly. Take it without hesitation.' Then, starting from the first, he gave to all of them as much as they wished, and he himself also partook as much as he wished.

Atha naṃ bhattakiccāvasāne therā pucchiṃsu – “kadā, āvuso, lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhī”ti? Natthi me, bhante, lokuttaradhammoti. Jhānalābhīsi, āvusoti. Etampi, bhante, natthīti? Nanu, āvuso, pāṭihāriyanti. Sāraṇīyadhammo me, bhante, pūrito, tassa [P 3.0343] me pūritakālato paṭṭhāya sacepi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ hoti, pattagataṃ na khīyatīti. Sādhu sādhu, sappurisa, anucchavikamidaṃ tuyhanti. Idaṃ tāva pattagataṃ na khīyatīti ettha vatthu.

Then, after the meal, the elders asked him, “Friend, when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma?” “Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane Dhamma.” “Are you an attainer of jhāna, friend?” “This too, venerable sirs, I do not have.” “Surely, friend, this must be a miraculous power?” “Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the principle of amiability. From the time I fulfilled this, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the almsfood in my bowl would not be exhausted.” “Good, good, noble one, this is fitting for you.” This, to begin with, is the story concerning 'what has gone into the bowl is not exhausted'.

Ayameva pana thero cetiyapabbate giribhaṇḍamahāpūjāya dānaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “imasmiṃ dāne kiṃ varabhaṇḍa”nti pucchi. Dve sāṭakā, bhanteti. Ete mayhaṃ pāpuṇissantīti? Taṃ sutvā amacco rañño ārocesi – “eko daharo evaṃ vadatī”ti. “Daharassa evaṃ cittaṃ, mahātherānaṃ pana sukhumasāṭakā [M 3.0093] vaṭṭantī”ti vatvā “mahātherānaṃ dassāmī”ti ṭhapesi. Tassa bhikkhusaṅghe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhite dentassa matthake ṭhapitāpi te sāṭakā hatthaṃ nārohanti, aññeva ārohanti. Daharassa dānakāle pana hatthaṃ āruḷhā. So tassa hatthe ṭhapetvā amaccassa mukhaṃ oloketvā daharaṃ nisīdāpetvā dānaṃ datvā saṅghaṃ vissajjetvā daharassa santike nisīditvā “kadā, bhante, imaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijjhitthā”ti āha. So pariyāyenapi asantaṃ avadanto “natthi mayhaṃ, mahārāja, lokuttaradhammo”ti āha. Nanu, bhante, pubbeva avacutthāti. Āma, mahārāja, sāraṇīyadhammapūrako ahaṃ, tassa me dhammassa pūritakālato paṭṭhāya bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātīti. “Sādhu sādhu, bhante, anucchavikamidaṃ tumhāka”nti vatvā pakkāmi. Idaṃ bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṭṭhāne aggabhaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇātīti ettha vatthu.

Moreover, this same elder went to the donation site during the great offering of goods at Cetiyapabbata and asked, “What is the finest item in this donation?” When told, “Two cloths, venerable sir,” he stated, “These will come to me.” Hearing this, a minister reported to the king, “A young monk speaks thus.” The king, thinking, “Such is the mind of a young one, but fine cloths are fitting for the great elders,” set them aside for the great elders. When the monastic community stood in order and the king was giving, though those cloths were placed on top, they did not come to his hand; only other cloths did. But at the time of giving to the young monk, they ascended to his hand. The king, having placed them in his hand, looked at the minister's face, had the young monk sit down, gave the donation, dismissed the Saṅgha, and then sat near the young monk and asked, “Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?” Not wishing to speak even indirectly of what was not present, the monk replied, “Great king, I have no supramundane Dhamma.” “But, venerable sir, did you not say so before?” “Yes, great king. I am one who has fulfilled the principle of amiability. From the time that principle was fulfilled, in any place where goods are distributed, the finest item comes to me.” “Good, good, venerable sir, this is fitting for you,” the king said and departed. This is the story concerning 'in a place where goods are distributed, he obtains the finest item'.

Brāhmaṇatissabhaye pana bhātaragāmavāsino nāgattheriyā anārocetvāva palāyiṃsu. Therī paccūsasamaye “ativiya [P 3.0344] appanigghoso gāmo, upadhāretha tāvā”ti daharabhikkhuniyo āha. Tā gantvā sabbesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgamma theriyā ārocesuṃ. Sā sutvā “mā tumhe tesaṃ gatabhāvaṃ cintayittha, attano uddesaparipucchāyonisomanasikāresuyeva yogaṃ karothā”ti vatvā bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ [V 3.0096] pārupitvā attadvādasamā gāmadvāre nigrodharukkhamūle aṭṭhāsi. Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā dvādasannampi bhikkhunīnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ datvā, “ayye, aññattha mā gacchatha, niccaṃ idheva āgaccheyyāthā”ti āha. Theriyā pana kaniṭṭhabhātā nāgatthero nāma atthi. So “mahantaṃ bhayaṃ, na sakkā yāpetuṃ, paratīraṃ gamissāmī”ti attadvādasamova attano vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhanto “theriṃ disvā gamissāmī”ti bhātaragāmaṃ āgato. Therī “therā āgatā”ti sutvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ ayyā”ti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Sā “ajja ekadivasaṃ vihāreva vasitvā sve gamissathā”ti āha. Therā vihāraṃ agamiṃsu.

Now, due to the danger from the thief Brāhmaṇa Tissa, the residents of Bhātaragāma fled without informing the elder nun Nāgā. At dawn, the elder nun said to the young nuns, “The village is unusually quiet—first, go and investigate.” They went, discovered that everyone had fled, and came back and reported to the elder nun. Hearing this, she said, “Do not worry about their departure. Apply yourselves only to your own recitation, questioning, and wise attention.” Then, at the time for the almsround, she robed herself and, as one of twelve, stood at the village gate under a banyan tree. The deity dwelling in the tree gave almsfood to all twelve nuns and said, “Noble ladies, do not go elsewhere—always come here.” Now, the elder nun had a younger brother, the elder Nāga. He thought, “The danger is great; it is not possible to carry on here. I will go to the other shore.” As one of twelve, he left his dwelling place, thinking, “I will see the elder nun before I go,” and came to Bhātaragāma. Hearing that the elders had come, the elder nun went to them and asked, “What is it, venerable sirs?” He explained the situation. She said, “Stay in the monastery for one day today, and go tomorrow.” The elders went to the monastery.

Therī punadivase rukkhamūle piṇḍāya caritvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Thero “vaṭṭissati therī”ti vatvā tuṇhī aṭṭhāsi. Dhammiko, tāta, piṇḍapāto, kukkuccaṃ akatvā paribhuñjathāti[M 3.0094]. Vaṭṭissati therīti? Sā pattaṃ gahetvā ākāse khipi, patto ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Thero “sattatālamatte ṭhitampi bhikkhunībhattameva therī”ti vatvā “bhayaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ na hoti, bhaye vūpasante ariyavaṃsaṃ kathayamāno, ‘bho piṇḍapātika, bhikkhunībhattaṃ bhuñjitvā vītināmayitthā’ti cittena anuvadiyamāno santhambhituṃ na sakkhissāmi, appamattā hotha [P 3.0345] theriyo”ti maggaṃ paṭipajji.

The next day, the elder nun, having gone for alms at the foot of the tree, approached the elder and said, “Please partake of this almsfood.” The elder, asking, “Will this be proper, elder nun?” remained silent. “The almsfood is righteous, dear brother; partake of it without scruple.” “Will it be proper, elder nun?” She took the bowl and threw it into the air; the bowl remained suspended in the air. The elder said, “Even standing at a height of seven palm trees, it is still a nun's almsfood, elder nun. This danger will not last forever. When the danger has subsided, and I am speaking on the noble lineage, if I am reproached in my mind with the thought, ‘Oh, this alms-goer sustained himself by eating a nun's almsfood,’ I will not be able to remain composed. Be heedful, elder nuns,” and he set out on the path.

Rukkhadevatāpi “sace thero theriyā hatthato piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjissati, na taṃ nivattessāmi. Sace na paribhuñjissati, nivattessāmī”ti cintayamānā ṭhatvā therassa gamanaṃ disvā rukkhā oruyha “pattaṃ, bhante, dethā”ti vatvā pattaṃ gahetvā theraṃ rukkhamūlaṃyeva ānetvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā piṇḍapātaṃ datvā katabhattakiccaṃ paṭiññaṃ kāretvā dvādasa bhikkhuniyo dvādasa ca bhikkhū satta vassāni upaṭṭhahi. Idaṃ devatā ussukkaṃ āpajjantīti ettha vatthu. Tatra hi therī sāraṇīyadhammapūrikā ahosi.

The tree-deity also stood there thinking, “If the elder partakes of the almsfood from the elder nun's hand, I will not turn him back. If he does not partake, I will turn him back.” Seeing the elder's departure, she descended from the tree and said, “Venerable sir, give me the bowl.” Taking the bowl, she brought the elder back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, and gave him the almsfood. After he had finished his meal, she made him give a promise, and for seven years she attended upon the twelve nuns and the twelve monks. This is the story concerning 'deities take an interest'. Indeed, in that case, the elder nun was one who had fulfilled the qualities conducive to amiability.

Akhaṇḍānītiādīsu yassa sattasu āpattikkhandhesu ādimhi vā ante vā sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti, tassa sīlaṃ pariyante chinnasāṭako viya khaṇḍaṃ nāma. Yassa pana vemajjhe bhinnaṃ, tassa chiddasāṭako viya chiddaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa paṭipāṭiyā dve tīṇi bhinnāni, tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ vā kucchiyaṃ vā uṭṭhitena visabhāgavaṇṇena kāḷarattādīnaṃ aññataravaṇṇā gāvī viya sabalaṃ [V 3.0097] nāma hoti. Yassa antarantarā bhinnāni, tassa antarantarā visabhāgabinduvicitrā gāvī viya kammāsaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa pana sabbena sabbaṃ abhinnāni, tassa tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni nāma honti. Tāni panetāni taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissabhāvakaraṇato bhujissāni, buddhādīhi viññūhi pasatthattā viññuppasatthāni, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattā “idaṃ nāma tvaṃ āpannapubbo”ti kenaci parāmaṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ca aparāmaṭṭhāni, upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiṃ vā saṃvattayantīti samādhisaṃvattanikānīti vuccanti.

Regarding 'unbroken,' and so forth: For any monk whose training rule among the seven groups of offenses is broken at the beginning or at the end, his virtue is called 'broken,' like a cloth cut at the edge. For one whose training rule is broken in the middle, his virtue is called 'pierced,' like a cloth with a hole. For one for whom two or three training rules are broken in succession, his virtue is called 'spotted,' like a cow that has a dissimilar-colored mark of black, red, or the like, on its back or belly. For one for whom training rules are broken intermittently, his virtue is called 'mottled,' like a cow variegated with dissimilar spots. But for one whose training rules are entirely unbroken, those virtues are called 'unbroken,' 'unpierced,' 'unspotted,' and 'unmottled.' Furthermore, these virtues, because they liberate from the state of being a slave to craving and bring about a state of freedom, are called 'liberating.' Because they are praised by the wise, beginning with the Buddha, they are called 'praised by the wise.' Because they are not grasped by craving and views, and because it is impossible for anyone to wrongly assess them by saying, 'You have previously committed this offense,' they are called 'ungrasped.' And because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration, they are called 'conducive to concentration.'

Sīlasāmaññagato [M 3.0095][P 3.0346] viharatīti tesu tesu disābhāgesu viharantehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ samānabhāvūpagatasīlo viharati. Sotāpannādīnañhi sīlaṃ samuddantarepi devalokepi vasantānaṃ aññesaṃ sotāpannādīnaṃ sīlena samānameva hoti, natthi maggasīle nānattaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘He dwells having attained commonality in virtue’ means: he dwells having virtue that has reached a state of sameness with the monks dwelling in those various regions. Indeed, the virtue of stream-enterers and so forth is exactly the same as the virtue of other stream-enterers and so forth who dwell even in the middle of the ocean or in the deva world. There is no difference in the virtue of the path. This was said in reference to that.

Yāyaṃ diṭṭhīti maggasampayuttā sammādiṭṭhi. Ariyāti niddosā. Niyyātīti niyyānikā. Takkarassāti yo tathākārī hoti. Dukkhakkhayāyāti sabbadukkhakkhayatthaṃ. Diṭṭhisāmaññagatoti samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ upagato hutvā viharatīti.

‘This view’ means: right view associated with the path. ‘Noble’ means: faultless. ‘Leads out’ means: it is emancipating. ‘For one who acts accordingly’ means: for one who acts in that way. ‘For the destruction of suffering’ means: for the purpose of the destruction of all suffering. ‘Having attained commonality of view’ means: having reached a state of same view, he dwells.

2. Dutiyasāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on States of Conciliation

12. Dutiye yo te dhamme pūreti, taṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyaṃ karontīti piyakaraṇā. Garuṃ karontīti garukaraṇā. Saṅgahāyāti saṅgaṇhanatthāya. Avivādāyāti avivadanatthāya. Sāmaggiyāti samaggabhāvatthāya. Ekībhāvāyāti ekabhāvatthāya ninnānākaraṇāya. Saṃvattantīti vattanti pavattanti.

12. In the second sutta: Whichever monk fulfills those dhammas, they make him dear to his companions in the holy life; therefore, they are called 'endearing.' They make him respected; therefore, they are called 'respect-inspiring.' ‘For cohesion’ means for the purpose of mutual support. ‘For non-dispute’ means for the purpose of not causing disputes. ‘For harmony’ means for the purpose of a state of harmony. ‘For unification’ means for the purpose of a state of oneness, not for creating separateness. ‘They conduce to’ means they exist and they proceed.

3. Nissāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Nissāraṇīya Sutta

13. Tatiye nissāraṇīyā dhātuyoti nissaraṇadhātuyova. Mettā hi kho me cetovimuttīti ettha paccanīkadhammehi vimuttattā tikacatukkajjhānikā mettāva mettācetovimutti nāma[V 3.0098]. Bhāvitāti vaḍḍhitā. Bahulīkatāti punappunaṃ katā. Yānīkatāti yuttayānasadisā katā. Vatthukatāti [P 3.0347] patiṭṭhā katā. Anuṭṭhitāti adhiṭṭhitā. Paricitāti samantato citā ācitā upacitā. Susamāraddhāti suppaguṇakaraṇena suṭṭhu samāraddhā. Pariyādāya tiṭṭhatīti pariyādiyitvā gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Mā hevantissa vacanīyoti yasmā abhūtabyākaraṇaṃ byākaroti, tasmā “mā evaṃ bhaṇī”ti vattabbo. Yadidaṃ mettācetovimuttīti yā ayaṃ mettācetovimutti, idaṃ nissaraṇaṃ byāpādassa, byāpādato nissaṭāti attho. Yo pana mettāya tikacatukkajjhānato vuṭṭhito saṅkhāre sammasitvā tatiyamaggaṃ patvā “puna [M 3.0096] byāpādo natthī”ti tatiyaphalena nibbānaṃ passati, tassa cittaṃ accantanissaraṇaṃ byāpādassa. Etenupāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

13. In the third sutta, 'the elements of escape' are indeed the elements of liberation. Here, in the passage 'the liberation of mind through loving-kindness,' because it is liberated from opposing states, loving-kindness associated with the three-fold and four-fold jhānas is called 'the liberation of mind through loving-kindness.' 'Developed' means increased. 'Made much of' means done again and again. 'Made into a vehicle' means made similar to a vehicle yoked with a thoroughbred horse. 'Made a foundation' means made a basis. 'Steadfastly established' means resolved upon. 'Familiarized' means accumulated and built up from all around. 'Well undertaken' means well commenced by means of making it proficient. 'It remains, having encompassed' means it remains, having pervaded and grasped. 'He should not be spoken to thus' means: because he makes an untrue declaration, he should be told, "Do not speak thus." 'That is, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness' means: whatever this liberation of mind through loving-kindness is, this is the escape from ill will; the meaning is that one has escaped from ill will. As for the one who, having arisen from the three-fold or four-fold jhāna on loving-kindness, contemplates the formations, attains the third path, and sees Nibbāna with the third fruit, thinking, "There is no more ill will," for him, that mind is the utter escape from ill will. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Animittācetovimuttīti balavavipassanā. Dīghabhāṇakā pana arahattaphalasamāpattīti vadanti. Sā hi rāganimittādīnañceva rūpanimittādīnañca niccanimittādīnañca abhāvā animittāti vuttā. Nimittānusārīti vuttappabhedaṃ nimittaṃ anusaraṇasabhāvaṃ.

'The signless liberation of mind' is powerful insight. The reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya, however, say it is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, it is called 'signless' because of the absence of the sign of lust and so on, the sign of form and so on, and the sign of permanence and so on. 'Following after the sign' means having the nature of following after the sign with the distinctions mentioned.

Asmīti asmimāno. Ayamahamasmīti pañcasu khandhesu ayaṃ nāma ahaṃ asmīti. Ettāvatā arahattaṃ byākataṃ hoti. Vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallanti vicikicchābhūtaṃ kathaṃkathāsallaṃ. Mā hevantissa vacanīyoti sace te paṭhamamaggavajjhā vicikicchā uppajjati, arahattabyākaraṇaṃ micchā hoti, tasmā “mā abhūtaṃ gaṇhī”ti vāretabbo. Asmīti [P 3.0348] mānasamugghātoti arahattamaggo. Arahattamaggaphalavasena hi nibbāne diṭṭhe puna asmimāno natthīti arahattamaggo “asmīti mānasamugghāto”ti vutto. Iti imasmiṃ sutte abhūtabyākaraṇaṃ nāma kathitaṃ.

'I am' is the conceit 'I am.' 'I am this' means: 'This being here in the five aggregates, I am.' By this much, Arahantship is declared. 'The dart of doubt, of "how? how?"' is the dart of questioning which is doubt. 'He should not be spoken to thus' means: if for you doubt—which is to be cut off by the first path—should arise, the declaration of Arahantship is mistaken. Therefore, he should be prevented, with the words, "Do not take up what is not real." 'The uprooting of the conceit "I am"' is the path of Arahantship. For when Nibbāna is seen by the power of the fruit of the path of Arahantship, there is again no conceit 'I am'; therefore, the path of Arahantship is called 'the uprooting of the conceit "I am".' Thus, in this sutta, what is called an untrue declaration has been taught.

4. Bhaddakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bhaddaka Sutta

14. Catutthe na bhaddakanti na laddhakaṃ. Tattha yo hi bhītabhīto marati, tassa na bhaddakaṃ maraṇaṃ hoti. Yo apāye paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhāti, tassa na bhaddikā kālakiriyā hoti. Kammārāmotiādīsu āramaṇaṃ ārāmo, abhiratīti attho. Vihārakaraṇādimhi navakamme ārāmo assāti kammārāmo. Tasmiṃyeva kamme ratoti kammarato. Tadeva kammārāmataṃ punappunaṃ yuttoti [V 3.0099] anuyutto. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ettha ca bhassanti ālāpasallāpo. Niddāti soppaṃ. Saṅgaṇikāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikā. Sā “ekassa dutiyo hoti, dvinnaṃ hoti tatiyako”tiādinā nayena veditabbā. Saṃsaggoti dassanasavanasamullāpasambhogakāyasaṃsaggavasena pavatto saṃsaṭṭhabhāvo. Papañcoti taṇhādiṭṭhimānavasena pavatto madanākārasaṇṭhito kilesapapañco. Sakkāyanti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyāti hetunā nayena sakalavaṭṭadukkhassa parivaṭumaparicchedakaraṇatthaṃ. Magoti magasadiso. Nippapañcapadeti nibbānapade. Ārādhayīti paripūrayi taṃ sampādesīti.

14. In the fourth sutta, `na bhaddakaṃ` means not good. Therein, for one who dies terrified, their death is not good. For one who takes rebirth in a plane of misery, their passing away is not a good death. In `kammārāmo` and so forth, `āramaṇaṃ`, `ārāmo`, and `abhirati` mean delight; this is the meaning. One who has delight in new work, such as constructing a monastery, is a `kammārāmo`. One who delights in that very work is a `kammarato`. One who is repeatedly engaged in that very delight in work is an `anuyutto`. This method should be understood for all terms. And here, `bhassaṃ` means initial talk and repeated talk. `Niddā` means sleeping. `Saṅgaṇikā` means delighting in company. This should be understood by the method of: 'for one there is a second; for two there is a third,' and so on. `Saṃsaggo` is the state of being associated that occurs by way of association through seeing, hearing, conversing together, using things in common, and bodily contact. `Papañco` is the defilement-proliferation which occurs by way of craving, views, and conceit, and is established in the manner of intoxication. `Sakkāyaṃ` is the cycle of the three planes. `Sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā` (for the right ending of suffering) means for the purpose of making a boundary known as the end to all the suffering of the cycle, by a proper cause and method. `Mago` means like a deer. `Nippapañcapade` means in the state of Nibbāna. `Ārādhayi` means fulfilled it, accomplished it.

5. Anutappiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Anutappiya Sutta

15. Pañcame [M 3.0097][P 3.0349] anutappāti anusocitabbā anutāpakārī. Imesu dvīsupi suttesu gāthāsu ca vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

15. In the fifth sutta, `anutappā` means one who is to be grieved over, one who causes remorse. In both these suttas and in the verses, the cycle and the ending of the cycle have been taught.

6. Nakulapitusuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe bāḷhagilānoti adhimattagilāno. Etadavocāti sāmikassa bhesajjaṃ katvā byādhiṃ vūpasametuṃ asakkontī idāni sīhanādaṃ naditvā saccakiriyāya byādhiṃ vūpasametuṃ santike nisīditvā etaṃ “mā kho tva”ntiādivacanaṃ avoca. Sāpekkhoti sataṇho. Na nakulamātāti ettha na-kāro na sakkhatīti evaṃ parapadena yojetabbo. Santharitunti nicchiddaṃ kātuṃ, saṇṭhapetunti attho. Veṇiṃ olikhitunti eḷakalomāni kappetvā vijaṭetvā veṇiṃ kātuṃ.

16. In the sixth sutta, `bāḷhagilāno` means exceedingly ill. `Etadavoca` means: being unable to pacify the illness by preparing medicine for her husband, she now uttered a bold speech like a lion's roar and, sitting near him, spoke the words beginning with `mā kho tvaṃ` in order to pacify the illness by an act of truth. `Sāpekho` means with craving. In `na nakulamātā`, the letter `na` should be connected with the following word, as in `na sakkhi` (was not able). `Santharituṃ` means to make it without a hole, to establish it; this is the meaning. `Veṇiṃ olikhituṃ` means to prepare and arrange sheep's wool, to clean it, and to make a braid.

Aññaṃ gharaṃ gamissatīti aññaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhissati. Soḷasa vassāni gahaṭṭhakaṃ brahmacariyaṃ samāciṇṇanti ito soḷasavassamatthake gahaṭṭhabrahmacariyavāso samāciṇṇo. Dassanakāmatarāti atirekena dassanakāmā. Imehi tīhi aṅgehi sīhanādaṃ naditvā “iminā saccena tava sarīre byādhi phāsu hotū”ti saccakiriyaṃ akāsi.

`Aññaṃ gharaṃ gamissati` means she will take another husband. `Soḷasa vassāni gahaṭṭhakaṃ brahmacariyaṃ samāciṇṇaṃ` means that for sixteen years, the noble life of a householder has been well practiced. `Dassanakāmatarā` means exceedingly desirous of seeing. With these three factors, having uttered a lion's roar, she performed an act of truth, saying, 'By this truth, may the illness in your body be eased!'

Idāni bhagavantaṃ sakkhiṃ katvā attano sīlādiguṇehipi saccakiriyaṃ kātuṃ siyā kho [V 3.0100] pana tetiādimāha. Tattha paripūrakārinīti samattakārinī. Cetosamathassāti samādhikammaṭṭhānassa. Ogādhappattāti ogādhaṃ anuppavesaṃ pattā. Patigādhappattāti [P 3.0350] patigādhaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ pattā. Assāsappattāti assāsaṃ avassayaṃ pattā. Vesārajjappattāti somanassañāṇaṃ pattā. Aparappaccayāti parappaccayo vuccati parasaddhā parapattiyāyanā, tāya virahitāti attho. Imehi tīhi aṅgehi attano guṇe ārabbha saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Gilānā vuṭṭhitoti gilāno hutvā vuṭṭhito. Yāvatāti yattikāyo. Tāsaṃ aññatarāti tāsaṃ antare ekā. Anukampikāti hitānukampikā. Ovādikāti ovādadāyikā. Anusāsikāti anusiṭṭhidāyikā.

Now, having made the Blessed One a witness, in order to perform an act of truth by means of her own virtues such as morality, she spoke the words beginning with `siyā kho pana te`. Therein, `paripūrakārinī` means one who is accustomed to making things complete. `Cetosamathassa` means of the meditation subject of serenity. `Ogādhappattā` means having reached the state of entering. `Patigādhappattā` means having reached establishment. `Assāsappattā` means having reached relief, a state of reliance. `Vesārajjappattā` means having attained knowledge associated with joy. `Aparappaccayā`: faith caused by another is called `parappaccayo`; the meaning is being devoid of that faith which is `parapattiyāyanā` (going by another's report). With these three factors, taking her own virtues such as morality and concentration as object, she performed an act of truth. `Gilānā vuṭṭhito` means having been ill, he arose. `Yāvatā` means however many. `Tāsaṃ aññatarā` means one among them. `Anukampikā` means one who compassionately looks after one's welfare. `Ovādikā` means one who gives exhortation. `Anusāsikā` means one who gives instruction.

7. Soppasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Soppa Sutta

17. Sattame [M 3.0098] paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ekībhāvāya dhammanijjhānakkhantito phalasamāpattivihārato vuṭṭhito. Yathāvihāranti attano attano vasanavihāraṃ. Navāti pabbajjāya navakā. Te pañcasatamattā ahesuṃ. Kākacchamānāti kākasaddaṃ karontā dante khādantā. Therāti thirabhāvaṃ pattā. Tena noti tena nu. Seyyasukhādīni heṭṭhā vuttatthāneva. Raṭṭhikoti yo raṭṭhaṃ bhuñjati. Pettaṇikoti yo pitarā bhuttānubhuttaṃ bhuñjati. Senāpatikoti senāya jeṭṭhako. Gāmagāmaṇikoti gāmabhojako. Pūgagāmaṇikoti gaṇajeṭṭhako. Avipassako [P 3.0351] kusalānaṃ dhammānanti kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anesako agavesako hutvā. Bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānanti sattatiṃsāya bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ.

17. In the seventh sutta, 'emerged from seclusion' (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito) means: having arisen from the abiding in the attainment of fruition, from the delight in reflecting on the Dhamma in solitude. 'According to their dwelling' (yathāvihāraṃ) means: to their own respective dwelling. 'New' (navā) means: new by way of ordination. They were five hundred in number. 'Making a cawing sound' (kākacchamānā) means: making a sound like a crow's caw while gnashing their teeth. 'Elders' (therā) means: those who have attained the state of an elder. 'Tena no' means: tena nu. 'The bliss of sleep, etc.' (seyyasukhādīni) has the meaning as stated below. 'A provincial governor' (raṭṭhiko) means: he who enjoys the country. 'An inheritor' (pettaṇiko) means: he who enjoys what was enjoyed and repeatedly enjoyed by his father. 'A commander' (senāpatiko) means: the chief of the army. 'A village headman' (gāmagāmaṇiko) means: one who enjoys a village. 'A guild leader' (pūgagāmaṇiko) means: the chief of a group. 'Not a seer of wholesome states' (avipassako kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ) means: being one who does not seek or search for wholesome states. 'Of the states belonging to enlightenment' (bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ) means: of the thirty-seven states belonging to enlightenment.

8. Macchabandhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Macchabandha Sutta

18. Aṭṭhame macchikanti macchaghātakaṃ. Hatthinā yātīti hatthiyāyī. Paratopi eseva nayo. Vajjheti vadhitabbe. Vadhāyanīteti vadhāya upanīte. Pāpakena manasāti lāmakena vadhakacittena. Pāḷiyaṃ pana vadhāyupanīteti likhanti. Māgavikoti migaghātako. Ko pana vādo manussabhūtanti yo manussabhūtaṃ pāpakena manasā anupekkhati, tassa sampattiyā abhāve kimeva vattabbaṃ. Idaṃ pāpakassa kammuno aniṭṭhaphalabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yesaṃ pana tādisaṃ kammaṃ karontānampi yasapaṭilābho hoti, tesaṃ taṃ akusalaṃ nissāya kusalaṃ vipaccatīti veditabbaṃ[V 3.0101]. Tena panassa akusalakammena upahatattā vipāko na ciraṭṭhitiko hoti. Imasmiṃ sutte akusalapakkhova kathito.

18. In the eighth sutta, 'a fisherman' (macchikaṃ) means: a fish-killer. 'He who goes by elephant' (hatthinā yāti) is a `hatthiyāyī`. In the later words also, this is the method. 'To be killed' (vajjhe) means: those who are to be killed. 'Brought for killing' (vadhāyanīte) means: brought for the purpose of killing. 'With a base mind' (pāpakena manasā) means: with a base, killing mind. But in the Pāḷi text, they write 'vadhāyūpanīto'. 'A hunter' (māgaviko) means: a deer-killer. 'What then is to be said of one who is a human being?' (ko pana vādo manussabhūtaṃ) means: for one who regards a human being with a base mind, what is to be said in the absence of their success? This was said to show the state of having an undesirable result from a base action. However, for those who, even while doing such an action, obtain renown, it should be known thus: for them, a wholesome action ripens depending on that unwholesome action. But for that person, because of being oppressed by that unwholesome action, its result is not long-lasting. In this sutta, only the unwholesome side was taught.

9. Paṭhamamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

19. Navame nātiketi evaṃnāmake gāme. Giñjakāvasatheti iṭṭhakāmaye pāsāde. Amatogadhāti nibbānogadhā, nibbānapatiṭṭhāti attho. Bhāvetha noti bhāvetha nu. Maraṇassatinti maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ. Aho vatāti patthanatthe nipāto. Bahuṃ [P 3.0352] vata me kataṃ assāti [M 3.0099] tumhākaṃ sāsane mama kiccaṃ bahu kataṃ assa. Tadantaranti taṃ antaraṃ khaṇaṃ okāsaṃ. Assasitvā vā passasāmīti ettha assāso vuccati anto pavisanavāto, passāso bahi nikkhamanavāto. Iti ayaṃ bhikkhu yāva anto paviṭṭhavāto bahi nikkhamati, bahi nikkhanto vāto anto pavisati, tāva jīvitaṃ patthento evamāha. Dandhanti mandaṃ garukaṃ asīghappavattaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayāyāti arahattaphalatthāya. Imasmiṃ sutte maraṇassati arahattaṃ pāpetvā kathitāti.

19. In the ninth sutta, 'at Nātika' (nātike) means: in a village of that name. 'In the brick hall' (giñjakāvasathe) means: in a mansion made of brick. 'Immersed in the deathless' (amatogadhā) means: immersed in Nibbāna, established in Nibbāna—this is the meaning. 'Do you develop?' (bhāvetha no) means: bhāvetha nu. 'Mindfulness of death' (maraṇassatiṃ) means: the meditation subject of mindfulness of death. 'Aho vata' is a particle that occurs in the sense of longing. 'Oh, may much have been done by me!' (bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assā) means: may much of my duty, which is for my own welfare, have been done in your dispensation. 'In that interval' (tadantaraṃ) means: that interval, moment, or opportunity. 'Having breathed in or I shall breathe out' (assasitvā vā passasāmi): here, 'in-breath' (assāso) is said to be the in-going breath; 'out-breath' (passāso) is said to be the out-going breath. Thus this monk, desiring life for as long as the in-breath goes out and the out-breath comes in, spoke thus. 'Slowly' (dandhaṃ) means: gently, heavily, not proceeding swiftly. 'For the destruction of the taints' (āsavānaṃ khayāya) means: for the sake of the fruit of arahantship. In this sutta, mindfulness of death is taught as having been made to lead to arahantship.

10. Dutiyamaraṇassatisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

20. Dasame patigatāyāti paṭipannāya. Iti paṭisañcikkhatīti evaṃ paccavekkhati. So mamassa antarāyoti ettha tividho antarāyo jīvitantarāyo, samaṇadhammantarāyo, puthujjanakālakiriyaṃ karontassa saggantarāyo ceva maggantarāyo cāti. Taṃ sabbampi sandhāyevamāha. Byāpajjeyyāti ajiṇṇakādivasena vipajjeyya. Adhimattoti balavā. Chandoti kattukamyatāchando. Vāyāmoti payogavīriyaṃ. Ussāhoti ussāpanavīriyaṃ. Ussoḷhīti sampādanavīriyaṃ. Appaṭivānīti anukkaṇṭhanā appaṭisaṅgharaṇā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

20. In the tenth sutta, 'patigatāya' means having arrived. 'Iti paṭisañcikkhati' means he considers in this way. Herein, 'so mamassa antarāyo' refers to a threefold obstacle: an obstacle to life, an obstacle to the practice of a recluse, and for one who dies the death of an ordinary person, an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the path. Referring to all this, he spoke thus. 'Byāpajjeyya' means may one perish by way of indigestion and so on. 'Adhimatto' means strong. 'Chando' means the desire to act. 'Vāyāmo' means the energy of application. 'Ussāho' means the energy of exertion. 'Ussoḷhī' means the energy of accomplishment. 'Appaṭivānī' means not cutting short, not holding back. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Sāraṇīyavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on Conduciveness to Amity.

3. Anuttariyavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Unsurpassed

1-2. Sāmakasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Sāmaka Sutta, etc.

21-22. Tatiyassa [V 3.0102][P 3.0353] paṭhame sāmagāmaketi sāmakānaṃ ussannattā evaṃladdhanāme gāmake. Pokkharaṇiyāyanti pokkharaṇiyānāmake vihāre. Abhikkantāya rattiyāti rattiyā paṭhamayāmaṃ atikkamma majjhimayāme sampatte. Abhikkantavaṇṇāti abhikkantaatimanāpavaṇṇā. Kevalakappanti sakalakappaṃ. Pokkharaṇiyaṃ obhāsetvāti pokkharaṇiyānāmakaṃ mahāvihāraṃ attano obhāsena pharitvā. Samanuññoti samānaanuñño samānacitto. Dovacassatāti dubbacabhāvo. Pāpamittatāti lāmakamittatā[M 3.0100]. Imasmiṃ sutte parihāniyadhammāva kathitā. Dutiye aparihāniyadhammā lokuttaramissakā kathitā.

21-22. In the first of the third, 'Sāmagāmake' means in the small village that obtained its name thus because of the abundance of Sāmāka grain. 'Pokkharaṇiyāyaṃ' means in the monastery named Pokkharaṇiyā. 'When the night was advanced' (abhikkantāya rattiyā) means when, having passed the first watch of the night, the middle watch was reached. 'Abhikkantavaṇṇā' means having a surpassing and very pleasing complexion. 'Kevalakappaṃ' means the entire.
