Tassa na evaṃ hoti atthi me seyyoti vātiādīhi seyyassa seyyohamasmīti mānādayo tayo mānā paṭikkhittā. Na hi khīṇāsavassa “atthi mayhaṃ seyyo, atthi sadiso, atthi hīno”ti māno hoti. Natthi me seyyotiādīhipi teyeva [M 3.0118] paṭikkhittā. Na hi khīṇāsavassa “ahameva seyyo, ahaṃ sadiso, ahaṃ hīno, aññe seyyādayo natthī”ti evaṃ māno hoti.

49. In the seventh, vusitavā means one who has completed the living of the holy life. Katakaraṇīyo means one who, having done what was to be done by means of the four paths, is established. Ohitabhāro means one who, having put down the burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, and the burden of formations, is established. Anuppattasadattho means: sadattho (one's own goal) is said to be Arahantship; he has attained it—this is the meaning. Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano means one whose fetter of existence is destroyed. Sammadaññāvimutto means liberated by knowing rightly with reason and cause. For such a one, it does not occur "There is one better than me," and so on. By this, the three conceits, beginning with "I am superior to the superior," are rejected. Indeed, for one whose cankers are destroyed, the conceit "There is one superior to me, there is one equal, there is one inferior" does not occur. By "There is none superior to me," and so on, those very same conceits are rejected. Indeed, for one whose cankers are destroyed, the conceit "I alone am superior, I am equal, I am inferior; there are no others who are superior, and so on" does not occur.

Acirapakkantesūti [P 3.0381] arahattaṃ byākaritvā aciraṃyeva pakkantesu. Aññaṃ byākarontīti arahattaṃ kathenti. Hasamānakā maññe aññaṃ byākarontīti hasamānā viya kathenti. Vighātaṃ āpajjantīti dukkhaṃ āpajjanti.

Acirapakkantesu means: when they had departed not long after having declared Arahantship. Aññaṃ byākaronti means: they speak of Arahantship. Hasamānakā maññe aññaṃ byākaronti means: they speak as if laughing. Vighātaṃ āpajjanti means: they come to suffering.

Na ussesu na omesu, samatte nopanīyareti ettha ussāti ussitatā seyyapuggalā. Omāti hīnā. Samattoti sadiso. Iti imesu tīsupi seyyahīnasadisesu khīṇāsavā mānena na upanīyare, na upanenti, na upagacchantīti attho. Khīṇā jātīti khīṇā tesaṃ jāti. Vusitaṃ brahmacariyanti vutthaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Caranti saṃyojanavippamuttāti sabbasaṃyojanehi vimuttā hutvā caranti. Suttepi gāthāyampi khīṇāsavo kathito.

In the passage Na ussesu na omesu, samatte nopanīyare, ussā means exalted, superior persons. Omā means inferior persons. Samatto means an equal person. Thus, in regard to these three—the superior, inferior, and equal—the one whose cankers are destroyed is not led by conceit, does not bring himself near, does not approach; this is the meaning. Khīṇā jāti means: their birth is destroyed. Vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ means: the holy life of the path has been lived. Caranti saṃyojanavippamuttā means: having become liberated from all fetters, they fare on. The one whose cankers are destroyed is spoken of in both the sutta and the gāthā.

8. Indriyasaṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Restraint of the Senses

50. Aṭṭhame hatūpanisaṃ hotīti hatūpanissayaṃ hoti. Sīlavipannassāti vipannasīlassa. Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti taruṇavipassanāñāṇaṃ. Nibbidāvirāgoti ettha nibbidā balavavipassanā, virāgo ariyamaggo. Vimuttiñāṇadassananti ettha vimuttīti arahattaphalaṃ, ñāṇadassananti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Upanissayasampannaṃ hotīti sampannaupanissayaṃ hoti. Imasmiṃ sutte sīlānurakkhaṇaindriyasaṃvaro kathito.

50. In the eighth discourse, hatūpanisaṃ hoti means it has its strong cause destroyed. Sīlavipannassa means for one whose virtue is corrupted. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ is tender insight-knowledge. In nibbidā virāgo, nibbidā is strong insight; virāgo is the Noble Path. In vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ, vimuttiṃ is the fruit of Arahantship; ñāṇadassanaṃ is reviewing knowledge. Upanissayasampannaṃ hoti means it has a complete, strong cause. In this discourse, the restraint of the senses which protects virtue is taught.

9. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

51. Navame [V 3.0121] kittāvatāti kittakena. Assutañcevāti aññasmiṃ kāle assutapubbaṃ. Na sammosaṃ gacchantīti vināsaṃ na gacchanti. Cetaso samphuṭṭhapubbāti cittena phusitapubbā. Samudācarantīti [P 3.0382] manodvāre caranti. Aviññātañca vijānātīti aññasmiṃ kāle aviññātakāraṇaṃ jānāti. Pariyāpuṇātīti vaḷañjeti katheti. Desetīti pakāseti. Paraṃ vācetīti paraṃ uggaṇhāpeti.

51. In the ninth discourse, kittāvatā means by what measure. Assutañceva means not heard before at another time. Na sammosaṃ gacchanti means they do not go to destruction. Cetaso samphuṭṭhapubbā means previously reached by the mind. Samudācaranti means they occur at the mind-door. Aviññātañca vijānāti means at another time, one knows a cause that was not known. Pariyāpuṇāti means one masters and speaks of it. Deseti means one makes it clear. Paraṃ vāceti means one causes another to learn.

Āgatāgamāti [M 3.0119] dīghādīsu yo koci āgamo āgato etesanti āgatāgamā. Dhammadharāti suttantapiṭakadharā. Vinayadharāti vinayapiṭakadharā. Mātikādharāti dvepātimokkhadharā. Paripucchatīti anusandhipubbāparaṃ pucchati. Paripañhatīti idañcidañca pucchissāmīti paritulati paricchindati. Idaṃ, bhante, kathanti, bhante, idaṃ anusandhipubbāparaṃ kathaṃ hotīti pucchati. Imassa kvatthoti imassa bhāsitassa ko atthoti pucchati. Avivaṭanti avivaritaṃ. Vivarantīti pākaṭaṃ karonti. Kaṅkhāṭhāniyesūti kaṅkhāya kāraṇabhūtesu. Tattha yasmiṃ dhamme kaṅkhā uppajjati, sveva kaṅkhāṭhāniyo nāmāti veditabbo.

Āgatāgamā means: for them, there is some oral tradition that has come down from the Dīgha Nikāya and so on; therefore, they are called āgatāgama. Dhammadharā means bearers of the Suttanta Piṭaka. Vinayadharā means bearers of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Mātikādharā means bearers of the two Pātimokkhas. Paripucchati means one asks about the before and after of the connection. Paripañhati means, thinking, 'I will ask about this meaning and that meaning,' one weighs and delimits. Idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ means one asks, 'Venerable sir, how is this before and after of the connection?' Imassa ko attho means one asks, 'What is the meaning of this spoken text?' Avivaṭaṃ means that which has not been investigated by wisdom. Vivarantī means they make it manifest. Kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu means in things that have become a cause for doubt. Therein, it should be known thus: whatever teaching doubt arises in, that very teaching is called a cause of doubt.

10. Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

52. Dasame bhogādhippāyāti bhogasaṃharaṇatthaṃ ṭhapitādhippāyā pavattaajjhāsayā. Paññūpavicārāti paññavanto bhaveyyāmāti evaṃ paññatthāya pavattūpavicārā. Ayameva nesaṃ vicāro citte upavicarati. Balādhiṭṭhānāti [P 3.0383] balakāyādhiṭṭhānā. Balakāyañhi laddhā te laddhapatiṭṭhā nāma honti. Pathavibhinivesāti pathavisāmino bhavissāmāti evaṃ pathaviatthāya katacittābhinivesā. Issariyapariyosānāti rajjābhisekapariyosānā. Abhisekañhi patvā te pariyosānappattā nāma honti. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

52. In the tenth discourse, `bhogādhippāyā` means: they have an intention established for the purpose of accumulating possessions, an existing inclination. `Paññūpavicārā` means: they have an existing investigation for the sake of wisdom, thinking, 'May we become wise.' This very investigation arises close to their minds. `Balādhiṭṭhānā` means: they have the host of troops as their foundation. Indeed, having obtained the host of troops, they are called 'those who have gained a foundation.' `Pathavibhinivesā` means: they have a mental adherence made for the sake of the earth, thinking, 'We shall become lords of the earth.' `Issariyapariyosānā` means: they have the royal consecration as their culmination. Indeed, having reached the consecration, they are called 'those who have reached the culmination.' In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Sesapadesu panettha ayamadhippāyo – brāhmaṇā tāva mante labhitvā laddhapatiṭṭhā nāma honti, gahapatikā yaṃkiñci sippaṃ, itthī kuladāyajjasāmikaṃ puttaṃ, corā yaṃkiñci āvudhasatthaṃ[V 3.0122], samaṇā sīlaparipuṇṇā laddhapatiṭṭhā nāma honti. Tasmā mantādhiṭṭhānātiādīni vuttāni.

Furthermore, in the remaining terms here, this is the intention: Firstly, brahmins, having obtained the Vedas, are called 'those who have gained a foundation'; householders, having obtained some craft; a woman, having obtained a son who is the master of the clan's inheritance; thieves, having obtained some life-taking weapon; and ascetics, being complete in virtue, are called 'those who have gained a foundation.' Therefore, such things as 'establishment in the Vedas' and so on were spoken by the Blessed One.

Brāhmaṇānañca “yaññaṃ yajissāmā”ti cittaṃ abhinivisati, brahmaloke patte pariyosānappattā nāma honti. Tasmā te yaññābhinivesā brahmalokapariyosānāti vuttā. Kammantakaraṇatthāya mano etesaṃ abhinivisatīti kammantābhinivesā. Kamme niṭṭhite pariyosānappattā nāma hontīti niṭṭhitakammantapariyosānā.

And for brahmins, the mind adheres to the thought, 'We shall perform a sacrifice'; having reached the Brahma-world, they are called 'those who have reached the culmination.' Therefore, they are spoken of as 'those with adherence to sacrifice, with the Brahma-world as their culmination.' Their mind adheres for the purpose of doing work; therefore, they are 'those with adherence to work.' When the work is finished, they are called 'those who have reached the culmination'; therefore, they are 'those with finished work as their culmination.'

Purisādhippāyāti purisesu pavattaajjhāsayā. Alaṅkāratthāya mano upavicarati etissāti alaṅkārūpavicārā. Asapattī hutvā ekikāva [M 3.0120] ghare vaseyyanti evamassā cittaṃ abhinivisatīti asapattībhinivesā. Gharāvāsissariye laddhe pariyosānappattā nāma hontīti issariyapariyosānā.

‘Having men as her intention’ means she has an inclination that has arisen towards men. ‘Occupied with adornment’ means her mind is occupied for the purpose of adornment. Her mind adheres thus: 'Being without a co-wife, may I live alone in the house'; therefore, she is one with ‘adherence to being without a co-wife.’ Having obtained mastery in the household life, she is called 'one who has reached the culmination'; therefore, she is one with ‘mastery as her culmination.’

Parabhaṇḍassa [P 3.0384] ādāne adhippāyo etesanti ādānādhippāyā. Gahane nilīyanaṭṭhāne etesaṃ mano upavicaratīti gahanūpavicārā. Andhakāratthāya etesaṃ cittaṃ abhinivisatīti andhakārābhinivesā. Adassanappattā pariyosānappattā hontīti adassanapariyosānā.

‘Having taking as their intention’ means they have an intention to take another's property. ‘Occupied with the thicket’ means their mind is occupied in a thicket, a hiding place. ‘Adherence to darkness’ means their mind adheres for the purpose of darkness. Having reached a state of not being seen, they are called 'those who have reached the culmination'; therefore, they are ‘those with not being seen as their culmination.’

Adhivāsanakkhantiyañca sucibhāvasīle ca adhippāyo etesanti khantisoraccādhippāyā. Akiñcanabhāve niggahaṇabhāve cittaṃ etesaṃ abhinivisatīti ākiñcaññābhinivesā. Nibbānappattā pariyosānappattā hontīti nibbānapariyosānā.

‘Having patience and gentleness as their intention’ means they have an intention for enduring patience and for virtue which is the state of purity. ‘Adherence to nothingness’ means their mind adheres to the state of being without possessions and the state of being without oppression. Having reached Nibbāna, they are called 'those who have reached the culmination'; therefore, they are ‘those with Nibbāna as their culmination.’

11. Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Appamāda Sutta

53. Ekādasame samadhiggayhāti suṭṭhu gaṇhitvā. Jaṅgalānaṃ pāṇānanti pathavītalacārīnaṃ sapādakapāṇānaṃ. Padajātānīti padāni. Samodhānaṃ gacchantīti odhānaṃ upanikkhepaṃ gacchanti. Aggamakkhāyatīti seṭṭhaṃ akkhāyati. Pabbajalāyakoti pabbajatiṇacchedako. Odhunātīti heṭṭhā mukhaṃ dhunāti. Nidhunātīti ubhohi passehi dhunāti. Nicchādetīti bāhāya vā paharati, rukkhe vā paharati. Ambapiṇḍiyāti ambaphalapiṇḍiyā. Vaṇṭūpanibandhanānīti [P 3.0385] vaṇṭe upanibandhanāni[V 3.0123], vaṇṭe vā patiṭṭhitāni. Tadanvayāni bhavantīti vaṇṭānuvattakāni bhavanti, ambapiṇḍidaṇḍakānuvattakāni bhavantītipi attho. Khuddarājānoti khuddakarājāno, pakatirājāno vā.

53. In the eleventh sutta, 'having encompassed' means having grasped well. 'Of jungle creatures' means of creatures with feet that move on the surface of the earth. 'Kinds of footprints' means footprints. 'They come to a convergence' means they go to a collection, they are included. 'Is called the chief' means it is said to be the best. 'A reaper of grass' means a cutter of grass. 'He shakes down' means he shakes it facing downwards. 'He shakes thoroughly' means he shakes it on both sides. 'He strips' means he strikes it with his arm or strikes it on a tree. 'A cluster of mangoes' means a cluster of mango fruit. 'Bound to the stalk' means bound on the stem, or established on the stem. 'They follow it' means they follow the stem; the meaning can also be taken as they follow the stalk of the mango cluster. 'Minor kings' means petty kings, or ordinary kings.

12. Dhammikasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta

54. Dvādasame sabbasoti sabbesu. Sattasu vihāresūti sattasu pariveṇesu. Paribhāsatīti paribhavati bhayaṃ upadaṃseti. Vihiṃsatīti viheṭheti. Vitudatīti vijjhati. Roseti vācāyāti vācāya ghaṭṭeti. Pakkamantīti disā pakkamanti. Na saṇṭhahantīti nappatiṭṭhahanti. Riñcantīti [M 3.0121] chaḍḍenti vissajjenti. Pabbājeyyāmāti nīhareyyāma. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Alanti yuttametaṃ, yaṃ taṃ pabbājeyyunti attho. Kiṃ te imināti kiṃ tava iminā jātibhūmiyaṃ vāsena. Tīradassiṃ sakuṇanti disākākaṃ. Muñcantīti disādassanatthaṃ vissajjenti. Sāmantāti avidūre. Samantātipi pāṭho, samantatoti attho. Abhinivesoti pattharitvā ṭhitasākhānaṃ niveso. Mūlasantānakānanti mūlānaṃ niveso.

54. In the twelfth sutta, 'in all' means in all. 'In the seven residences' means in the seven monastic compounds. 'He reproaches' means he oppresses, he shows danger. 'He harms' means he harasses. 'He pierces' means he stabs. 'He angers with speech' means he provokes with speech. 'They depart' means they depart to the various directions. 'They do not stand' means they are not established. 'They abandon' means they give up, they release. 'We should banish' means we should expel. The word 'handa' is a particle that occurs in the sense of determination. 'Enough' means it is proper that they should banish him; this is the meaning. 'What is this to you?' means what benefit is there for you from this dwelling in your land of birth? 'A shore-seeing bird' means a direction-crow. 'They release' means they release it for the purpose of seeing the direction. 'Nearby' means not far. 'Samantā' is also a reading; the meaning is 'from all around'. 'Settling' means the settling-place of branches that stand having spread out. 'Of the root-lineage' means the settling-place of the roots.

Āḷhakathālikāti taṇḍulāḷhakassa bhattapacanathālikā. Khuddaṃ madhunti khuddamakkhikāhi kataṃ daṇḍakamadhuṃ. Anelakanti [P 3.0386] niddosaṃ. Na ca sudaṃ aññamaññassa phalāni hiṃsantīti aññamaññassa koṭṭhāse phalāni na hiṃsanti. Attano koṭṭhāsehi mūlaṃ vā tacaṃ vā pattaṃ vā chindanto nāma natthi, attano attano sākhāya heṭṭhā patitāneva paribhuñjanti. Aññassa koṭṭhāsato aññasa koṭṭhāsaṃ parivattitvā gatampi “na amhākaṃ sākhāya phala”nti ñatvā no khādanti. Yāvadatthaṃ bhakkhitvāti kaṇṭhappamāṇena khāditvā. Sākhaṃ bhañjitvāti chattappamāṇamattaṃ chinditvā chāyaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Yatra hi nāmāti yo hi nāma. Pakkamissatīti pakkanto. Nādāsīti devatāya ānubhāvena phalameva na gaṇhi. Evañhi sā adhiṭṭhāsi.

'A pot for an āḷhaka' means a pot for cooking rice from one āḷhaka of rice-grains. 'Honey from small bees' means stalk-honey made by small bees. 'Without blemish' means faultless. 'And they do not harm one another's fruits' means they do not harm the fruits in one another's portion. There is no one who cuts a root, bark, or leaf from their own portions; they only consume what has fallen beneath their own respective branches. Even a fruit that has rolled from another's portion to another's portion, knowing 'this is not a fruit of our branch,' they do not eat it. 'Having eaten as much as needed' means having eaten to the measure of the throat. 'Having broken a branch' means having cut a leaf the size of an umbrella, made shade, and then departed. 'Whoever indeed' means who indeed. 'Will depart' means departed. 'He did not take' means by the power of the deity, he did not take the fruit. For indeed, she had resolved thus.

Tenupasaṅkamīti janapadavāsīhi gantvā, “mahārāja, rukkho phalaṃ na gaṇhi, amhākaṃ nu kho doso tumhāka”nti vutte “neva mayhaṃ doso atthi, na jānapadānaṃ, amhākaṃ vijite adhammo nāma na vattati, kena nu kho kāraṇena rukkho na phalito, sakkaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchissāmī”ti [V 3.0124] cintetvā yena sakko devānamindo tenupasaṅkami. Pavattesīti parivattesi. Ummūlamakāsīti uddhaṃmūlaṃ akāsi. Api nu tvanti api nu tava. Aṭṭhitāyevāti aṭṭhitāya eva. Sacchavīnīti samānacchavīni pakatiṭṭhāne ṭhitāni. Na paccakkosatīti nappaṭikkosati. Rosantanti ghaṭṭentaṃ. Bhaṇḍantanti paharantaṃ.

'He approached him' means: The country-dwellers went and said, 'Great king, the tree did not bear fruit. Is it our fault, or is it yours?' When this was said, he thought, 'The fault is neither mine nor the country-dwellers. In our kingdom, unrighteousness does not occur. For what reason, then, has the tree not borne fruit? I will approach Sakka and ask.' Having thought thus, he approached Sakka, the lord of the gods. 'Overturned' means turned over. 'Uprooted' means made the root go upwards. 'And you?' means 'and yours?'. 'While not standing firm' means while being unstable. 'Of the same skin' means having the same skin, standing in their natural place. 'Does not revile in return' means does not scold back. 'The one who is angry' means the one who is provoking. 'The one who is quarreling' means the one who is striking.

Sunettoti [P 3.0387] nettā vuccanti akkhīni, tesaṃ sundaratāya sunetto. Titthakaroti sugatiogāhanatitthassa kārako. Vītarāgoti vikkhambhanavasena [M 3.0122] vigatarāgo. Pasavatīti paṭilabhati. Diṭṭhisampannanti dassanasampannaṃ, sotāpannanti attho. Khantinti attano guṇakhaṇanaṃ. Yathāmaṃ sabrahmacārīsūti yathā imaṃ sabrahmacārīsu akkosanaparibhāsanaṃ, aññaṃ evarūpaṃ guṇakhantiṃ na vadāmīti attho. Na no samasabrahmacārīsūti ettha samajano nāma sakajano vuccati. Tasmā na no sakesu samānabrahmacārīsu cittāni paduṭṭhāni bhavissantīti ayamettha attho.

'Sunetta' means: eyes are called 'nettā'; because of their beauty, he is Sunetto. 'A ford-maker' means a maker of a ford for descending into a good destination. 'Free from passion' means free from passion by way of suppression. 'He produces' means he obtains. 'Accomplished in view' means accomplished in vision; the meaning is a stream-enterer. 'Patience' means the endurance of one's own virtue. 'As I among fellow practitioners' means: the meaning is that I declare this person among fellow practitioners as one who has the endurance of virtue. 'Not for us among equal fellow practitioners' means: here, 'samajana' is said to be one's own people. Therefore, the meaning here is: 'Our minds will not be corrupted towards our own, equal fellow practitioners.'

Jotipālo ca govindoti nāmena jotipālo ṭhānena mahāgovindo. Sattapurohitoti reṇuādīnaṃ sattannaṃ rājūnaṃ purohito. Ahiṃsakā atītaṃseti ete cha satthāro atītaṃse ahiṃsakā ahesuṃ. Nirāmagandhāti kodhāmagandhena nirāmagandhā. Karuṇevimuttāti karuṇajjhāne adhimuttā, karuṇāya ca karuṇāpubbabhāge ca ṭhitā. Yeteti ete, ayameva vā pāṭho. Na sādhurūpaṃ āsīdeti sādhusabhāvaṃ na ghaṭṭeyya. Diṭṭhiṭṭhānappahāyinanti [P 3.0388] dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatappahāyinaṃ. Sattamoti arahattato paṭṭhāya sattamo. Avītarāgoti avigatarāgo. Etena anāgāmibhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Pañcindriyā mudūti pañca vipassanindriyāni mudūni. Tassa hi tāni sakadāgāmiṃ upādāya mudūni nāma honti. Vipassanāti saṅkhārapariggahañāṇaṃ. Pubbeva upahaññatīti paṭhamataraññeva upahaññati. Akkhatoti guṇakhaṇanena akkhato anupahato hutvā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Jotipāla and Govinda' means Jotipāla by name, Mahāgovinda by position. 'Priest of seven' means the priest of the seven kings beginning with Reṇu. 'Non-violent in the past' means these six teachers were non-violent in the past. 'Without the raw stench' means without the raw stench of anger. 'Intent on compassion' means intent on the compassion-jhāna, and established in compassion and the preliminary part of compassion. 'Those who' means these; or this itself is the reading. 'One should not assail a virtuous person' means one should not clash with a person of virtuous nature. 'Of those who abandon the bases of views' means of those who abandon the sixty-two wrong views. 'The seventh' means the seventh starting from Arahantship. 'Not free from passion' means with passion not gone. By this, he rejects the state of a non-returner. 'The five faculties are soft' means the five insight-faculties are soft. Indeed, for him, those faculties are called 'soft' in comparison to a once-returner. 'Insight' means the knowledge that comprehends formations. 'Is afflicted beforehand' means is afflicted at the very first. 'Unharmed' means having become un-dug, unharmed by the destruction of virtue. The rest is clear everywhere.

Dhammikavaggo pañcamo.

The fifth chapter.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The first fifty is completed.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

6. Mahāvaggo

6. The Great Division

1. Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

55. Chaṭṭhassa [V 3.0125][M 3.0123] paṭhame soṇoti sukhumālasoṇatthero. Sītavaneti evaṃnāmake susāne. Tasmiṃ kira paṭipāṭiyā pañca caṅkamanapaṇṇasālāsatāni māpitāni, tesu thero attano sappāyacaṅkamanaṃ gahetvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Tassa āraddhavīriyassa hutvā caṅkamato pādatalāni bhijjiṃsu, jāṇūhi caṅkamato jāṇukānipi hatthatalānipi bhijjiṃsu, chiddāni ahesuṃ. Evaṃ āraddhavīriyo viharanto obhāsanimittamattakampi dassetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tassa vīriyena kilamitakāyassa koṭiyaṃ pāsāṇaphalake nisinnassa yo vitakko udapādi, taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho āyasmatotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha [P 3.0389] āraddhavīriyāti paripuṇṇapaggahitavīriyā. Na anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccatīti sace hi ahaṃ ugghaṭitaññū vā assaṃ vipañcitaññū vā neyyo vā, nūna me cittaṃ vimucceyya. Addhā panasmi padaparamo, yena me cittaṃ na vimuccatīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā saṃvijjanti kho panātiādīni cintesi. Tattha bhogāti upayogatthe paccattaṃ.

2. In the first of the sixth, 'Soṇa' refers to the delicate Elder Soṇa. 'In Sītavana' means in the charnel ground of that name. There, it is said, five hundred leaf-hut walking paths were built in succession, and in them the elder, having taken a suitable walking path for himself, practiced the duties of a monk. As he was walking with strenuous effort, the soles of his feet cracked; and as he walked on his knees, his kneecaps and the palms of his hands also cracked and became perforated. Dwelling with such intense effort, he could not produce even the slightest sign of light. Then, while his body was exhausted from exertion, as he sat on a stone slab at the end of the walking path, the thought that arose in him is shown by the passage beginning, 'Then to the venerable...' Here, 'with strenuous effort' means with fully undertaken and exerted energy. 'The mind is not freed from the taints through non-clinging' means: he reflected, 'If I were one of quick understanding, or one of expanded understanding, or one who needs to be led, surely my mind would be freed. Truly, I must be one for whom the text is the highest resort, which is why my mind is not freed.' Having made this determination, he reflected, 'Yet there exist...' Here, 'bhogā' is in the nominative case with the meaning of 'for use'.

Pāturahosīti therassa cittācāraṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ soṇo ajja sītavane padhānabhūmiyaṃ nisinno imaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi, gantvāssa vitakkaṃ sahotthaṃ gaṇhitvā vīṇopamaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessāmī”ti pamukhe pākaṭo ahosi. Paññatte āsaneti padhānikabhikkhū attano vasanaṭṭhāne ovadituṃ āgatassa buddhassa bhagavato nisīdanatthaṃ yathālābhena āsanaṃ paññāpetvāva padhānaṃ karonti, aññaṃ alabhamānā purāṇapaṇṇānipi santharitvā upari saṅghāṭiṃ paññapenti. Theropi āsanaṃ paññāpetvā padhānaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “paññatte āsane”ti.

6. 'He appeared' means: Knowing the elder's train of thought, he became manifest before him, having thought, 'This Soṇa, sitting today in the striving-ground in Sītavana, is thinking this thought. I will go, and having seized his thought as if it were stolen goods, I will teach him the meditation subject of the lute simile.' 'On the prepared seat' means: Monks engaged in striving, when the Blessed Buddha comes to their dwelling place to advise them, first prepare a seat for him to sit on according to what is available, and only then do they practice their striving. If they cannot find anything else, they spread out even old leaves and place their outer robe on top. The elder, too, had prepared a seat before he engaged in his striving. It is with reference to this that it was said: 'on the prepared seat'.

Taṃ kiṃ maññasīti satthā “imassa bhikkhuno avasesakammaṭṭhānehi attho natthi, ayaṃ gandhabbasippe [V 3.0126] cheko ciṇṇavasī, attano visaye kathiyamānaṃ [M 3.0124] khippameva sallakkhessatī”ti vīṇopamaṃ kathetuṃ “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”tiādimāha. Vīṇāya tantissare kusalatā nāma vīṇāya vādanakusalatā, so ca tattha kusalo. Mātāpitaro hissa “amhākaṃ putto aññaṃ sippaṃ sikkhanto kāyena kilamissati, idaṃ pana sayane [P 3.0390] nisinneneva sakkā uggaṇhitu”nti gandhabbasippameva uggaṇhāpesuṃ. Tassa –

1. 'What do you think?' means: The Teacher, thinking, 'This monk has no need for the remaining meditation subjects; he is skilled in the art of music and has mastery from practice. When taught about a matter in his own domain, he will quickly understand,' in order to teach the lute simile, said, 'What do you think?' and so on. Skill in the sound of the strings of a lute is called skill in playing the lute, and he was skilled in that. His parents had thought, 'While our son learns another art, his body will become weary. But this one can be learned even while sitting in bed,' so they had him learn only the art of music. For him—

“Satta sarā tayo gāmā, mucchanā ekavīsati;

Ṭhānā ekūnapaññāsa, iccete saramaṇḍalā”ti. –

55. "Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one modulations, forty-nine positions—thus these are the circles of notes."

Ādikaṃ gandhabbasippaṃ sabbameva paguṇaṃ ahosi. Accāyatāti atiāyatā kharamucchanā. Saravatīti sarasampannā. Kammaññāti kammakkhamā kammayoggā. Atisithilāti mandamucchanā. Same guṇe patiṭṭhitāti majjhime sare ṭhapetvā mucchitā.

The entire art of music, beginning with the aforementioned, was well-practiced by him. `Accāyatā` means excessively stretched, played harshly. `Saravatī` means endowed with sound. `Kammaññā` means workable, suitable for the task. `Atisithilā` means played gently. `Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā` means established in the middle tone and played.

Accāraddhanti atigāḷhaṃ. Uddhaccāya saṃvattatīti uddhatabhāvāya saṃvattati. Atilīnanti atisithilaṃ. Kosajjāyāti kusītabhāvatthāya. Vīriyasamathaṃ adhiṭṭhahāti vīriyasampayuttaṃ samathaṃ adhiṭṭhaha, vīriyaṃ samathena yojehīti attho. Indriyānañca samataṃ paṭivijjhāti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samataṃ samabhāvaṃ adhiṭṭhāhi. Tattha saddhaṃ paññāya, paññañca saddhāya, vīriyaṃ samādhinā, samādhiñca vīriyena yojayatā indriyānaṃ samatā adhiṭṭhitā nāma hoti. Sati pana sabbatthikā, sā sadā balavatīyeva vaṭṭati. Tañca pana tesaṃ yojanāvidhānaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.60-62) pakāsitameva. Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhīti tasmiñca samabhāve sati yena ādāse mukhabimbeneva nimittena uppajjitabbaṃ, taṃ samathanimittaṃ vipassanānimittaṃ magganimittaṃ phalanimittañca [P 3.0391] gaṇhāhi nibbattehīti evamassa satthā arahatte pakkhipitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi.

`Accāraddhaṃ` means excessively strenuous. `Uddhaccāya saṃvattati` means it leads to a state of agitation. `Atilīnaṃ` means excessively slack. `Kosajjāya` means for the purpose of a state of laziness. `Vīriyasamathaṃ adhiṭṭhaha` means: 'Establish tranquility conjoined with energy'; the meaning is, 'Yoke energy with concentration.' `Indriyānañca samataṃ paṭivijjha` means: 'Establish the balance of the faculties.' Therein, the balance of the faculties is said to be established by one who yokes faith with wisdom, and wisdom with faith; energy with concentration, and concentration with energy. But mindfulness is needed in all matters; it is fitting that it is always strong. The method of combining these is explained in the Visuddhimagga. `Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇhāhi` means: 'And when that state of balance is present, grasp the sign by which it is to be produced—like the reflection of a face in a mirror—that is, the sign of tranquility, the sign of insight, the sign of the path, and the sign of the fruit; bring it into being.' Thus the Teacher, placing him in Arahantship, taught him the meditation subject.

Tattha ca nimittaṃ aggahesīti samathanimittañca vipassanānimittañca aggahesi. Cha ṭhānānīti cha kāraṇāni. Adhimutto hotīti paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā ṭhito hoti. Nekkhammādhimuttotiādi sabbaṃ arahattavaseneva vuttaṃ. Arahattañhi sabbakilesehi nikkhantattā nekkhammaṃ, teheva pavivittattā paviveko, byāpajjhābhāvato abyāpajjhaṃ, taṇhākkhayante uppannattā [M 3.0125] taṇhākkhayo[V 3.0127], upādānakkhayante uppannattā upādānakkhayo, sammohābhāvato asammohoti vuccati.

`Tattha ca nimittaṃ aggahesi` means he grasped the sign of tranquility and the sign of insight. `Cha ṭhānāni` means six causes. `Adhimutto hoti` means he stands, having penetrated and directly experienced it. The entire passage beginning with `Nekkhammādhimutto` is spoken solely by way of Arahantship. Indeed, Arahantship is called `nekkhamma` (renunciation) because it is an escape from all defilements; `paviveka` (seclusion) because it is seclusion from them; `abyāpajjha` (non-affliction) because of the absence of affliction; `taṇhākkhaya` (destruction of craving) because it arises upon the destruction of craving; `upādānakkhaya` (destruction of clinging) because it arises upon the destruction of clinging; and `asammoha` (non-delusion) because of the absence of delusion.

Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakanti paṭivedharahitaṃ kevalaṃ paṭivedhapaññāya asammissakaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ. Paṭicayanti punappunaṃ karaṇena vaḍḍhiṃ. Vītarāgattāti maggapaṭivedhena rāgassa vigatattāyeva nekkhammasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sacchikatvā ṭhito hoti, phalasamāpattivihārena viharati, tanninnamānasoyeva ca hotīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

`Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ` means mere worldly faith, devoid of penetration, unmixed with the wisdom of penetration. `Paṭicayaṃ` means growth through repeated action. `Vītarāgattā` means: because lust has departed through the penetration of the path, he stands, having penetrated and directly realized Arahantship, which is called renunciation. He abides by abiding in the attainment of fruition, and he has a mind inclined towards that—this is the meaning. In the remaining passages, this is the method.

Lābhasakkārasilokanti catupaccayalābhañca tesaññeva sukatabhāvañca vaṇṇabhaṇanañca. Nikāmayamānoti icchamāno patthayamāno. Pavivekādhimuttoti paviveke adhimutto arahanti evaṃ arahattaṃ byākarotīti attho.

As for 'gain, honor, and fame': it means the gain of the four requisites, the state of those very requisites being well-made, and the speaking of their praise. As for 'desiring': it means wishing, longing. As for 'inclined to seclusion': by stating 'I am inclined to seclusion,' he thus declares Arahantship. This is the meaning.

Sīlabbataparāmāsanti sīlañca vatañca parāmasitvā gahitaṃ gahaṇamattaṃ. Sārato [P 3.0392] paccāgacchantoti sārabhāvena jānanto. Abyāpajjhādhimuttoti abyāpajjhaṃ arahattaṃ byākaroti. Imināva nayena sabbaṭṭhānesu attho daṭṭhabbo. Apicettha “nekkhammādhimuttoti imasmiṃyeva arahattaṃ kathitaṃ, sesesu pañcasu nibbāna”nti eke vadanti. Apare “asammohādhimuttoti ettheva nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ, sesesu arahatta”nti vadanti. Ayaṃ panettha sāro – sabbesveva tesu arahattampi nibbānampi kathitamevāti.

As for 'attachment to rites and rituals': it is the mere grasping that is grasped by misapprehending precepts and vows. As for 'knowing as essence': it means knowing in terms of essence. As for 'inclined to non-affliction': he declares the Arahantship that is without affliction. By this very method, the meaning should be understood in all instances. Furthermore, some say here: 'As for "inclined to renunciation," in this term alone is Arahantship spoken of; in the remaining five, Nibbāna is spoken of.' Others say: 'As for "inclined to non-delusion," in this very term is Nibbāna spoken of; in the remaining terms, Arahantship is spoken of.' But this is the essential point here: in all of them, both Arahantship and Nibbāna are indeed spoken of.

Bhusāti balavanto dibbarūpasadisā. Nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyantīti etassa khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ gahetvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Kilesā hi uppajjamānā cittaṃ gaṇhanti nāma. Amissīkatanti kilesā hi ārammaṇena saddhiṃ cittaṃ missaṃ karonti, tesaṃ abhāvā amissīkataṃ. Ṭhitanti patiṭṭhitaṃ. Āneñjappattanti acalappattaṃ. Vayañcassānupassatīti tassa cesa cittassa uppādampi vayampi passati. Bhusā vātavuṭṭhīti balavā vātakkhandho. Neva sampakampeyyāti ekabhāgena cāletuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Na sampakampeyyāti thūṇaṃ viya sabbabhāgato kampetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya. Na sampavedheyyāti vedhetvā pavedhetvā pātetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya.

As for 'mighty': they are powerful, like divine forms. As for 'they do not overwhelm his mind': they are not able to seize the mind of this one whose taints are destroyed and remain. Indeed, it is said that defilements, when arising, seize the mind. As for 'unmixed': indeed, defilements make the mind mixed with the object; due to their absence, it is unmixed. As for 'established': it is firmly established. As for 'attained to the imperturbable': it has reached the unshakable. As for 'and he observes its passing away': this one sees both the arising and the passing away of that mind. As for 'a fierce wind and rain': a powerful mass of wind. As for 'it would not shake': it could not cause it to be moved on one side. As for 'it would not cause to tremble': it could not cause it to shake from all parts, like a post. As for 'it would not cause to be agitated': having shaken and shaken violently, it could not cause it to fall.

Nekkhammaṃ [M 3.0126] adhimuttassāti arahattaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitassa khīṇāsavassa. Sesapadesupi [P 3.0393] arahattameva [V 3.0128] kathitaṃ. Upādānakkhayassa cāti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Asammohañca cetasoti cittassa ca asammohaṃ adhimuttassa. Disvā āyatanuppādanti āyatanānaṃ uppādañca vayañca disvā. Sammā cittaṃ vimuccatīti sammā hetunā nayena imāya vipassanāpaṭipattiyā phalasamāpattivasena cittaṃ vimuccati, nibbānārammaṇe adhimuccati. Atha vā iminā khīṇāsavassa paṭipadā kathitā. Tassa hi āyatanuppādaṃ disvā imāya vipassanāya adhigatassa ariyamaggassānubhāvena sabbakilesehi sammā cittaṃ vimuccati. Evaṃ tassa sammā vimuttassa…pe… na vijjati. Tattha santacittassāti nibbutacittassa. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

As for 'of one inclined to renunciation': it means of one with taints destroyed who stands firm, having penetrated Arahantship. By the remaining terms also, only Arahantship is spoken of. As for 'and of the destruction of clinging': the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. As for 'and non-delusion of mind': it means of one inclined to the non-delusion of the mind. As for 'having seen the arising of the sense-bases': it means having seen the arising and passing away of the sense-bases. As for 'the mind is rightly liberated': the mind is liberated rightly—that is, by cause and by method—by this practice of insight, by way of the attainment of fruition; it is inclined towards Nibbāna as its object. Alternatively, by this, the practice of one whose taints are destroyed is taught. Indeed, for that one, having seen the arising of the sense-bases, by the power of the noble path attained through this insight, the mind is rightly liberated from all defilements. For that monk with a peaceful mind, meaning a stilled mind, there is no accumulation for what has been done, and there is nothing further to be done. The rest here has a plain meaning.

2. Phaggunasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Phagguna Sutta

56. Dutiye samadhosīti uṭṭhānākāraṃ dassesi. Paṭikkamantīti parihāyanti. No abhikkamantīti na vaḍḍhanti. Sīsaveṭhanaṃ dadeyyāti sīsaṃ veṭhetvā daṇḍakena samparivattakaṃ bandheyya. Indriyāni vippasīdiṃsūti tasmiṃ maraṇasamaye cha indriyāni vippasannāni ahesuṃ. Atthupaparikkhāyāti atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ upaparikkhane. Anuttare upadhisaṅkhayeti nibbāne. Avimuttaṃ hotīti arahattaphalena adhimuttaṃ hoti.

56. In the second, by 'he settled', he showed the aspect of exertion. 'They decline' means they diminish. 'They do not advance' means they do not increase. 'He would give a head-binding' means he would bind his head by wrapping it and, with a stick, turning it back and forth. 'His faculties became serene' means at that time of death, his six faculties were especially clear. 'By examination of the goal' means by investigating what is beneficial and not beneficial, what is a cause and not a cause. 'In the supreme destruction of attachments' means in Nibbāna. 'He is resolved' means he is inclined by the fruit of Arahantship.

3. Chaḷabhijātisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sutta on the Six High Births

57. Tatiye chaḷabhijātiyoti cha jātiyo. Tatridanti tatrāyaṃ. Luddāti dāruṇā. Bhikkhū [P 3.0394] kaṇṭakavuttikāti samaṇā nāmete. Ekasāṭakāti ekeneva pilotikakhaṇḍena purato paṭicchādanakā. Akāmakassa bilaṃ olaggeyyunti satthe gacchamāne goṇamhi mate gomaṃsamūlaṃ uppādanatthāya vibhajitvā khādamānā ekassa gomaṃsaṃ anicchantasseva koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā “ayañca te khāditabbo, mūlañca dātabba”nti taṃ koṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ bilaṃ olaggeyyuṃ, balakkārena hatthe ṭhapeyyunti attho. Akhettaññunāti abhijātipaññattiyā khettaṃ ajānantena. Taṃ suṇāhīti taṃ mama paññattiṃ suṇāhi. Kaṇhābhijātikoti kāḷakajātiko. Kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyatīti kaṇhasabhāvo hutvā jāyati nibbattati, kaṇhābhijātiyaṃ vā jāyati. Nibbānaṃ [V 3.0129][M 3.0127] abhijāyatīti nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti, ariyabhūmisaṅkhātāya vā nibbānajātiyā jāyati.

57. In the third, 'six high births' means six births. 'Therein this' means among those. 'Cruel' means harsh. 'Monks of thorn-like livelihood' means these are ascetics only by name. 'Wearing a single cloth' means they are covered in front by only a single piece of rag. 'They would force a portion on an unwilling person' means when a caravan is travelling, if an ox dies, they, dividing the beef to generate its value and eating it, would make a portion for one who does not want the beef and would force that portion, called a share, on him, saying, 'This must be eaten by you, and its value must be given.' The meaning is that they would forcibly place it in his hand. 'By one who does not know the field' means by one who does not know the field for the designation of birth. 'Listen to that' means listen to that designation of mine. 'Of dark birth' means one of black birth. 'He is born into a dark state' means having a dark nature, he is born, he arises; or he is born into a dark birth. 'He is born into Nibbāna' means he reaches Nibbāna, or he is born with the Nibbāna-nature, which is called the noble ground.

4. Āsavasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sutta on the Taints

58. Catutthe saṃvarā pahātabbāti saṃvarena pahātabbā. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Paṭisaṅkhāti paṭisañjānitvā, paccavekkhitvāti attho. Yonisoti upāyena pathena. Ettha ca asaṃvare ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā yoniso paṭisaṅkhāti veditabbā. Sā cāyaṃ “varaṃ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho”tiādinā ādittapariyāyena (saṃ. ni. 4.235) veditabbā. Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto [P 3.0395] viharatīti ettha cakkhumeva indriyaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ, saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, pidahanato thakanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhundriye saṃvaro cakkhundriyasaṃvaro. Javane uppajjamānopi hesa tasmiṃ dvāre kilesānaṃ uppattivāraṇato cakkhundriyasaṃvaroti vuccati. Saṃvutoti tena saṃvarena upeto. Tathā hi “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti imassa vibhaṅge “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā saṃvarīti saṃvuto, thakesi pidahīti vuttaṃ hoti. Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvutoti cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātaṃ satikavāṭaṃ cakkhudvāre gharadvāre kavāṭaṃ viya saṃvari thakesi pidahīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayamevettha attho sundarataro. Tathā hi “cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ asaṃvutassa viharato, saṃvutassa viharato”ti etesu padesu ayamevattho dissatīti.

58. In the fourth, 'taints to be abandoned by restraint' means they are to be abandoned by means of restraint. This same method applies in the remaining cases as well. 'Here' means in this Dispensation. 'By reflection' means having known and having reviewed; this is the meaning. 'Wisely' means by a proper means, by a proper path. And here, the reflection on the danger in non-restraint should be understood as 'wise reflection'. And this should be understood through the Discourse on Burning, which begins: 'Better, monks, that the eye faculty be scorched with a red-hot iron rod that is burning, blazing, and glowing, than that there be the grasping of signs and features in forms cognizable by the eye.' Regarding 'he dwells restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty': here, the eye itself is the faculty, hence 'eye faculty'. It is 'restraint' (saṃvaro) because of restraining (saṃvaraṇa); it is said to mean closing (pidahana) and blocking (thakana). This is a term for mindfulness. Restraint at the eye faculty is 'restraint of the eye faculty'. For although it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called 'restraint of the eye faculty' because it prevents the arising of defilements at that door. 'Restrained' (saṃvuto) means endowed with that restraint. For so it is said in the Vibhaṅga on 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha': 'He is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha... possessed of it.' Alternatively, saṃvuto means 'he has restrained' (saṃvari); that is to say, 'he has blocked, he has closed'. 'Restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty' means he has restrained—blocked, closed—the door-leaf of mindfulness, called 'restraint of the eye faculty', at the eye door, like a door-leaf at a house door. This is what is meant. Here, this latter meaning is more beautiful. For indeed, in these phrases, 'of one dwelling with the eye faculty unrestrained' and 'of one dwelling restrained', this is the very meaning that is seen.

Yaṃ hissātiādimhi yaṃ cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ assa bhikkhuno asaṃvutassa athaketvā apidahitvā viharantassāti attho. Yekārassa vā esa yanti ādeso, ye assāti attho. Āsavā vighātapariḷāhāti cattāro āsavā ca aññe ca vighātakarā kilesapariḷāhā vipākapariḷāhā vā. Cakkhudvārasmiñhi iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ āpāthagataṃ kāmassādavasena assādayato abhinandato kāmāsavo uppajjati, “īdisaṃ aññasmimpi sugatibhave labhissāmī”ti bhavapatthanāya assādayato bhavāsavo [M 3.0128] uppajjati, sattoti vā sattassāti vā gaṇhato diṭṭhāsavo uppajjati, sabbeheva sahajātaṃ aññāṇaṃ avijjāsavoti cattāro āsavā uppajjanti[V 3.0130]. Etehi sampayuttā apare kilesā vighātapariḷāhā āyatiṃ vā tesaṃ vipākā tehipi asaṃvutasseva viharato uppajjeyyunti vuccanti. Evaṃsa [P 3.0396] teti evaṃ assa te, etenupāyena na honti, no aññathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso sotindriyasaṃvarasaṃvutotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ime vuccanti āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbāti imesu chasu dvāresu cattāro cattāro katvā catuvīsati āsavā saṃvarena pahātabbāti vuccanti.

In the phrase beginning `yaṃ hissa`, the meaning is: for that monk who dwells unrestrained, not having blocked or closed the restraint of the eye faculty, those taints arise. Alternatively, this `yaṃ` is a substitute for `ye`; the meaning is 'which taints for him'. 'Taints, distresses, and torments' means the four taints and other distress-causing defilement-torments or resultant torments. For when a pleasant object comes into the range of the eye door, for one who savors and delights in it with the taste for sensual pleasure, the taint of sensual pleasure arises. For one who savors it with a wish for future existence, thinking, 'May I obtain such as this in another good destination,' the taint of existence arises. For one who grasps it as 'a being' or 'belonging to a being', the taint of views arises. The ignorance that is co-nascent with all of them is the taint of ignorance. Thus, the four taints arise. It is said that other defilements associated with these, which are distresses and torments, or their future results, would arise for one dwelling unrestrained. Regarding `evaṃsa te`: thus for him, by this method they do not arise, not otherwise; this is what is meant. This same method applies also to the phrases beginning 'by reflection, wisely, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the ear faculty'. 'These are called the taints to be abandoned by restraint' means that in these six doors, taking four taints for each, twenty-four taints are said to be 'abandoned by restraint'.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvarantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.18) sīlakathāya vuttameva. Yaṃ hissāti yañhi cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātādīsu vā aññataraṃ assa. Appaṭisevatoti evaṃ yoniso appaṭisevantassa. Imasmiṃ vāre aladdhaṃ cīvarādiṃ patthayato laddhaṃ vā assādayato kāmāsavassa uppatti veditabbā, īdisaṃ aññasmimpi sugatibhave labhissāmīti bhavapatthanāya assādayato bhavāsavassa, ahaṃ labhāmi na labhāmīti vā mayhaṃ vā idanti attasaññaṃ adhiṭṭhahato diṭṭhāsavassa, sabbeheva pana sahajāto avijjāsavoti evaṃ catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ uppatti vighātapariḷāhāva navavedanuppādanatopi veditabbā. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbāti ime ekamekasmiṃ paccaye cattāro cattāro katvā soḷasa āsavā iminā ñāṇasaṃvarasaṅkhātena paccavekkhaṇapaṭisevanena pahātabbāti vuccanti.

Whatever should be said regarding 'reflecting wisely on the robe' and so forth has all been stated in the section on virtue in the Visuddhimagga. Regarding 'whatever there is for him': whatever requisite, whether a robe, almsfood, or another, there is for him. Regarding 'not making use of it': for one who does not make use of it thus wisely. In this case, for one who longs for an unattained robe and so forth, or who delights in what has been attained, the arising of the taint of sensual desire should be understood. For one who delights with the longing for existence, thinking, 'I will obtain such a requisite in another happy existence,' the arising of the taint of existence should be understood. For one who establishes the perception of self, thinking, 'I gain,' 'I do not gain,' or 'This is mine,' the arising of the taint of views should be understood. Moreover, delusion co-arisen with all of them is the taint of ignorance. Thus the arising of the four taints, which are vexations and feverish states, should also be understood from the production of new feelings. As to 'These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by use': this means that these sixteen taints—making four for each requisite—are said to be abandoned by this reflective use, which is called restraint by knowledge.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassāti upāyena pathena paccavekkhitvā khantā hoti sītassa, sītaṃ khamati sahati, na avīrapuriso viya appamattakenapi sītena calati kampati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vijahati. Uṇhādīsupi [P 3.0397] eseva nayo. Ettha ca vacanameva vacanapathoti veditabbo. Dukkhānantiādīsu dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhā, bahalaṭṭhena tibbā, pharusaṭṭhena kharā, tikhiṇaṭṭhena kaṭukā, assādavirahato asātā, manaṃ avaḍḍhanato amanāpā, pāṇaharaṇasamatthatāya pāṇaharāti veditabbā. Yaṃ hissāti sītādīsu yaṃkiñci ekadhammampi assa. Anadhivāsatoti anadhivāsentassa akkhamantassa[M 3.0129]. Āsavuppatti panettha evaṃ veditabbā – sītena phuṭṭhassa uṇhaṃ patthayato kāmāsavo uppajjati, evaṃ sabbattha. “Natthi sugatibhave sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā”ti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavāsavo, mayhaṃ sītaṃ uṇhanti gāho diṭṭhāsavo, sabbeheva sampayutto avijjāsavoti. Ime vuccantīti ime sītādīsu ekamekassa vasena cattāro cattāro [V 3.0131] katvā aneke āsavā imāya khantisaṃvarasaṅkhātāya adhivāsanāya pahātabbāti vuccantīti attho.

Regarding 'reflecting wisely, one becomes patient with cold': having reflected by means and by path, one becomes patient with cold; one endures and bears the cold, and does not waver or tremble like a man without fortitude at even a slight chill, nor does one abandon the meditation subject. The same method applies to heat and so forth. And here, the word itself should be understood as the 'path of words'. Regarding 'painful' and so on: they are called 'painful' (dukkhā) because they are difficult to bear; 'intense' (tibbā) because they are dense; 'harsh' (kharā) because they are rough; 'sharp' (kaṭukā) because they are piercing; 'unpleasant' (asātā) due to the absence of gratification; 'disagreeable' (amanāpā) because they do not enhance the mind; and 'life-destroying' (pāṇaharā) due to their ability to take away life—thus they should be understood. Regarding 'whatever there is for him': whatever single phenomenon among cold and so forth there may be for him. Regarding 'not enduring': for one not enduring, not tolerating. Here, the arising of taints should be understood thus: for one touched by cold and longing for heat, the taint of sensual desire arises; so it is in all cases. For one longing for existence, thinking, 'There is no cold or heat in a happy existence,' the taint of existence arises. The grasping, 'My cold, my heat,' is the taint of views. Delusion conjoined with all of them is the taint of ignorance. As to 'these are called': this is the meaning: these many taints—making four for each case of cold and so forth—are said to be abandoned by this endurance, which is called restraint by patience.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetīti ahaṃ samaṇoti na caṇḍassa hatthissa āsanne ṭhātabbaṃ. Tatonidānañhi maraṇampi maraṇamattampi dukkhaṃ bhaveyyāti evaṃ upāyena pathena paccavekkhitvā caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjeti paṭikkamati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Caṇḍanti duṭṭhaṃ vāḷaṃ. Khāṇunti khadirakhāṇukādiṃ. Kaṇṭakaṭṭhānanti yattha kaṇṭakā vijjhanti, taṃ okāsaṃ. Sobbhanti [P 3.0398] sabbato chinnataṭaṃ. Papātanti ekato chinnataṭaṃ. Candanikanti ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ chaḍḍanaṭṭhānaṃ. Oḷigallanti tesaṃyeva kaddamādīnaṃ sandanokāsaṃ. Taṃ jaṇṇumattampi asucibharitaṃ hoti. Dvepi cetāni ṭhānāni amanussussadaṭṭhānāni honti, tasmā vajjetabbāni. Anāsaneti ettha ayuttaṃ āsanaṃ anāsanaṃ, taṃ atthato aniyatavatthubhūtaṃ rahopaṭicchannāsananti veditabbaṃ. Agocareti etthapi ayutto gocaro agocaro. So vesiyādibhedato pañcavidho. Pāpake mitteti lāmake dussīle mittapatirūpake amitte. Pāpakesūti lāmakesu. Okappeyyunti saddaheyyuṃ adhimucceyyuṃ “addhā ayamāyasmā akāsi vā karissati vā”ti. Yaṃ hissāti hatthiādīsu yaṃkiñci ekampi assa. Āsavuppatti panettha evaṃ veditabbā – hatthiādinidānena dukkhena phuṭṭhassa sukhaṃ patthayato kāmāsavo uppajjati, “natthi sugatibhave īdisaṃ dukkha”nti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavāsavo, maṃ hatthī maddati maṃ assoti gāho diṭṭhāsavo, sabbeheva sampayutto avijjāsavoti. Ime vuccantīti ime hatthiādīsu ekekassa vasena cattāro cattāro katvā aneke āsavā iminā sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhātena parivajjanena pahātabbāti vuccanti.

Regarding 'reflecting wisely, one avoids a fierce elephant': thinking, 'I am a monk,' one should not stand near a fierce elephant. For from that cause, death or suffering equivalent to death might arise. Thus, having reflected by means and by path, one avoids and retreats from a fierce elephant. This is the method in all cases. 'Fierce' means a vicious wild animal. 'A stump' refers to an acacia stump and so forth. 'A thorny place' means a place where thorns pierce. 'A chasm' means a bank cut away on all sides. 'A precipice' means a bank cut away on one side. 'A cesspool' is a place for discarding things like leftover water, fetal waste, and other impurities. 'A sewer' is a place where their sludge and so forth flows. It is filled with filth, even if only knee-deep. Both these places can be haunts of non-human beings, and therefore should be avoided. Regarding 'an unsuitable seat': here, an improper seat is an unsuitable seat; it should be understood in meaning as a secluded and concealed seat that is the basis for an undetermined offense. Regarding 'an unsuitable resort': here too, an improper resort is an unsuitable resort. It is of five kinds, distinguished by prostitutes and so forth. 'Evil companions' means wretched, immoral false friends or enemies. 'Among the wicked' means among the wretched. 'They would be convinced' means they would believe or conclude, thinking, 'Surely this venerable one has done or will do an improper act.' Regarding 'whatever there is for him': whatever single one among elephants and the like there may be for him. Here, the arising of taints should be understood as follows: for one afflicted by suffering with a cause such as an elephant, and who longs for happiness, the taint of sensual desire arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, 'There is no such suffering in a happy existence,' the taint of existence arises. The grasping, 'An elephant tramples me, a horse tramples me,' is the taint of views. Delusion conjoined with all of them is the taint of ignorance. As to 'these are called': this means that these many taints—making four for each case of elephants and so forth—are said to be abandoned by this avoidance, which is called restraint by virtue.

Paṭisaṅkhā [P 3.0399] yoniso uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetīti “itipāyaṃ vitakko akusalo, itipi sāvajjo, itipi dukkhavipāko, so ca kho [M 3.0130] attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.207-208) nayena yoniso kāmavitakke ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti, cittaṃ āropetvā na vāseti, abbhantare vā na vāsetīti attho. Anadhivāsento kiṃ karotīti? Pajahati. Kiṃ kacavaraṃ viya piṭakenāti? Na hi, api ca kho naṃ vinodeti tudati vijjhati nīharati. Kiṃ balibaddaṃ viya patodenāti? Na hi, atha kho naṃ byantīkaroti vigatantaṃ karoti, yathāssa antopi nāvasissati [V 3.0132] antamaso bhaṅgamattampi, tathā naṃ karoti. Kathaṃ pana naṃ tathā karotīti? Anabhāvaṃ gameti anu anu abhāvaṃ gameti, vikkhambhanappahānena yathā suvikkhambhito hoti, tathā karoti. Sesavitakkadvayepi eseva nayo. Uppannuppanneti uppanne uppanne, uppannamatteyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakiṃ vā uppanne vinodetvā dutiye vāre ajjhupekkhitā na hoti, satakkhattumpi uppanne uppanne vinodetiyeva. Pāpake akusale dhammeti teyeva kāmavitakkādayo, sabbepi vā nava mahāvitakke. Tattha tayo vuttā, avasesā “ñātivitakko, janapadavitakko, amarāvitakko, parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko, lābhasakkārasilokappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko, anavaññattippaṭisaṃyutto vitakko”ti (mahāni. 207) ime cha. Yaṃ hissāti etesu vitakkesu yaṃkiñci assa. Kāmavitakko panettha kāmāsavo eva, tabbiseso bhavāsavo, taṃsampayutto diṭṭhāsavo, sabbavitakkesu avijjā avijjāsavoti evaṃ āsavuppatti veditabbā. Ime [P 3.0400] vuccantīti ime kāmavitakkādivasena vuttappakārā āsavā iminā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vitakke ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇasahitena vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vinodanena pahātabbāti vuccanti.

The meaning of 'reflecting wisely, one does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought' is: having wisely reflected on the drawback in sensual thoughts according to the method beginning 'this thought is unwholesome, blameworthy, has painful results, and leads to self-affliction,' one does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought in that particular object. The meaning is that one does not place the mind on it, nor does one allow it to dwell internally. What does one do by not tolerating it? One abandons it. Does one discard it like rubbish with a basket? No, but rather one dispels it, pierces it, and expels it. Does one drive it away like an ox with a goad? No, but rather one brings it to an end, makes it cease, so that not even a trace remains inside, not even the slightest fragment. How does one accomplish this? One brings it to non-existence, brings it to non-existence again and again; by suppression-abandonment, one makes it thoroughly suppressed. The same method applies to the remaining two kinds of thoughts. The meaning of 'whenever they arise' is: when they arise, when they arise; that is to say, as soon as they arise. Having dispelled it once when it arises, one is not indifferent on a second occasion; even if it arises a hundred times, one dispels it each time. 'Evil unwholesome states' refers to those very sensual thoughts and so forth, or all nine great thoughts. Among them, three have been mentioned, while the remaining six are: thoughts of kinship, thoughts of homeland, thoughts of immortality, thoughts connected with compassion for others, thoughts connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thoughts connected with not being despised. The meaning of 'whatever' is: any one of these thoughts that might arise for him. Here, the sensual thought is just the taint of sensuality; its specific aspect is the taint of existence; the view conjoined with it is the taint of views; in all thoughts, ignorance is the taint of ignorance—thus, the arising of taints should be understood. The meaning of 'these are called' is that these taints, described by way of sensual thought and so on, are said to be abandoned by this act of dispelling, which is accompanied by reflection on the drawback in each respective thought.

Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetīti abhāvanāya ādīnavaṃ bhāvanāya ca ānisaṃsaṃ upāyena pathena paccavekkhitvā satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Bojjhaṅgānaṃ bhāvanā heṭṭhā vitthāritāva. Yaṃ hissāti etesu bojjhaṅgesu yaṃkiñci assa. Āsavuppattiyaṃ panettha imesaṃ ariyamaggasampayuttānaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ abhāvitattā ye uppajjeyyuṃ kāmāsavādayo āsavā, bhāvayato evaṃsa te [M 3.0131] na hontīti ayaṃ nayo veditabbo. Ime vuccantīti ime kāmāsavādayo āsavā imāya lokuttarāya bojjhaṅgabhāvanāya pahātabbāti vuccanti. Imehi chahākārehi pahīnāsavaṃ bhikkhuṃ thomento yato kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha yatoti sāmivacane to-kāro, yassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Porāṇā pana yamhi kāleti vaṇṇayanti. Ye āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā, te saṃvarā pahīnā hontīti ye āsavā saṃvarena pahātabbā, te saṃvareneva pahīnā honti, na appahīnesuyeva pahīnasaññī hotīti.

Reflecting wisely, one develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness—this means: having reflected on the drawback in not developing it and the benefit in developing it, by a suitable means and path, one develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This same method applies in all cases. The development of the enlightenment factors has already been explained in detail below. 'Whatever' means whatever one among these enlightenment factors there may be for him. Here, regarding the arising of taints: because these enlightenment factors associated with the noble path have not been developed, taints such as the taint of sensuality would arise. For one who develops them thus, those taints, as well as distresses and fevers, do not arise. This method should be understood. 'These are called' means: these taints, such as the taint of sensuality, are said to be abandoned by this supramundane development of the enlightenment factors.

5. Dārukammikasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Dārukammika Sutta

59. Pañcame dārukammikoti dāruvikkayena pavattitājīvo eko upāsako. Kāsikacandananti [V 3.0133] saṇhacandanaṃ. Aṅgenāti aguṇaṅgena, sukkapakkhe guṇaṅgena. Nemantanikoti nimantanaṃ gaṇhanako. Saṅghe dānaṃ dassāmīti bhikkhusaṅghassa dassāmi. So evaṃ vatvā satthāraṃ abhivādetvā pakkāmi. Athassa [P 3.0401] aparabhāge pañcasatā kulūpakā bhikkhū gihibhāvaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. So “kulūpakabhikkhū te vibbhantā”ti vutte “kiṃ ettha mayha”nti vatvā cittuppādavemattamattampi na akāsi. Idaṃ sandhāya satthā saṅghe te dānaṃ dadato cittaṃ pasīdissatīti āha.

5. In the fifth sutta, 'dārukammika' means a lay follower who made a living by selling firewood. 'Kāsika sandalwood' means fine sandalwood. 'Aṅgena' means with a defective part; during the bright fortnight, with a good part. 'Nemantanika' means one who accepts invitations. 'I will give a gift to the Saṅgha' means 'I will give to the community of monks.' Having said this, he paid homage to the Teacher and departed. Later, five hundred monks who frequented his family returned to the lay state. When it was said, 'Those monks who frequented your family have disrobed,' he replied, 'What is that to me?' and did not show even the slightest change of mind. With reference to this, the Teacher said, 'His mind will be serene when giving a gift to the Saṅgha.'

6. Hatthisāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Hatthisāriputta Sutta

60. Chaṭṭhe abhidhammakathanti abhidhammamissakaṃ kathaṃ. Kathaṃ opātetīti tesaṃ kathaṃ vicchinditvā attano kathaṃ katheti. Therānaṃ bhikkhūnanti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, therehi bhikkhūhi saddhinti attho. Yā ca therānaṃ abhidhammakathā, taṃ ayampi kathetuṃ sakkotīti attho. Cetopariyāyanti cittavāraṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Soratasoratoti sūrato viya sūrato, soraccasamannāgato viyāti attho. Nivātanivātoti nivāto viya nivāto, nivātavutti viyāti attho. Upasantupasantoti upasanto viya upasanto[M 3.0132]. Vapakassateva satthārāti satthu santikā apagacchati. Saṃsaṭṭhassāti pañcahi saṃsaggehi saṃsaṭṭhassa. Vissaṭṭhassāti vissajjitassa. Pākatassāti pākatindriyassa.

59. In the sixth, 'abhidhammakathā' means a talk mixed with Abhidhamma. 'Kathaṃ opātetīti' means having cut off their talk, he speaks his own talk. 'Therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ' is a genitive case in the sense of instrumentality, meaning 'with the monks who are elders.' It means he is also capable of discussing the Abhidhamma topics the elders speak of. 'Cetopariyāya' means the sphere of the mind. 'Idha' means in this world. 'Soratasorato' means 'gentle as gentle,' which means like one who is gentle, possessed of gentleness. 'Nivātanivāto' means 'humble as humble,' which means like the humble, behaving humbly. 'Upasantupasanto' means 'peaceful as peaceful,' which means like the peaceful. 'Vapakassateva satthārā' means he goes away from the Teacher's presence. 'Saṃsaṭṭhassa' means associated through the five kinds of association. 'Vissaṭṭhassa' means released. 'Pākatassa' means with evident faculties.

Kiṭṭhādoti kiṭṭhakhādako. Antaradhāpeyyāti nāseyya. Gopasūti gāvo ca ajikā ca. Sippisambukanti [P 3.0402] sippiyo ca sambukā ca. Sakkharakaṭhalanti sakkharā ca kaṭhalāni ca. Ābhidosikanti abhiññātadosaṃ kudrūsakabhojanaṃ. Nacchādeyyāti na rucceyya. Tattha yadetaṃ purisaṃ bhuttāvinti upayogavacanaṃ, taṃ sāmiatthe daṭṭhabbaṃ. Amuṃ hāvuso, purisanti, āvuso, amuṃ purisaṃ.

'Kiṭṭhādo' means one who eats grain plants. 'Antaradhāpeyya' means one should destroy. 'Gopasu' means cows and goats. 'Sippisambuka' means oysters and snails. 'Sakkharakaṭhala' means gravel and potsherds. 'Ābhidosika' means food made from kudrūsaka grain with a known fault. 'Nacchādeyya' means it would not be agreeable. There, the accusative case in the phrase 'purisaṃ bhuttāvi' is to be understood in the sense of the genitive. 'Amuṃ hāvuso, purisaṃ' means, 'Friend, of that man.'

Sabbanimittānanti sabbesaṃ niccanimittādīnaṃ nimittānaṃ. Animittaṃ cetosamādhinti balavavipassanāsamādhiṃ. Cīrikasaddoti jhallikasaddo. Sarissati nekkhammassāti pabbajjāya guṇaṃ sarissati. Arahataṃ ahosīti bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahantānaṃ antare eko arahā ahosi. Ayañhi thero satta vāre gihī hutvā satta vāre pabbaji. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle [V 3.0134] kiresa ekassa bhikkhuno gihibhāve vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. So teneva kammena arahattassa upanissaye vijjamāneyeva satta vāre gihibhāve ca pabbajjāya ca sañcaranto sattame vāre pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti.

'Sabbanimittānaṃ' means of all signs, such as the sign of permanence and so on. 'Animittaṃ cetosamādhi' means powerful insight concentration. 'Cīrikasadda' means the sound of crickets. 'Sarissati nekkhammassa' means he will recollect the virtue of going forth. 'Arahataṃ ahosi' means he became one Arahant among the Blessed One's Arahant disciples. This elder, indeed, was a householder seven times and went forth seven times. For what reason? It is said that during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, he spoke to a certain monk in praise of the householder life. Because of that very kamma, although the supporting condition for Arahantship was present, wandering back and forth between the householder life and the ordained life seven times, in the seventh instance, having gone forth, he attained Arahantship.

7. Majjhesuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Sutta on the Middle

61. Sattame pārāyane metteyyapañheti pārāyanasamāgamamhi metteyyamāṇavassa pañhe. Ubhonte viditvānāti dve ante dve koṭṭhāse jānitvā. Majjhe mantā na lippatīti mantā vuccati paññā, tāya ubho ante viditvā majjhe na lippati, vemajjheṭṭhāne na lippati. Sibbanimaccagāti [P 3.0403] sibbanisaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ atīto. Phassoti phassavasena nibbattattā ayaṃ attabhāvo. Eko antoti ayameko koṭṭhāso. Phassasamudayoti phasso samudayo assāti phassasamudayo, imasmiṃ attabhāve katakammaphassapaccayā nibbatto anāgatattabhāvo. Dutiyo antoti dutiyo koṭṭhāso. Phassanirodhoti nibbānaṃ. Majjheti sibbinitaṇhaṃ chetvā dvidhākaraṇaṭṭhena nibbānaṃ majjhe nāma hoti. Taṇhā hi [M 3.0133] naṃ sibbatīti taṇhā naṃ attabhāvadvayasaṅkhātaṃ phassañca phassasamudayañca sibbati ghaṭṭeti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Tassa tasseva bhavassa abhinibbattiyā. Yadi hi taṇhā na sibbeyya, tassa tassa bhavassa nibbatti na bhaveyya. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne koṭimajjhikūpamaṃ gaṇhanti. Dvinnañhi kaṇḍānaṃ ekato katvā majjhe suttena saṃsibbitānaṃ koṭi majjhanti vuccati. Sutte chinne ubho kaṇḍāni ubhato patanti. Evamettha kaṇḍadvayaṃ viya vuttappakārā dve antā, sibbitvā ṭhitasuttaṃ viya taṇhā, sutte chinne kaṇḍadvayassa ubhatopatanaṃ viya taṇhāya niruddhāya antadvayaṃ niruddhameva hoti. Ettāvatāti ettakena iminā ubho ante viditvā taṇhāya majjhe anupalittabhāvena abhiññeyyaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ abhijānāti nāma, tīraṇapariññāya ca pahānapariññāya ca parijānitabbaṃ lokiyasaccadvayaṃ parijānāti nāma. Diṭṭheva [P 3.0404] dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Dukkhassantakaro hotīti vaṭṭadukkhassa koṭikaro paricchedaparivaṭumakaro hoti nāma.

61. In the seventh, in the Pārāyana, 'the Metteyya question' means: in the Pārāyana assembly, the question of the youth Metteyya. 'Having known both ends' means: having known the two ends, the two portions. 'In the middle, one of wisdom is not smeared' means: wisdom is called 'mantā'; with that wisdom, having known both ends, one is not smeared in the middle, one is not smeared in the central position. 'Having overcome the seamstress' means: having gone beyond craving, which is called the seamstress. 'Contact' means: this present individual existence, because it is produced through the power of contact. 'One end' means: this is one portion. 'The origin of contact' means: contact is its origin, thus it is the 'origin of contact'; the future individual existence is produced conditioned by contact together with kamma performed in this present individual existence. 'The second end' means: this is the second portion. 'The cessation of contact' is Nibbāna. 'Middle' means: Nibbāna is called the middle because it has the meaning of making two by cutting craving, the seamstress. 'For craving sews it' means: craving sews and connects it, that is, contact and the origin of contact, which are designated as the pair of individual existences. For what reason? For the production of that very existence. Indeed, if craving did not sew, the production of that existence would not occur. In this place, they take up the simile of the end and the middle. Of two edges brought together and sewn in the middle with a thread, the end is called the middle. When the thread is cut, both edges fall to either side. Thus, herein, the two ends of the aforesaid kind are to be seen like the pair of edges, and craving is to be seen like the thread that has sewn them. Just as the pair of edges falls to either side when the thread is cut, so too, when craving has ceased, the pair of ends ceases indeed. 'To this extent' means: by this much, having known both ends and by being unsmeared by craving in the middle, one is said to know through direct knowledge the doctrine of the Four Truths, which is to be directly known. One is said to fully understand the two worldly truths, which are to be fully understood through the full understanding of scrutinizing and the full understanding of abandoning. 'In this very life' means: in this very present individual existence. 'He becomes an end-maker of suffering' means: one becomes a maker of the end, a maker of the limit and conclusion, of the suffering of the round of existences.

Dutiyavāre tiṇṇaṃ kaṇḍānaṃ vasena upamā veditabbā. Tiṇṇañhi kaṇḍānaṃ suttena saṃsibbitānaṃ sutte chinne tīṇi kaṇḍāni tīsu ṭhānesu patanti, evamettha kaṇḍattayaṃ viya atītānāgatapaccuppannā khandhā, suttaṃ viya taṇhā. Sā hi atītaṃ paccuppannena, paccuppannañca anāgatena [V 3.0135] saddhiṃ saṃsibbati. Sutte chinne kaṇḍattayassa tīsu ṭhānesu patanaṃ viya taṇhāya niruddhāya atītānāgatapaccuppannā khandhā niruddhāva honti.

In the second instance, the simile should be understood by means of three edges. For when three edges are sewn together with a thread, if the thread is cut, the three edges fall in three places. Thus, herein, the past, future, and present aggregates are to be seen as the triad of edges, and craving as the thread. Indeed, that craving sews the past together with the present, and the present with the future. Just as the triad of edges falls in three places when the thread is cut, so too, when craving has ceased, the past, future, and present aggregates are indeed ceased.

Tatiyavāre adukkhamasukhā majjheti dvinnaṃ vedanānaṃ antaraṭṭhakabhāvena majjhe. Sukhañhi dukkhassa, dukkhaṃ vā sukhassa antaraṃ nāma natthi. Taṇhā sibbinīti vedanāsu nandirāgo vedanānaṃ upacchedaṃ nivāretīti tā sibbati nāma.

In the third instance, 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant is in the middle' means: it is in the middle because of its nature of standing between the two feelings. For pleasure is not what is called the interval of pain, nor is pain the interval of pleasure. 'Craving is the seamstress' means: delight-lust in feelings prevents the cutting off of feelings; therefore, it is said to sew them.

Catutthavāre viññāṇaṃ majjheti paṭisandhiviññāṇampi sesaviññāṇampi nāmarūpapaccayasamudāgatattā nāmarūpānaṃ majjhe nāma.

In the fourth instance, 'consciousness is in the middle' means: both rebirth-linking consciousness and the remaining consciousness are called 'in the middle' of name-and-form, because they have arisen from name-and-form as their condition.

Pañcamavāre viññāṇaṃ majjheti kammaviññāṇaṃ majjhe, ajjhattikāyatanesu vā manāyatanena kammassa gahitattā idha yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ majjhe nāma, manodvāre vā āvajjanassa ajjhattikāyatananissitattā javanaviññāṇaṃ majjhe nāma.

In the fifth instance, 'consciousness is in the middle' means: kamma-consciousness is in the middle. Or, because kamma is grasped by the mind-base among the internal sense bases, herein any consciousness whatsoever is called 'middle'. Or, because adverting at the mind-door is dependent on an internal sense base, impulsion-consciousness is called 'middle'.

Chaṭṭhavāre [M 3.0134] sakkāyoti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Sakkāyasamudayoti samudayasaccaṃ. Sakkāyanirodhoti nirodhasaccaṃ. Pariyāyenāti [P 3.0405] tena tena kāraṇeneva. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the sixth instance, 'identity' is the round of the three planes. 'The origin of identity' is the truth of origin. 'The cessation of identity' is the truth of cessation. 'By way of' means by that very reason. The remainder should be understood everywhere in the manner already stated.

8. Purisindriyañāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Sutta on the Knowledge of the Faculties of Persons

62. Aṭṭhame aññataroti devadattapakkhiko eko. Samannāharitvāti āvajjitvā. Idaṃ so “kiṃ nu kho bhagavatā jānitvā kathitaṃ, udāhu ajānitvā, ekaṃsikaṃ vā kathitaṃ udāhu vibhajjakathita”nti adhippāyena pucchati. Āpāyikoti apāye nibbattanako. Nerayikoti nirayagāmī. Kappaṭṭhoti kappaṭṭhiyakammassa katattā kappaṃ ṭhassati. Atekicchoti na sakkā tikicchituṃ. Dvejjhanti dvidhābhāvaṃ. Vālaggakoṭinittudanamattanti vālassa aggakoṭiyā dassetabbamattakaṃ, vālaggakoṭinipātamattakaṃ vā. Purisindriyañāṇānīti purisapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattañāṇāni, indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvajānanañāṇānīti attho.

62. In the eighth [sutta], 'a certain one' (aññataro) means a certain monk who was in Devadatta's faction. 'Having considered' (samannāharitvā) means having adverted. He asks with this intention: 'Was this spoken by the Blessed One having known, or was it spoken without knowing? Was it spoken definitively, or was it spoken having analyzed it?' 'Destined for the lower realms' (āpāyiko) means one who will be reborn in the lower realms. 'Hell-bound' (nerayiko) means one who will go to hell. 'Fixed for an aeon' (kappaṭṭho) means he will remain for an aeon because of having done an action that lasts for an aeon. 'Incurable' (atekiccho) means it is not possible to cure. 'Duality' (dvejjaṃ) means a state of twofoldness. 'Just the measure of the tip of a hair' (vālaggakoṭinittudanamattaṃ) means an amount that can be shown by the tip of a hair, or an amount of space just enough to place the tip of a hair. 'Knowledge of the faculties of persons' (purisindriyañāṇāni) means the knowledges of the superiority and inferiority of the faculties of male persons, that is, the knowledges of knowing the sharp and dull states of the faculties.

Vijjamānā kusalāpi dhammā akusalāpi dhammāti ettakā kusalā dhammā vijjanti, ettakā [V 3.0136] akusalā dhammāti jānāmi. Antarahitāti adassanaṃ gatā. Sammukhībhūtāti samudācāravasena pākaṭā jātā. Kusalamūlanti kusalajjhāsayo. Kusalā kusalanti tamhā kusalajjhāsayā aññampi kusalaṃ nibbattissati. Sāradānīti sārādāni gahitasārāni, saradamāse vā nibbattāni. Sukhasayitānīti [P 3.0406] sukhasannicitāni. Sukhetteti maṇḍakhette. Nikkhittānīti vuttāni. Sappaṭibhāgāti sarikkhakā. Abhido addharattanti abhiaddharattaṃ addharatte abhimukhībhūte. Bhattakālasamayeti rājakulānaṃ bhattakālasaṅkhāte samaye. Parihānadhammoti ko evaṃ bhagavatā ñātoti? Ajātasatturājā. So hi pāpamittaṃ nissāya maggaphalehi parihīno. Aparepi suppabuddhasunakkhattādayo bhagavatā ñātāva. Aparihānadhammoti evaṃ bhagavatā ko ñāto? Susīmo paribbājako aññe ca evarūpā. Parinibbāyissatīti evaṃ ko ñāto bhagavatāti? Santatimahāmatto aññe ca evarūpā.

'Wholesome states exist, unwholesome states exist' (vijjamānā kusalāpi dhammā akusalāpi dhammā) means: I know that 'this many wholesome states exist, and this many unwholesome states exist.' 'Disappeared' (antarahitā) means gone from sight. 'Manifest' (sammukhībhūtā) means having become manifest by way of repeated occurrence. 'Root of wholesomeness' (kusalamūlaṃ) means wholesome inclination. 'Wholesome from wholesome' (kusalā kusalaṃ) means that from that wholesome inclination, other wholesome [states] will also arise. 'Autumnal' (sāradāni) means having an extracted essence, or produced in the autumn month. 'Well-stored' (sukhasayitāni) means well-accumulated. 'In a fertile field' (sukhette) means in a good field. 'Placed' (nikkhittāni) means sown. 'Of similar kind' (sappaṭibhāgā) means similar. 'Approaching midnight' (abhido addharattaṃ) means when midnight is approaching. 'At mealtime' (bhattakālasamaye) means at the time designated as mealtime for royal families. 'Of a nature to decline' (parihānadhammo)—who is known by the Blessed One in this way? This is the question. King Ajātasattu. Indeed, he, relying on an evil friend, declined from the path and fruit. Others too, such as Suppabuddha and Sunakkhatta, are also known by the Blessed One. 'Not of a nature to decline' (aparihānadhammo)—who is known by the Blessed One in this way? This is the question. Susīma the wanderer and others of such a nature. 'Will attain final Nibbāna' (parinibbāyissati)—who is known by the Blessed One in this way? This is the question. Santati the great minister and others of such a nature.

9. Nibbedhikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Nibbedhika Sutta.

63. Navame [M 3.0135] anibbiddhapubbe appadālitapubbe lobhakkhandhādayo nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapariyāyo, nibbijjhanakāraṇanti attho. Nidānasambhavoti kāme nideti uppādanasamatthatāya niyyādetīti nidānaṃ. Sambhavati tatoti sambhavo, nidānameva sambhavo nidānasambhavo. Vemattatāti nānākaraṇaṃ.

63. In the ninth [sutta], because it pierces and splits the aggregates of greed and so on, which have not been pierced before, not been split before, it is called the 'Discourse on Piercing' (nibbedhikapariyāyo). The meaning is: the cause of piercing. 'Originating from the source' (nidānasambhava) means: it brings forth (nideti), it delivers (niyyādeti) sensual pleasures (kāme) by its capacity to produce them; therefore, it is 'nidāna' (source). From that, it arises (sambhavati); therefore, it is 'sambhava' (origin). The source itself is the origin; hence, nidānasambhavo. 'Diversity' (vemattatā) means making various.

Kāmaguṇāti kāmayitabbaṭṭhena kāmā, bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā “antaguṇa”ntiādīsu viya. Cakkhuviññeyyāti cakkhuviññāṇena passitabbā. Iṭṭhāti pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu mā vā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Kantāti kamanīyā. Manāpāti manavaḍḍhanakā. Piyarūpāti piyajātikā. Kāmūpasañhitāti [P 3.0407] ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānena kāmena upasañhitā. Rajanīyāti rāguppattikāraṇabhūtā. Nete kāmāti na ete kamanaṭṭhena kāmā nāma honti. Saṅkapparāgoti saṅkappavasena uppannarāgo. Kāmoti ayaṃ kāmappahānāya paṭipannehi pahātabbo. Kamanaṭṭhena kāmā nāma. Citrānīti citravicitrārammaṇāni.

'Strands of sensual pleasure' (kāmaguṇā) are 'kāmā' in the sense of being desirable, and 'guṇā' in the sense of binding, as in 'antaguṇaṃ', etc. 'Cognizable by the eye' (cakkhuviññeyyā) means to be seen by eye-consciousness. 'Agreeable' (iṭṭhā) means: whether they are sought for or not, they are agreeable objects. This is the meaning. 'Pleasing' (kantā) means desirable. 'Lovely' (manāpā) means that which increases [delight in] the mind. 'Endearing in form' (piyarūpā) means of a nature to be loved. 'Connected with sensual desire' (kāmūpasañhitā) means connected with the sensual desire that arises having taken them as an object. 'Alluring' (rajanīyā) means being a cause for the arising of lust. 'These are not sensual pleasures' (nete kāmā) means: these are not called 'kāmā' in the sense of desiring. 'Thought-lust' (saṅkapparāgo) means lust arisen by way of thought. 'Sensual pleasure' (kāmo) means: this [thought-lust] is to be abandoned by those practicing for the abandonment of sensual desire; it is called 'kāma' in the sense of desiring. 'Varied' (citrāni) means varied and diverse objects.

Phassoti sahajātaphasso. Kāmayamānoti kāmaṃ kāmayamāno. Tajjaṃ tajjanti tajjātikaṃ tajjātikaṃ. Puññabhāgiyanti dibbe kāme patthetvā sucaritapāripūriyā devaloke nibbattassa [V 3.0137] attabhāvo puññabhāgiyo nāma, duccaritapāripūriyā apāye nibbattassa attabhāvo apuññabhāgiyo nāma. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kāmānaṃ vipākoti ayaṃ duvidhopi kāmapatthanaṃ nissāya uppannattā kāmānaṃ vipākoti vuccati. So imaṃ nibbedhikanti so bhikkhu imaṃ chattiṃsaṭṭhānesu nibbijjhanakaṃ seṭṭhacariyaṃ jānāti. Kāmanirodhanti kāmānaṃ nirodhane evaṃ laddhanāmaṃ. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne brahmacariyasaṅkhāto maggova kāmanirodhoti vutto.

'Contact' (phasso) means co-nascent contact. 'Desiring' (kāmayamāno) means one who desires sensual pleasure. 'Suitable for that, suitable for that' (tajjaṃ tajjaṃ) means of that kind, of that kind. 'Meritorious portion' (puññabhāgiyaṃ) means: having aspired to divine sensual pleasures, the state of existence of one who is reborn in the deva world due to the perfection of good conduct is called a 'meritorious portion'.
