Then, having sent a group of monks, they have the boundary rectified, they have the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies established, in places where those of wrong livelihood are numerous they send those who teach the noble lineage and have the noble lineage taught, and they have the evil monks censured by masters of the Vinaya. The evil monks, too, thinking, 'The Saṅgha is heedful; it is not possible for us to go about by forming factions,' break up and flee. Thus, in this context, growth and decline should be understood.

Samaggātiādīsu cetiyapaṭijagganatthaṃ vā bodhigharauposathāgāracchādanatthaṃ vā katikavattaṃ vā ṭhapetukāmatāya “saṅgho sannipatatū”ti bheriyā vā ghaṇṭiyā vā ākoṭitamattāya “mayhaṃ cīvarakammaṃ atthi, mayhaṃ patto pacitabbo, mayhaṃ navakammaṃ atthī”ti vikkhepaṃ karontā na samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Sabbaṃ pana taṃ kammaṃ [P 4.0018] ṭhapetvā “ahaṃ purimataraṃ, ahaṃ purimatara”nti ekappahāreneva sannipatantā samaggā sannipatanti nāma. Sannipatitā pana cintetvā mantetvā kattabbaṃ katvā ekatova avuṭṭhahantā na samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Evaṃ vuṭṭhitesu hi ye paṭhamaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ evaṃ hoti “amhehi bāhirakathāva sutā, idāni vinicchayakathā bhavissatī”ti. Ekappahāreneva vuṭṭhahantā samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma. Apica “asukaṭṭhāne vihārasīmā ākulā, uposathappavāraṇā ṭhitā, asukaṭṭhāne vejjakammādikārakā pāpabhikkhū ussannā”ti sutvā “ko gantvā tesaṃ niggahaṃ karissatī”ti vutte “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti vatvā gacchantāpi samaggā vuṭṭhahanti nāma.

23. Regarding 'in concord' and so on, the decision should be understood in this way. If, for the purpose of maintaining a cetiya, or for roofing the Bodhi-house or the Uposatha-house, or with the desire to establish a code of conduct, it is announced, 'Let the Saṅgha assemble,' and upon the mere striking of a drum or a bell, some, making distractions by saying, 'I have robe-work to do,' 'My bowl must be fired,' or 'I have new work to do,' they are not called 'assembling in concord.' But, having set aside all such work, those who assemble all at once, thinking, 'I will assemble first, I will assemble first,' are called 'assembling in concord.' Furthermore, having assembled, after thinking, consulting, and doing what should be done, if they do not rise up all together, they are not called 'rising up in concord.' For among those who have risen up in this way, for those who go first, this thought occurs: 'Only the external talk was heard by us; now the talk of the decision will take place.' Those who rise up all at once are called 'rising up in concord.' Moreover, having heard, 'In such-and-such a place the monastery boundary is disturbed, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are suspended, in such-and-such a place evil monks who perform medical practice and so on are numerous,' when it is asked, 'Who will go and censure them?' those who go, saying, 'I first, I first,' are also called 'rising up in concord.'

Āgantukaṃ pana disvā “imaṃ pariveṇaṃ yāhi, etaṃ pariveṇaṃ yāhi, ayaṃ ko”ti avatvā sabbe vattaṃ karontāpi, jiṇṇapattacīvarakaṃ disvā tassa bhikkhācāravattena pattacīvaraṃ pariyesantāpi, gilānassa gilānabhesajjaṃ pariyesamānāpi, gilānameva anāthaṃ “asukapariveṇaṃ yāhī”ti avatvā attano attano pariveṇe paṭijaggantāpi, eko olīyamānako [M 3.0158] gantho hoti, paññavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ saṅgaṇhitvā tena taṃ ganthaṃ ukkhipāpentāpi samaggā saṅghakaraṇīyāni karonti nāma.

Furthermore, on seeing a visiting monk, without saying, 'Go to this cell,' 'Go to that cell,' or 'Who is this?,' all perform their duties; on seeing a monk with a worn-out bowl and robe, they search for a bowl and robe for him by means of the alms-round duty; they search for medicine for the sick; on seeing a sick and helpless monk, without saying, 'Go to such-and-such a cell,' they look after him in their own respective cells; when there is a text that is declining, they support a wise monk and through him have that text taken up—in all these cases, they are called 'performing the duties of the Saṅgha in concord.'

Appaññattantiādīsu navaṃ adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ vā sikkhāpadaṃ vā gaṇhantā appaññattaṃ paññāpenti nāma purāṇasanthatavatthusmiṃ sāvatthiyaṃ bhikkhū viya. Uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ sāsanaṃ dīpentā paññattaṃ samucchindanti nāma, vassasataparinibbute bhagavati vesālikā vajjiputtakā [V 3.0160] viya. Khuddānukhuddakā pana āpattiyo sañcicca vītikkamantā yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya na vattanti nāma assajipunabbasukā viya. Tathā akarontā pana apaññattaṃ na paññāpenti, paññattaṃ na samucchindanti[P 4.0019], yathāpaññattesu sikkhāpadesu samādāya vattanti nāma āyasmā upaseno viya, āyasmā yaso kākaṇḍakaputto viya, āyasmā mahākassapo viya ca. Vuddhiyevāti sīlādiguṇehi vuddhiyeva, no parihāni.

Regarding 'what is not enacted' and so on, the decision should be understood in this way. Those who take up a new, unrighteous code of conduct or training rule are called 'enacting what has not been enacted,' like the monks in Sāvatthī in the case of the old felt cloth. Those who propound the Dispensation as being against the Dhamma and against the Vinaya are called 'cutting off what has been enacted,' like the Vajjian sons in Vesālī one hundred years after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. Furthermore, those who intentionally transgress minor and very minor offenses, and do not practice in accordance with the training rules as they were enacted, having undertaken them, are like Assaji and Punabbasuka. On the other hand, those who do not act thus do not enact what has not been enacted, do not cut off what has been enacted, and practice in accordance with the training rules as they were enacted, having undertaken them, like the Venerable Upasena, the Venerable Yasa son of Kākaṇḍaka, and the Venerable Mahākassapa. 'Growth indeed' means growth only in qualities such as virtue; not decline.

Therāti thirabhāvappattā therakārakehi guṇehi samannāgatā. Bahū rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū. Ciraṃ pabbajitānaṃ etesanti cirapabbajitā. Saṅghassa pitiṭṭhāne ṭhitāti saṅghapitaro. Pitiṭṭhāne ṭhitattā saṅghaṃ pariṇenti, pubbaṅgamā hutvā tīsu sikkhāsu pavattentīti saṅghapariṇāyakā.

`Thera` (elder) means one who has reached a state of steadfastness, endowed with qualities that make one an elder. Because they know many nights, they are called `rattaññū` (of long standing). Because they have been gone forth for a long time, they are called `cirapabbajitā` (long-ordained). Because they stand in the position of a father to the Saṅgha, they are called `saṅghapitaro` (fathers of the Saṅgha). Because they stand in the position of a father, they lead the Saṅgha; having become foremost, they cause others to practice in the three trainings, therefore they are called `saṅghapariṇāyakā` (leaders of the Saṅgha).

Ye tesaṃ sakkārādīni na karonti, ovādatthāya dve tayo vāre upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchanti, tepi tesaṃ ovādaṃ na denti, paveṇikathaṃ na kathenti, sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ na sikkhāpenti. Te tehi vissaṭṭhā sīlādīhi dhammakkhandhehi sattahi ca ariyadhanehīti evamādīhi guṇehi parihāyanti. Ye pana tesaṃ sakkārādīni karonti, upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ te “evaṃ te abhikkamitabba”ntiādikaṃ ovādaṃ denti, paveṇikathaṃ kathenti, sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sikkhāpenti, terasahi dhutaṅgehi dasahi kathāvatthūhi anusāsanti. Te tesaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā sīlādīhi guṇehi vaḍḍhamānā sāmaññatthaṃ anupāpuṇanti. Evamettha hānivuddhiyo daṭṭhabbā.

Those junior monks who do not give respect and so on to those elders, and do not go to attend on them two or three times for the sake of receiving admonition—to them, those elders also give no admonition, do not speak the traditional talk, and do not have them learn the essential Dhamma discourse. They, having been abandoned by those elders, decline from qualities such as the aggregates of Dhamma beginning with virtue, and from the seven noble treasures. But for those junior monks who do give respect and so on to those elders and go to attend on them, the elders give admonition, such as, 'Thus you should advance,' they speak the traditional talk, they have them learn the essential Dhamma discourse, and they instruct them with the thirteen ascetic practices and the ten topics of discourse. They, having stood in the elders' admonition and growing in qualities such as virtue, gradually attain the goal of recluseship. Thus, in this context, decline and growth should be seen.

Punabbhavo sīlamassāti ponobbhavikā, punabbhavadāyikāti attho, tassā ponobbhavikāya. Na vasaṃ gacchissantīti ettha ye catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ kāraṇā upaṭṭhākānaṃ padānupadikā hutvā gāmato gāmaṃ vicaranti[P 4.0020], te tassā [M 3.0159] vasaṃ gacchanti nāma. Itare na gacchanti. Tattha hānivuddhiyo pākaṭāyeva.

'Ponobbhavikā' means that renewed existence is its nature; that is to say, it is a giver of renewed existence. Regarding 'they will not come under its control,' those who, for the sake of the four requisites, wander from village to village, having become followers in the footsteps of their supporters—they are said to come under its control. Others do not. Therein, decline and growth are indeed evident.

Āraññakesūti pañcadhanusatikapacchimesu. Sāpekkhāti sālayā. Gāmantasenāsanesu hi jhānaṃ appetvāpi tato vuṭṭhitamattova itthipurisadārakadārikādisaddaṃ suṇāti, yenassa adhigatavisesopi hāyatiyeva. Araññasenāsane niddāyitvāpi pabuddhamatto sīhabyagghamorādīnaṃ saddaṃ suṇāti, yena araññe pītiṃ paṭilabhitvā tameva sammasanto aggaphale patiṭṭhāti. Iti bhagavā [V 3.0161] gāmantasenāsane jhānaṃ appetvā nisinnabhikkhuto araññe niddāyamānameva pasaṃsati. Tasmā tameva atthavasaṃ paṭicca “āraññakesu senāsanesu sāpekkhā bhavissantī”ti āha.

'In wilderness dwellings' means in those at a minimum of five hundred bow-lengths. 'With expectation' means with longing. For in dwellings near a village, even having entered jhāna, just as soon as one emerges from it, one hears the sounds of women, men, boys, and girls, by which even the special attainment one has gained indeed declines. In a wilderness dwelling, even having slept, just upon awakening one hears the sounds of lions, tigers, peacocks, and so on, by which, having obtained joy in the wilderness and contemplating that very thing, one becomes established in the highest fruit. Thus, the Blessed One praises the very monk who is sleeping in the wilderness over a monk seated in a dwelling near a village having entered jhāna. Therefore, on account of that very benefit, he said, 'They will have longing for wilderness dwellings.'

Paccattaññeva satiṃ upaṭṭhāpessantīti attanāva attano abbhantare satiṃ upaṭṭhapessanti. Pesalāti piyasīlā. Idhāpi sabrahmacārīnaṃ āgamanaṃ anicchantā nevāsikā assaddhā honti appasannā, vihāraṃ sampattabhikkhūnaṃ paccuggamana-pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇa-āsanapaññāpanatālavaṇṭaggahaṇādīni na karonti. Atha nesaṃ avaṇṇo uggacchati “asukavihāravāsino bhikkhū assaddhā appasannā vihāraṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ vattappaṭivattampi na karontī”ti. Taṃ sutvā pabbajitā vihāradvārena gacchantāpi vihāraṃ na pavisanti. Evaṃ anāgatānaṃ anāgamanameva hoti. Āgatānaṃ pana phāsuvihāre [P 4.0021] asati yepi ajānitvā āgatā, te “vasissāmāti tāvacintetvā āgatamhā, imesaṃ pana nevāsikānaṃ iminā nīhārena ko vasissatī”ti nikkhamitvā gacchanti. Evaṃ so vihāro aññesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anāvāsova hoti. Tato nevāsikā sīlavantānaṃ dassanaṃ alabhantā kaṅkhāvinodakaṃ vā ācārasikkhāpakaṃ vā madhuradhammasavanaṃ vā na labhanti. Tesaṃ neva aggahitadhammaggahaṇaṃ na gahitasajjhāyakaraṇaṃ hoti. Iti nesaṃ hāniyeva hoti, na vuddhi.

'They will establish mindfulness right within themselves' means they will establish mindfulness within themselves by themselves. 'Pesalā' means those of amiable virtue. Here too, the resident monks, not wishing for the arrival of fellow monastics, become faithless and uninspired; they do not perform such duties as going out to meet the monks who have arrived at the monastery, taking their bowl and robe, preparing a seat, or taking a fan. Then a bad reputation arises for them: 'The monks residing in such-and-such monastery are faithless and uninspired; they do not perform even the major and minor duties for those who have entered the monastery.' Hearing that, monastics, even while passing by the monastery gate, do not enter the monastery. Thus, for those who have not yet come, there is only non-arrival. As for those who have come, since there is no comfortable dwelling, even those who came without knowing, thinking, 'We came having first intended to stay, but with this manner of these resident monks, who will stay?' leave and go. Thus that monastery becomes indeed an unsuitable dwelling for other monks. Then the resident monks, not obtaining the sight of virtuous ones, do not obtain the dispelling of their doubts, or instruction in proper conduct, or the hearing of the sweet Dhamma. For them there is neither the grasping of the ungrasped Dhamma nor the recitation of what has been grasped. Thus for them there is only decline, not growth.

Ye pana sabrahmacārīnaṃ āgamanaṃ icchanti, te saddhā honti pasannā, āgatānaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ paccuggamanādīni katvā senāsanaṃ paññapetvā denti[M 3.0160], te gahetvā bhikkhācāraṃ pavisanti, kaṅkhaṃ vinodenti, madhuradhammassavanaṃ labhanti. Atha nesaṃ kittisaddo uggacchati “asukavihāre bhikkhū evaṃ saddhā pasannā vattasampannā saṅgāhakā”ti. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū dūratopi āgacchanti. Tesaṃ nevāsikā vattaṃ karonti, samīpaṃ gantvā vuḍḍhataraṃ āgantukaṃ vanditvā nisīdanti, navakatarassa santike āsanaṃ gahetvā nisīditvā “imasmiṃ vihāre vasissatha, gamissathā”ti pucchanti. “Gamissāmā”ti vutte “sappāyaṃ senāsanaṃ, sulabhā bhikkhā”tiādīni vatvā gantuṃ na denti. Vinayadharo ce hoti, tassa santike vinayaṃ sajjhāyanti. Suttantādidharo ce, tassa santike taṃ taṃ dhammaṃ sajjhāyanti. Te āgantukatherānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇanti. Āgantukā “ekaṃ dve divasāni vasissāmāti āgatamhā, imesaṃ pana sukhasaṃvāsatāya dasa dvādasa vassāni vasimhā”ti vattāro honti. Evamettha hānivuddhiyo veditabbā.

But those who wish for the arrival of their fellow monastics are faithful and inspired. For the fellow monastics who have arrived, having performed the duties of going out to meet them and so on, they prepare and give them lodging. Taking them, they enter the alms-round, dispel their doubts, and obtain the hearing of the sweet Dhamma. Then the sound of their fame arises: 'In such-and-such monastery, the monks are so faithful, inspired, accomplished in their duties, and supportive.' Hearing that, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform their duties towards them; approaching, they pay respects to a more senior visitor and sit down. Having taken a seat near a more junior one, they sit and ask, 'Will you stay in this monastery, or will you go?' When it is said, 'We will go,' they say, 'The lodging is suitable, alms are easy to obtain,' and so on, and do not let them go. If there is a master of the Vinaya, they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If there is one who holds the Suttas and so on, they recite that particular Dhamma in his presence. They, abiding in the instruction of the visiting elders, attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. The visitors become speakers of this: 'We came thinking, "We will stay for one or two days," but because of the pleasant co-residence with these monks, we have stayed for ten or twelve years.' Thus, herein, decline and growth should be understood.

4. Dutiyasattakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Sutta of the Septet

24. Catutthe [V 3.0162][P 4.0022] na kammārāmāti ye divasaṃ cīvarakamma-kāyabandhanaparissāvana-dhammakaraṇa-sammajjani-pādakaṭhalikādīneva karonti, te sandhāyesa paṭikkhepo. Yo pana tesaṃ karaṇavelāya evaṃ etāni karoti, uddesavelāya uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, sajjhāyavelāya sajjhāyati, cetiyaṅgaṇavattavelāya cetiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ karoti, manasikāravelāya manasikāraṃ karoti, na so kammārāmo nāma.

24. In the fourth, 'delighting in work' is a rejection made in reference to those who spend their day just doing tasks like making robes, waistbands, water filters, water pots, brooms, and foot-scrapers. However, one who does these tasks only at the appropriate time, takes up a lesson at the time for lessons, recites at the time for recitation, performs duties in the stupa courtyard at the time for duties, and applies his mind to his meditation subject at the time for mental application—such a one is not called 'one who delights in work.'

Yo itthivaṇṇapurisavaṇṇādivasena ālāpasallāpaṃ karontoyeva rattindivaṃ vītināmeti, evarūpe bhasse pariyantakārī na hoti, ayaṃ bhassārāmo nāma. Yo pana rattindivaṃ dhammaṃ katheti, pañhaṃ vissajjeti, ayaṃ appabhassova bhasse pariyantakārīyeva. Kasmā? “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti (ma. ni. 1.273) vuttattā.

One who spends day and night engaged in talk and conversation about the beauty of women, the beauty of men, and so on, and does not make a limit to such talk—this person is called 'one who delights in talk.' However, one who spends day and night teaching the Dhamma or answering questions—this person is of little speech and indeed makes a limit to talk. Why? Because it is said: 'When you have gathered, monks, two things are to be done: either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence' (MN 26).

Yo ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi thinamiddhābhibhūto niddāyatiyeva, ayaṃ niddārāmo nāma. Yassa pana karajakāyagelaññena cittaṃ bhavaṅgaṃ [M 3.0161] otarati, nāyaṃ niddārāmo. Tenevāha – “abhijānāmahaṃ, aggivessana[P 4.0023], gimhānaṃ pacchime māse pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno niddaṃ okkamitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387).

One who, whether standing, walking, or sitting, is overcome by sloth and torpor and just sleeps—this is called one who delights in sleep. But when one's mind sinks into the life-continuum due to an affliction of the physical body, this is not called delighting in sleep. Therefore, it is said: 'I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of summer, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, spreading my outer robe folded fourfold, lying down on my right side, mindful and clearly comprehending, I fell asleep' (MN 36).

Yo “ekassa dutiyo, dvinnaṃ tatiyo, tiṇṇaṃ catuttho”ti evaṃ saṃsaṭṭhova viharati, ekako assādaṃ na labhati, ayaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo. Yo pana catūsu iriyāpathesu ekakova assādaṃ labhati, nāyaṃ saṅgaṇikārāmo.

One who lives mingled with others, thinking, 'A second for one, a third for two, a fourth for three,' and does not find delight in being alone—this is one who delights in company. But one who finds delight in being alone in the four postures is not one who delights in company.

Asantasambhāvanicchāya samannāgatā dussīlā pāpicchā nāma. Yesaṃ pāpakā mittā catūsu iriyāpathesu saha ayanato pāpasahāyā, ye ca tanninnatappoṇatappabbhāratāya pāpesu sampavaṅkā, te pāpamittā pāpasahāyā pāpasampavaṅkā nāma.

Immoral persons endowed with the desire to be esteemed for qualities they do not possess are called 'those of evil wishes.' Those who have evil friends are called 'evil companions' because they associate together in the four postures; and those who, due to their inclination, leaning, and tendency towards them, are bent towards evil persons—they are called 'evil friends,' 'evil companions,' and 'those bent towards evil.'

Oramattakenāti [V 3.0163] avaramattakena appamattakena. Antarāti arahattaṃ appatvāva etthantare. Vosānanti pariniṭṭhitabhāvaṃ “alamettāvatā”ti osakkanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāva sīlapārisuddhijjhānavipassanā sotāpannabhāvādīnaṃ aññataramattakena vosānaṃ nāpajjissanti, tāva vuddhiyeva bhikkhūnaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā, no parihānīti.

'By a small amount' means by an inferior, trifling amount. 'In the meantime' means before attaining Arahantship, in that interval. 'Conclusion' means the state of completion, or drawing back with the thought, 'This much is enough.' This is what is said: So long as monks do not reach a conclusion with some small measure of purity of virtue, jhāna, insight, the state of a stream-enterer, and so on, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.

7. Saññāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Saññā Sutta

27. Sattame aniccasaññādayo aniccānupassanādīhi sahagatasaññā.

27. In the seventh sutta, perceptions of impermanence and so on are perceptions accompanied by the contemplation of impermanence and so on.

8. Paṭhamaparihānisuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the First Sutta on Decline

28. Aṭṭhame uppannānaṃ saṅghakiccānaṃ nittharaṇena bhāraṃ vahantīti bhāravāhino. Te tena paññāyissantīti te therā tena attano therabhāvānurūpena kiccena paññāyissanti. Tesu yogaṃ [P 4.0024] āpajjatīti payogaṃ āpajjati, sayaṃ tāni kiccāni kātuṃ ārabhatīti.

28. In the eighth sutta, they are called burden-bearers because they bear the burden by bringing to completion the arisen duties of the Sangha. As to 'They will be known by that,' it means those elders will be known by that deed befitting their status as elders. As to 'He applies effort in regard to them,' it means he applies effort; he himself undertakes to perform those duties.

9. Dutiyaparihānisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Decline

29. Navame [M 3.0162] bhikkhudassanaṃ hāpetīti bhikkhusaṅghassa dassanatthāya gamanaṃ hāpeti. Adhisīleti pañcasīladasasīlasaṅkhāte uttamasīle. Ito bahiddhāti imamhā sāsanā bahiddhā. Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesatīti deyyadhammapaṭiggāhake pariyesati. Tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotīti tesaṃ bāhirānaṃ titthiyānaṃ datvā pacchā bhikkhūnaṃ deti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

29. In the ninth sutta, as to 'he neglects the seeing of bhikkhus,' it means he neglects going to see the Sangha of bhikkhus. As to adhisīle (in higher virtue), it means in the supreme virtue reckoned as the five precepts and the ten precepts. As to 'outside of this,' it means outside of this Dispensation. As to 'he seeks one worthy of offerings,' it means he searches for recipients of offerings. As to 'and there he performs a prior service,' it means having given to those outsiders, the sectarians, he gives to the bhikkhus afterwards. The rest is clear everywhere.

Vajjisattakavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the Seven Vajjian Principles.

4. Devatāvaggo

4. The Chapter on Deities

5. Paṭhamamittasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the First Sutta on a Friend

36. Catutthassa [V 3.0164] pañcame duddadanti duppariccajaṃ mahārahaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ. Dukkaraṃ karotīti kātuṃ asukaraṃ kammaṃ karoti. Dukkhamaṃ khamatīti sahāyassa atthāya duradhivāsaṃ adhivāseti. Guyhamassa āvikarotīti attano guyhaṃ tassa āvikaroti. Guyhamassa pariguhatīti tassa guyhaṃ aññesaṃ nācikkhati. Khīṇena nātimaññatīti tassa bhoge khīṇe tena khayena taṃ nātimaññati, tasmiṃ omānaṃ attani ca atimānaṃ na karoti.

36. In the fifth sutta of the fourth chapter, as to duddadaṃ (what is hard to give), it means a possession that is hard to relinquish and of great value. As to 'he does what is difficult,' it means he performs a deed that is not easy to do. As to 'he endures what is painful,' it means for the sake of a companion, he endures what is hard to bear. As to 'he reveals his secret to that one,' it means he discloses his own secret to that one. As to 'he conceals that one's secret,' it means he does not tell that one's secret to others. As to 'he does not despise him when he is ruined,' it means when his wealth is depleted, he does not despise him because of that depletion; he does not show contempt towards him nor conceit in himself.

6. Dutiyamittasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Second Sutta on a Friend

37. Chaṭṭhe vattāti vacanakusalo. Vacanakkhamoti vacanaṃ khamati, dinnaṃ ovādaṃ karoti. Gambhīranti guyhaṃ rahassaṃ jhānanissitaṃ vipassanāmaggaphalanibbānanissitaṃ.

37. In the sixth sutta, as to vattā (a speaker), it means one who is skilled in speech. As to vacanakkhamo (one who is patient with speech), it means he endures speech and carries out the advice that is given. As to gambhīraṃ (profound), it means hidden, secret, related to jhāna, and related to insight, the path, fruition, and Nibbāna.

7. Paṭhamapaṭisambhidāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the First Sutta on Analytical Knowledge

38. Sattame [P 4.0025] idaṃ me cetaso līnattanti uppanne cetaso līnatte “idaṃ me cetaso līnatta”nti yathāsabhāvato jānāti. Ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittaṃ nāma thinamiddhānugataṃ. Bahiddhā vikkhittaṃ nāma pañcasu kāmaguṇesu [M 3.0163] vikkhittaṃ. Vedanātiādīni papañcamūlavasena gahitāni. Vedanā hi taṇhāya mūlaṃ sukhavasena taṇhuppattito, saññā diṭṭhiyā mūlaṃ avibhūtārammaṇe diṭṭhiuppattito, vitakko mānassa mūlaṃ vitakkavasena asmīti mānuppattito. Sappāyāsappāyesūti upakārānupakāresu. Nimittanti kāraṇaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

38. In the seventh sutta, as to 'This is the sluggishness of my mind,' it means that when sluggishness of mind has arisen, one knows it according to its true nature as: 'This is the sluggishness of my mind.' What is called 'internally contracted' is a mind accompanied by sloth and torpor. What is called 'externally distracted' is a mind scattered among the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Feeling' and so on are taken by way of being the root of proliferation. For feeling is the root of craving, because craving arises by way of pleasant feeling. Perception is the root of wrong view, because wrong view arises in regard to an indistinct object. Thought is the root of conceit, because conceit arises by way of the thought, 'I am.' As to 'in the suitable and unsuitable,' it means in what is helpful and unhelpful. As to nimitta (sign), it means cause. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Devatāvaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Chapter on Deities.

5. Mahāyaññavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Great Sacrifice

1-2. Sattaviññāṇaṭṭhitisuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Stations of Consciousness and Others

44-45. Pañcamassa [V 3.0165] paṭhame viññāṇaṭṭhitiyoti paṭisandhiviññāṇassa ṭhānāni. Seyyathāpīti nidassanatthe nipāto, yathā manussāti attho. Aparimāṇesu hi cakkavāḷesu aparimāṇānaṃ manussānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena dvepi ekasadisā natthi. Yepi hi katthaci yamakabhātaro vaṇṇena vā saṇṭhānena vā sadisā honti, tesampi ālokitavilokitakathitahasitagamanaṭṭhānādīhi viseso hotiyeva. Tasmā nānattakāyāti vuttā. Paṭisandhisaññā pana nesaṃ tihetukāpi dvihetukāpi ahetukāpi hoti. Tasmā nānattasaññinoti vuttā. Ekacce ca devāti cha kāmāvacaradevā. Tesu hi kesañci kāyo nīlo hoti, kesañci pītakādivaṇṇo. Saññā pana tesaṃ dvihetukāpi tihetukāpi hoti, ahetukā natthi. Ekacce [P 4.0026] ca vinipātikāti catuapāyavinimuttā uttaramātā yakkhinī, piyaṅkaramātā, phussamittā, dhammaguttāti evamādikā aññe ca vemānikā petā. Etesañhi pītaodātakāḷamaṅguracchavisāmavaṇṇādivasena ceva kisa thūlarassadīghavasena ca kāyo nānā hoti, manussānaṃ viya dvihetukatihetukaahetukavasena saññāpi. Te pana devā viya na mahesakkhā, kapaṇamanussā viya appesakkhā dullabhaghāsacchādanā dukkhapīḷitā viharanti. Ekacce kāḷapakkhe dukkhitā juṇhapakkhe sukhitā honti. Tasmā sukhasamussayato vinipatitattā vinipātikāti vuttā. Ye panettha tihetukā, tesaṃ dhammābhisamayopi hoti piyaṅkaramātādīnaṃ viya.

44-45. In the first of the fifth chapter, 'stations of consciousness' are the abodes of rebirth-linking consciousness. The particle 'seyyathāpi' is used in the sense of an illustration; the meaning is 'just as humans'. Indeed, in the countless world-systems, among the countless human beings, there are not even two who are exactly alike in terms of color, form, and so on. For even if somewhere there are twin brothers who are similar in color or form, there is still a difference in their looking, glancing, speaking, laughing, walking, standing, and so on. Therefore, they are said to be 'of diverse bodies'. Their rebirth-linking perception, however, can be accompanied by three roots, two roots, or no roots. Therefore, they are said to be 'of diverse perceptions'. 'And some devas' refers to the six sense-sphere devas. For among them, the body of some is blue, while for others it is of a yellow or other color. Their perception, however, can be accompanied by two roots or three roots; it is never rootless. 'And some who have fallen into a woeful state' refers to those freed from the four woeful planes, such as the yakkhaṇī Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and other petas with celestial mansions. For their bodies are diverse in terms of color—yellow, white, black, the color of a bedbug, dark, and so on—and in terms of build—thin, stout, short, and tall. Like humans, their perception can also be accompanied by two roots, three roots, or no roots. They are not, however, powerful like devas; like destitute humans, they are of little power, find it difficult to obtain food and clothing, and live afflicted by suffering. Some are miserable during the dark fortnight and happy during the bright fortnight. Therefore, because they have fallen from an accumulation of happiness, they are called 'vinipātika' (those who have fallen). Among them, for those who are three-rooted, there can also be the comprehension of the Dhamma, as in the case of Piyaṅkaramātā and others.

Brahmakāyikāti [M 3.0164] brahmapārisajjabrahmapurohitamahābrahmāno. Paṭhamābhinibbattāti te sabbepi paṭhamajjhānena abhinibbattā. Brahmapārisajjā pana parittena abhinibbattā, tesaṃ kappassa tatiyo bhāgo āyuppamāṇaṃ. Brahmapurohitā majjhimena, tesaṃ upaḍḍhakappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo ca tesaṃ vipphārikataro hoti. Mahābrahmāno paṇītena, tesaṃ kappo āyuppamāṇaṃ, kāyo ca pana tesaṃ ativipphārikova hoti. Iti te kāyassa nānattā paṭhamajjhānavasena saññāya ekattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññinoti veditabbā.

'Brahmakāyika' refers to the Brahmās of the Retinue, the Brahmā Ministers, and the Great Brahmās. 'First arisen' means they are all born through the first jhāna. The Brahmās of the Retinue are born through the lesser [first jhāna]; their lifespan is one-third of an aeon. The Brahmā Ministers are born through the middling [first jhāna]; their lifespan is half an aeon, and their bodies are more expansive. The Great Brahmās are born through the sublime [first jhāna]; their lifespan is a full aeon, and their bodies are exceedingly expansive. Thus, because of the diversity of their bodies and the uniformity of their perception by means of the first jhāna, they should be understood as being 'of diverse bodies and uniform perception'.

Yathā [V 3.0166] ca te, evaṃ catūsu apāyesu sattā. Nirayesu hi kesañci gāvutaṃ, kesañci aḍḍhayojanaṃ, kesañci yojanaṃ attabhāvo hoti, devadattassa [P 4.0027] pana yojanasatiko jāto. Tiracchānesupi keci khuddakā, keci mahantā. Pettivisayesupi keci saṭṭhihatthā, keci asītihatthā honti, keci suvaṇṇā, keci dubbaṇṇā. Tathā kālakañcikā asurā. Apicettha dīghapiṭṭhikapetā nāma saṭṭhiyojanikāpi honti. Saññā pana sabbesampi akusalavipākāhetukāva hoti. Iti āpāyikāpi nānattakāyā ekattasaññinotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti.

Just as it is for them, so it is for beings in the four woeful planes. In the hells, the bodies of some are a gāvuta in size, some half a yojana, and some a full yojana; but Devadatta’s became one hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small, some large. In the realm of ghosts, some are sixty cubits tall, some eighty cubits; some are of good color, some of bad color. Likewise for the Kālakañcika asuras. Moreover, among them, there are ghosts called Dīghapiṭṭhika who are even sixty yojanas. The perception of all of them, however, is solely rootless, the result of unwholesome kamma. Thus, beings of the woeful planes are also counted as being 'of diverse bodies and uniform perception'.

Ābhassarāti daṇḍaukkāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati vissaratīti ābhassarā. Tesu pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyajjhānadvayaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā parittābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ dve kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Majjhimaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā appamāṇābhā nāma honti, tesaṃ cattāro kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Paṇītaṃ bhāvetvā upapannā ābhassarā nāma honti, tesaṃ aṭṭha kappā āyuppamāṇaṃ. Idha pana ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena sabbeva te gahitā. Sabbesañhi tesaṃ kāyo ekavipphārova hoti, saññā pana avitakkavicāramattā vā avitakkaavicārā vāti nānā.

'Ābhassarā' (Radiant) are so called because from their bodies radiance issues forth and scatters as if breaking off and falling, like the flame of a torch. Among them, in the fivefold jhāna system, those who are reborn having developed the pair of the second and third jhānas to a lesser degree are called Parittābhā (Of Limited Radiance); their lifespan is two aeons. Those reborn having developed them to a middling degree are called Appamāṇābhā (Of Immeasurable Radiance); their lifespan is four aeons. Those reborn having developed them to a sublime degree are called Ābhassarā (Radiant); their lifespan is eight aeons. Here, however, all of them are included by way of the highest designation. For the bodies of all of them are of a uniform radiance, but their perceptions are diverse: some are with only sustained application but without initial application, while others are without initial application and without sustained application.

Subhakiṇhāti subhena vokiṇṇā vikiṇṇā, subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanāti attho. Etesañhi na ābhassarānaṃ viya chijjitvā chijjitvā pabhā gacchati. Pañcakanaye pana parittamajjhimapaṇītassa catutthajjhānassa vasena soḷasabāttiṃsacatussaṭṭhikappāyukā parittaappamāṇasubhakiṇhā nāma hutvā nibbattanti. Iti sabbepi [P 4.0028] te ekattakāyā ceva catutthajjhānasaññāya [M 3.0165] ekattasaññino cāti veditabbā. Vehapphalāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitimeva bhajanti. Asaññasattā viññāṇābhāvā ettha saṅgahaṃ na gacchanti, sattāvāsesu gacchanti.

'Subhakiṇhā' means 'pervaded with beauty'; the meaning is that they are a single solid mass of beautiful bodily radiance and color. For their radiance, unlike that of the Ābhassarā brahmās, does not issue forth by breaking apart. In the fivefold jhāna system, by means of the fourth jhāna that is lesser, middling, and sublime, they are reborn as beings named Parittasubhā, Appamāṇasubhā, and Subhakiṇhā, with lifespans of sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four aeons respectively. Thus, all of them should be understood as having uniform bodies and, due to the perception of the fourth jhāna, uniform perception. The Vehapphalā brahmās also belong to the fourth station of consciousness. The non-percipient beings, due to the absence of consciousness, are not included here, but they are included among the abodes of beings.

Suddhāvāsā vivaṭṭapakkhe ṭhitā na sabbakālikā, kappasatasahassampi asaṅkheyyampi buddhasuññe loke na uppajjanti. Soḷasakappasahassaabbhantare buddhesu uppannesuyeva uppajjanti. Dhammacakkappavattissa bhagavato khandhāvāraṭṭhānasadisā honti. Tasmā neva viññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ na sattāvāsaṃ bhajanti. Mahāsīvatthero pana “na kho pana so, sāriputta, āvāso sulabharūpo, yo mayā anāvutthapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā aññatra suddhāvāsehi devehī”ti [V 3.0167] (ma. ni. 1.160) iminā suttena suddhāvāsāpi catutthaviññāṇaṭṭhitiṃ catutthasattāvāsañca bhajantīti vadati, taṃ appatibāhiyattā suttassa anuññātaṃ.

The Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) brahmās exist in the evolving phase of the world cycle; they are not perpetual. For a hundred thousand aeons or even an incalculable number of aeons, they do not arise in a world devoid of Buddhas. They arise only within an interval of sixteen thousand aeons when Buddhas have arisen. They are like the temporary camp-site of the Blessed One who turns the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they belong neither to a station of consciousness nor to an abode of beings. The Elder Mahāsīva, however, states that based on the sutta, 'Indeed, Sāriputta, that abode is not easily found which I have not previously dwelled in during this long time, apart from the Suddhāvāsa devas' (MN 1.160), the Suddhāvāsa abodes also belong to the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. Since this is not contradicted by the Sutta, it is permitted.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ yatheva saññāya, evaṃ viññāṇassāpi sukhumattā neva viññāṇaṃ nāviññāṇaṃ. Tasmā viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu na vuttaṃ. Dutiye samādhiparikkhārāti maggasamādhissa sambhārā.

Just as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is so called due to the subtlety of perception, so too, due to the subtlety of consciousness, it is neither consciousness nor non-consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness. In the second sutta, 'requisites for concentration' means the supports for the concentration of the path.

3. Paṭhamaaggisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the First Discourse on Fire

46. Tatiye sabbepi rāgādayo anuḍahanaṭṭhena aggī. Āhuneyyaggītiādīsu panettha āhunaṃ vuccati sakkāro, āhunaṃ arahantīti āhuneyyā. Mātāpitaro hi puttānaṃ bahupakārattā āhunaṃ arahanti, tesu vippaṭipajjamānā puttā nirayādīsu nibbattanti. Tasmā kiñcāpi mātāpitaro na [P 4.0029] anuḍahanti, anuḍahanassa pana paccayā honti. Iti anuḍahanaṭṭheneva āhuneyyaggīti vuccanti. Gahapatīti pana gehasāmiko vuccati, so mātugāmassa sayanavatthālaṅkārādianuppadānena bahupakāro. Taṃ aticaranto mātugāmo nirayādīsu nibbattati. Tasmā sopi purimanayeneva anuḍahanaṭṭhena gahapataggīti vutto. Dakkhiṇeyyaggīti ettha pana dakkhiṇāti cattāro paccayā, bhikkhusaṅgho dakkhiṇeyyo. So hi gihīnaṃ tīsu saraṇesu pañcasu sīlesu dasasu sīlesu mātāpitupaṭṭhāne dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇupaṭṭhāneti evamādīsu kalyāṇadhammesu niyojanena bahupakāro. Tasmiṃ micchāpaṭipannā gihī [M 3.0166] bhikkhusaṅghaṃ akkositvā paribhāsitvā nirayādīsu nibbattanti. Tasmā sopi purimanayeneva anuḍahanaṭṭhena dakkhiṇeyyaggīti vutto. Kaṭṭhato nibbatto pākatikova aggi kaṭṭhaggi nāma.

3. In the third [sutta], all lusts and so forth are fires in the sense of burning. In 'the fire worthy of offerings' (āhuneyyaggī) and so forth, 'offering' (āhuna) is said to be honor (sakkāra). Because they are worthy of offerings, they are called 'worthy of offerings' (āhuneyyā). Parents, because they are of great benefit to their children, are worthy of offerings. Children who act wrongly towards them are reborn in hell and so forth. Thus, although parents do not burn, they are conditions for burning. Therefore, they are called 'the fire worthy of offerings' precisely in the sense of burning. A householder (gahapati) is said to be the master of the house. He is of great benefit to his wife by providing beds, clothes, ornaments, and so forth. A wife who transgresses against him is reborn in hell and so forth. Thus, he too is called 'the householder’s fire' in the same way, in the sense of burning. Here, in 'the fire worthy of gifts' (dakkhiṇeyyaggī), dakkhiṇā refers to the four requisites, and the monastic community (bhikkhusaṅgho) is worthy of gifts (dakkhiṇeyyo). They are of great benefit to laypeople by guiding them in the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, service to parents, support of righteous ascetics and brahmins, and other such wholesome qualities. Laypeople who act wrongly towards them, having reviled and abused the monastic community, are reborn in hell and so forth. Therefore, they too are called 'the fire worthy of gifts' in the same way, in the sense of burning. The fire produced from wood, which is just an ordinary one, is called a wood fire.

4. Dutiyaaggisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Fire

47. Catutthe uggatasarīrassāti so kira brāhmaṇamahāsālo attabhāvenapi bhogehipi uggato sārappatto ahosi, tasmā uggatasarīrotveva paññāyittha. Upakkhaṭoti paccupaṭṭhito. Thūṇūpanītānīti yūpasaṅkhātaṃ thūṇaṃ upanītāni. Yaññatthāyāti vadhitvā yajanatthāya. Upasaṅkamīti so [V 3.0168] kira sabbaṃ taṃ yaññasambhāraṃ sajjetvā cintesi – “samaṇo kira gotamo mahāpañño, kiṃ nu kho me yaññassa vaṇṇaṃ kathessati udāhu avaṇṇaṃ, pucchitvā jānissāmī”ti iminā kāraṇena yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Aggissa [P 4.0030] ādānanti yaññayajanatthāya navassa maṅgalaggino ādiyanaṃ. Sabbena sabbanti sabbena sutena sabbaṃ sutaṃ sameti saṃsandati, ekasadisaṃ hotīti dasseti. Satthānīti vihiṃsanaṭṭhena satthāni viyāti satthāni. Sayaṃ paṭhamaṃ samārambhatīti attanāva paṭhamataraṃ ārabhati. Hantunti hanituṃ.

46. In the fourth [sutta], 'of one with an exalted body'—it is said that he was a wealthy brahmin, eminent both in person and in wealth, having attained the essence of prosperity; therefore he was known as 'one with an exalted body.' 'Prepared' means made ready. 'Brought to the pillar' means brought to the pillar known as a sacrificial post (yūpa). 'For the sake of sacrifice' means for the purpose of sacrificing after slaughter. 'He approached'—it is said that after preparing all the sacrificial materials, he thought: 'The ascetic Gotama is said to be of great wisdom. Will he speak in praise of my sacrifice or in dispraise? Having asked, I will know.' For this reason, he approached the Blessed One. 'Taking up fire' refers to the kindling of a new auspicious fire for the purpose of sacrifice. 'All with all' shows that all that is heard agrees with all that is heard, it harmonizes, it becomes of one kind. 'Weapons'—because of the meaning of harming, they are like weapons, and therefore are called weapons. 'He himself first begins' means he himself is the first to begin. `Hantun` means to kill.

Pahātabbāti pariharitabbā. Atohayanti ato hi mātāpitito ayaṃ. Āhutoti āgato. Sambhūtoti uppanno. Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, gahapataggīti ayaṃ puttadārādigaṇo yasmā, gahapati, viya gehasāmiko viya hutvā aggati vicarati, tasmā gahapataggīti vuccati. Attānanti cittaṃ. Damentīti indriyadamanena damenti. Samentīti rāgādisamanena samenti. Tesaññeva parinibbāpanena parinibbāpenti. Nikkhipitabboti yathā na vinassati, evaṃ ṭhapetabbo. Upavāyatanti upavāyatu. Evañca pana vatvā brāhmaṇo sabbesampi tesaṃ pāṇānaṃ jīvitaṃ datvā yaññasālaṃ viddhaṃsetvā satthu sāsane opānabhūto ahosīti.

4. 'Should be abandoned' means should be avoided. 'From this'—because this is from mother and father. 'Brought forth' means having come. 'Produced' means having arisen. This, brahmin, is called the householder's fire—this group of sons, wives, and so on, because, like a householder, like the master of the house, it moves about as the foremost. Therefore, it is called the householder's fire. 'The self' means the mind. 'They restrain' means they restrain by restraining the senses. 'They calm' means they calm by the calming of lust and so on. They completely quench by the complete quenching of those very things. 'Should be laid aside' means it should be kept in such a way that it does not perish. 'Let him blow' means let him blow. And having spoken thus, the brahmin, having given life to all those beings, destroyed the sacrificial hall, and became a wellspring in the Teacher's dispensation.

5-6. Saññāsuttadvayavaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Two Discourses on Perception

48-49. Pañcame [M 3.0167] amatogadhāti nibbānapatiṭṭhā. Amatapariyosānāti nibbānāvasānā. Chaṭṭhe methunadhammasamāpattiyāti methunadhammena samaṅgibhāvato. Nhārudaddulanti nhārukhaṇḍaṃ nhāruvilekhanaṃ vā. Anusandatīti [P 4.0031] pavattati. Natthi me pubbenāparaṃ visesoti natthi mayhaṃ pubbena abhāvitakālena saddhiṃ aparaṃ bhāvitakāle viseso. Lokacitresūti tidhātukalokasannivāsasaṅkhātesu lokacitresu. Ālasyeti ālasiyabhāve. Vissaṭṭhiyeti vissaṭṭhabhāve. Ananuyogeti yogassa ananuyuñjane. Ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānāpagatanti ahaṅkāradiṭṭhito ca mamaṅkārataṇhāto ca navavidhamānato ca apagataṃ. Vidhāsamatikkantanti tisso vidhā atikkantaṃ. Santanti tappaccanīkakilesehi santaṃ. Suvimuttanti pañcahi vimuttīhi suṭṭhu vimuttaṃ.

In the fifth, 'immersed in the deathless' means established in Nibbāna. 'Ending in the deathless' means culminating in Nibbāna. In the sixth, 'by the attainment of the sexual act' means from being endowed with the sexual act. 'A tangle of sinews' means a piece of sinew or a scraping of sinew. 'It flows on' means it proceeds. 'There is no distinction for me between before and after' means: for me, there is no distinction for the later time of development compared with the former time of non-development. 'In the world's variegatedness' means in the variegated worlds which are reckoned as the abodes of the three realms. 'In sloth' means in the state of laziness. 'In neglect' means in the state of neglect. 'In non-application' means in the non-application of effort. 'Devoid of 'I'-making, 'mine'-making, and conceit' means devoid of the view of 'I'-making, the craving of 'mine'-making, and the ninefold conceit. 'Having transcended distinctions' means having transcended the three distinctions. 'Peaceful' means peaceful from the opposing defilements. 'Well-liberated' means well liberated by the five liberations.

7. Methunasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on Sexual Intercourse

50. Sattame [V 3.0169] upasaṅkamīti bhuttapātarāso dāsakammakaraparivuto upasaṅkami. Bhavampinoti bhavampi nu. Brahmacārī paṭijānātīti “ahaṃ brahmacārī”ti evaṃ brahmacariyavāsaṃ paṭijānātīti pucchati. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “brāhmaṇasamaye vedaṃ uggaṇhantā aṭṭhacattālīsa vassāni brahmacariyaṃ caranti. Samaṇo pana gotamo agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto tīsu pāsādesu tividhanāṭakaratiyā abhirami, idāni kiṃ nu kho vakkhatī”ti imamatthaṃ sandhāyevaṃ pucchati. Tato bhagavā mantena kaṇhasappaṃ gaṇhanto viya amittaṃ gīvāya pādena akkamanto viya attano saṃkilesakāle chabbassāni padhānacariyāya rajjasukhaṃ vā pāsādesu nāṭakasampattiṃ vā ārabbha vitakkamattassāpi anuppannabhāvaṃ sandhāya sīhanādaṃ nadanto yañhi taṃ brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha [P 4.0032] dvayaṃdvayasamāpattinti dvīhi dvīhi samāpajjitabbabhāvaṃ. Dukkhasmāti sakalavaṭṭadukkhato. Sañjagghatīti hasitakathaṃ katheti. Saṃkīḷatīti keḷiṃ karoti. Saṃkeḷāyatīti mahāhasitaṃ hasati. Cakkhunā cakkhunti attano cakkhunā tassā cakkhuṃ paṭivijjhitvā upanijjhāyati. Tirokuṭṭaṃ vā tiropākāraṃ vāti parakuṭṭe vā parapākāre [M 3.0168] vā. Devoti eko devarājā. Devaññataroti aññataro devaputto. Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhinti arahattañceva sabbaññutaññāṇañca.

50. In the seventh discourse, 'he approached' means he approached having eaten his morning meal, surrounded by servants and workers. 'Does the venerable one also...?' means 'Does the venerable one also claim it?'. 'Do you claim to be a celibate?' means he asks, 'Do you declare the life of celibacy thus, saying, "I am a celibate"?'. It seems he thought thus: 'Brahmins, while learning the Vedas, practice celibacy for forty-eight years. But the ascetic Gotama, while living the household life, delighted in the three mansions with their threefold theatrical performances. Now, what will he declare?'. With this in mind, he asks. Then the Blessed One, like one seizing a black serpent with a mantra or treading on an enemy's neck with his foot, referring to the non-arising of even a mere thought concerning royal pleasure or the excellence of theatrical performances in the mansions during the six years of his striving at the time when he was subject to defilements, roaring a lion's roar, he spoke, beginning with 'That, O brahmin...' and so forth. There, 'a twofold attainment' means the state of being attainable by two and two. 'From suffering' means from all the suffering of the round of existence. 'He jests' means he speaks joking talk. 'He sports' means he engages in sport. 'He laughs loudly' means he laughs a great laugh. 'With the eye, the eye' means having pierced her eye with his own eye, he scrutinizes her. 'Beyond a wall or beyond a fence' means on the other side of another's wall or on the other side of another's fence. 'A deva' means one king of the devas. 'A certain deva' means a certain devaputta. 'Unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment' means both Arahantship and all-knowing knowledge.

8. Saṃyogasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Discourse on Connections

51. Aṭṭhame saṃyogavisaṃyoganti saṃyogavisaṃyogasādhakaṃ. Dhammapariyāyanti dhammakāraṇaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ itthindriyanti niyakajjhatte itthibhāvaṃ. Itthikuttanti itthikiriyaṃ. Itthākappanti nivāsanapārupanādiitthiākappaṃ. Itthividhanti itthiyā mānavidhaṃ. Itthichandanti itthiyā ajjhāsayacchandaṃ. Itthissaranti itthisaddaṃ. Itthālaṅkāranti itthiyā pasādhanabhaṇḍaṃ. Purisindriyādīsupi eseva nayo. Bahiddhā saṃyoganti purisena saddhiṃ samāgamaṃ. Ativattatīti anabhiratāti evaṃ vuttāya balavavipassanāya ariyamaggaṃ patvā ativattati. Imasmiṃ [P 4.0033] sutte vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

51. In the eighth discourse, 'bondage and non-bondage' means that which accomplishes bondage and non-bondage. 'The exposition of the Dhamma' means the reason for the teaching. 'The internal female faculty' means the state of being a woman within oneself. 'Feminine conduct' means feminine actions. 'Feminine appearance' means a woman's appearance, such as dressing and draping. 'The feminine manner' means a woman's manner of pride. 'Feminine desire' means a woman's desire which is her inclination. 'Feminine voice' means a woman's sound. 'Feminine adornment' means a woman's items for adornment. This same method applies to the male faculty and so on. 'External bondage' means association with a man. 'One transcends' means: not delighting, one transcends by reaching the noble path through powerful insight as has been stated. In this discourse, the cycle of existence and the freedom from it are taught.

9. Dānamahapphalasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Discourse on the Great Fruit of Giving

52. Navame [V 3.0170] sāpekhoti sataṇho. Paṭibaddhacittoti vipāke baddhacitto. Sannidhipekhoti nidhānapekho hutvā. Peccāti paralokaṃ gantvā. Taṃ kammaṃ khepetvāti taṃ kammavipākaṃ khepetvā. Iddhinti vipākiddhiṃ. Yasanti parivārasampadaṃ. Ādhipaccanti jeṭṭhabhāvakāraṇaṃ. Āgantā itthattanti itthabhāvaṃ ime pañcakkhandhe puna āgantā, na tatrūpapattiko na uparūpapattiko, heṭṭhāgāmīyeva hotīti attho. Sāhu dānanti dānaṃ nāmetaṃ sādhu bhaddakaṃ sundaraṃ. Tāni mahāyaññānīti tāni sappinavanītadadhimadhuphāṇitādīhi niṭṭhānaṃ gatāni mahādānāni. Cittālaṅkāracittaparikkhāranti samathavipassanācittassa alaṅkārabhūtañceva parivārabhūtañca. Brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyatanti na sakkā tattha dānena upapajjituṃ. Yasmā pana taṃ samathavipassanācittassa alaṅkārabhūtaṃ, tasmā tena dānālaṅkatena cittena jhānañceva ariyamaggañca nibbattetvā jhānena tattha upapajjati. Anāgāmī hotīti jhānānāgāmī nāma hoti. Anāgantā itthattanti puna itthabhāvaṃ na āgantā, uparūpapattiko [P 4.0034] vā tatrūpapattiko vā hutvā tattheva parinibbāyati. Iti imesu dānesu paṭhamaṃ taṇhuttariyadānaṃ, dutiyaṃ cittīkāradānaṃ, tatiyaṃ hirottappadānaṃ, catutthaṃ niravasesadānaṃ[M 3.0169], pañcamaṃ dakkhiṇeyyadānaṃ, chaṭṭhaṃ somanassupavicāradānaṃ, sattamaṃ alaṅkāraparivāradānaṃ nāmāti.

52. In the ninth discourse, 'with expectation' means with craving. 'With a bound mind' means having a mind bound to the result. 'Expecting to store up' means being one who expects a store. 'After passing away' means having gone to the next world. 'Having exhausted that kamma' means having exhausted the result of that kamma. 'Power' refers to the power of the result. 'Glory' means the accomplishment of a retinue. 'Sovereignty' refers to the making of the state of being a leader. 'Returning to this state' means returning again to this state of being, to these five aggregates; not being reborn in that same realm nor in a higher realm, one becomes one who comes to a lower realm. This is the meaning. 'Excellent is giving' means this giving is good and excellent. 'Those great sacrifices' refers to those great gifts completed with ghee, fresh butter, curd, honey, molasses, and so on. 'Adornment and equipment of the mind' means that which is both an adornment and a requisite for the mind of serenity and insight. 'Companionship with the devas of the Brahmā world' means it is not possible to be reborn there by means of giving. However, because that giving is an adornment for the mind of serenity and insight, therefore, with that mind adorned by giving, having produced both jhāna and the noble path, one is reborn there by means of jhāna. 'One becomes a non-returner' means one becomes a non-returner by means of jhāna. 'Not returning to this state' means not returning again to this state of being; having been reborn either in a higher realm or in that same realm, one attains final Nibbāna right there. Thus, among these gifts, the first is named the gift surpassing craving; the second, the gift of respect; the third, the gift of moral shame and dread; the fourth, the gift without remainder; the fifth, the gift to those worthy of offerings; the sixth, the gift with joyful reflection; and the seventh is named the gift that is an adornment and a requisite.

10. Nandamātāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Nandamātā Sutta

53. Dasamaṃ atthuppattivasena desitaṃ. Satthā kira vutthavasso pavāretvā dve aggasāvake ohāya “dakkhiṇāgiriṃ cārikaṃ gamissāmī”ti nikkhami, rājā pasenadi kosalo, anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati, visākhā mahāupāsikā, aññe ca bahujanā dasabalaṃ nivattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati “satthāraṃ nivattetuṃ nāsakkhi”nti raho cintayamāno nisīdi. Atha naṃ puṇṇā nāma dāsī disvā “kiṃ nu kho te, sāmi, na pubbe viya indriyāni vippasannānī”ti pucchi. Āma, puṇṇe, satthā cārikaṃ pakkanto, tamahaṃ nivattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃ. Na kho pana sakkā jānituṃ puna sīghaṃ āgaccheyya vā na vā, tenāhaṃ cintayamāno nisinnoti. Sacāhaṃ dasabalaṃ nivatteyyaṃ, kiṃ me kareyyāsīti? Bhujissaṃ taṃ karissāmīti. Sā gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “nivattatha, bhante”ti āha. Mama nivattanapaccayā [V 3.0171] tvaṃ kiṃ karissasīti? Tumhe, bhante, mama parādhīnabhāvaṃ jānātha, aññaṃ kiñci kātuṃ na sakkomi, saraṇesu pana patiṭṭhāya pañca sīlāni rakkhissāmīti. Sādhu sādhu puṇṇeti, satthā dhammagāravena ekapadasmiññeva nivatti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “dhammagaru, bhikkhave, tathāgato dhammagāravo”ti (a. ni. 5.99).

53. The tenth discourse was taught by way of an incident. It is said that the Master, having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā, leaving behind his two chief disciples, set out with the intention, “I will go on a journey to Dakkhiṇāgiri.” King Pasenadi of Kosala, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the great laywoman Visākhā, and many other people were unable to persuade the Ten-Powered One to turn back. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, “I was not able to persuade the Master to turn back,” sat reflecting in a secluded place. Then a female slave named Puṇṇā, seeing him, asked, “Master, why are your faculties not as serene as before?” “Yes, Puṇṇā, the Master has set out on a journey, and I was not able to persuade him to turn back. It is not possible to know whether he will return soon or not; for that reason, I am sitting here reflecting.” “If I were to persuade the Ten-Powered One to turn back, what would you do for me?” “I would set you free.” She went, paid homage to the Master, and said, “Venerable sir, please turn back.” “On account of my turning back, what will you do?” “Venerable sir, you know my state of dependence on others; I am not able to do anything else. However, having established myself in the refuges, I will observe the five precepts.” “Good, good, Puṇṇā!” The Master, out of reverence for the Dhamma, turned back at that very word. For this was said: “Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has respect for the Dhamma, has reverence for the Dhamma.”

Satthā nivattitvā jetavanamahāvihāraṃ pāvisi. Mahājano puṇṇāya sādhukārasahassāni adāsi. Satthā tasmiṃ samāgame dhammaṃ desesi, caturāsītipāṇasahassāni [P 4.0035] amatapānaṃ piviṃsu. Puṇṇāpi seṭṭhinā anuññātā bhikkhuniupassayaṃ gantvā pabbaji. Sammāsambuddho sāriputtamoggallāne āmantetvā “ahaṃ yaṃ disaṃ cārikāya nikkhanto, tattha na gacchāmi. Tumhe tumhākaṃ parisāya saddhiṃ taṃ disaṃ cārikaṃ gacchathā”ti vatvā uyyojesi. Imissaṃ atthuppattiyaṃ ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā sāriputtotiādi vuttaṃ.

The Master turned back and entered the Great Monastery of Jetavana. The great crowd of people gave thousands of acclamations to Puṇṇā. The Master delivered a discourse at that gathering, and eighty-four thousand living beings drank the beverage of the deathless. Puṇṇā, having been permitted by the great merchant, went to the bhikkhunī residence and went forth. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One summoned Sāriputta and Moggallāna and, saying, “I will not go to the region for which I set out on my journey. You, together with your retinue, should go on a journey to that region,” he sent them off. In connection with this incident, the passage beginning “At one time the Venerable Sāriputta…” and so on, was spoken.

Tattha veḷukaṇḍakīti veḷukaṇṭakanagaravāsinī. Tassa kira nagarassa pākāraguttatthāya pākārapariyantena veḷū ropitā, tenassa veḷukaṇṭakanteva [M 3.0170] nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Pārāyananti nibbānasaṅkhātapāraṃ ayanato pārāyananti laddhavohāraṃ dhammaṃ. Sarena bhāsatīti sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatale susaṃvihitārakkhaṭṭhāne nisinnā samāpattibalena rattibhāgaṃ vītināmetvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “imaṃ rattāvasesaṃ katarāya ratiyā vītināmessāmī”ti cintetvā “dhammaratiyā”ti katasanniṭṭhānā tīṇi phalāni pattā ariyasāvikā aḍḍhateyyagāthāsataparimāṇaṃ pārāyanasuttaṃ madhurena sarabhaññena bhāsati. Assosi khoti ākāsaṭṭhakavimānāni pariharitvā tassa pāsādassa uparibhāgaṃ gatena maggena naravāhanayānaṃ āruyha gacchamāno assosi. Kathāpariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno aṭṭhāsīti “kiṃ saddo esa bhaṇe”ti pucchitvā “nandamātāya upāsikāya sarabhaññasaddo”ti vutte otaritvā “idamavocā”ti idaṃ desanāpariyosānaṃ olokento avidūraṭṭhāne ākāse aṭṭhāsi.

Therein, ‘Veḷukaṇḍakī’ means a female resident of the city of Veḷukaṇṭaka. It is said that for the protection of that city's wall, bamboo was planted along the perimeter of the wall; hence its name became Veḷukaṇṭaka. ‘Pārāyana’ refers to the Dhamma that has gained the designation ‘Pārāyana’ because it is the way to reach the far shore, which is called Nibbāna. ‘She speaks with a voice’ means that, seated in a well-secured place on the upper floor of a seven-storied mansion, having spent the night-part by the power of meditative attainment, she emerged from that attainment and thought, “By what delight shall I spend the remainder of this night?” Having made the resolution, “With delight in the Dhamma,” she, a noble female disciple who had attained the three fruits, recites the Pārāyana Sutta, which has the measure of two hundred and fifty gāthās, with a sweet, melodious recitation. ‘He heard’ means that while traveling, having mounted a vehicle carried by men, along a path that went above that mansion, avoiding the mansions situated in the sky, he heard. ‘Waiting for the conclusion of the recitation, he stood still’ means that having asked, “Sirs, what is this sound?” and being told, “It is the sound of the melodious recitation of the lay follower Nandamātā,” he descended and, awaiting this conclusion of the discourse, stood in the sky in a place not far away.

Sādhu bhagini, sādhu bhaginīti “suggahitā te bhagini dhammadesanā [P 4.0036] sukathitā, pāsāṇakacetiye nisīditvā soḷasannaṃ pārāyanikabrāhmaṇānaṃ sammāsambuddhena kathitadivase ca ajja ca na kiñci antaraṃ passāmi, majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya te satthu kathitena saddhiṃ sadisameva kathita”nti vatvā sādhukāraṃ dadanto evamāha. Ko paneso bhadramukhāti imasmiṃ susaṃvihitārakkhaṭṭhāne [V 3.0172] evaṃ mahantena saddena ko nāmesa, bhadramukha, laddhamukha, kiṃ nāgo supaṇṇo devo māro brahmāti suvaṇṇapaṭṭavaṇṇaṃ vātapānaṃ vivaritvā vigatasārajjā tīṇi phalāni pattā ariyasāvikā vessavaṇena saddhiṃ kathayamānā evamāha. Ahaṃ te bhagini bhātāti sayaṃ sotāpannattā anāgāmiariyasāvikaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ maññamāno “bhaginī”ti vatvā puna taṃ paṭhamavaye ṭhitattā attano kaniṭṭhaṃ, attānaṃ pana navutivassasatasahassāyukattā mahallakataraṃ maññamāno “bhātā”ti āha. Sādhu bhadramukhāti, bhadramukha, sādhu sundaraṃ, svāgamanaṃ te āgamanaṃ, āgantuṃ yuttaṭṭhānamevasi āgatoti attho. Idaṃ te hotu ātitheyyanti idameva dhammabhaṇanaṃ tava atithipaṇṇākāro hotu, na hi te aññaṃ ito uttaritaraṃ dātabbaṃ passāmīti adhippāyo[M 3.0171]. Evañceva me bhavissati ātitheyyanti evaṃ attano pattidānaṃ yācitvā “ayaṃ te dhammakathikasakkāro”ti aḍḍhateḷasāni koṭṭhasatāni rattasālīnaṃ pūretvā “yāvāyaṃ upāsikā carati, tāva mā khayaṃ gamiṃsū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā pakkāmi. Yāva upāsikā aṭṭhāsi, tāva koṭṭhānaṃ heṭṭhimatalaṃ [P 4.0037] nāma daṭṭhuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya “nandamātāya koṭṭhāgāraṃ viyā”ti vohāro udapādi.

‘Excellent, sister! Excellent, sister!’ means that, giving his approval, he spoke thus: ‘Well-grasped by you, sister, is the Dhamma teaching, well-spoken. On the day the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One spoke to the sixteen Pārāyana brahmins while seated at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, and today—I see no difference at all. Like a piece of gold broken in the middle, what you have spoken is exactly the same as what was spoken by the Master.’ ‘But who is this, auspicious one?’: This means that the noble female disciple—who had attained the three fruits and was free from timidity—wishing to speak with Vessavaṇa, opened a golden-colored window in that well-secured place and, upon hearing such a loud voice, spoke thus: ‘Who is this, auspicious one? Is it a nāga, a supaṇṇa, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā?’ ‘I am your brother, sister’ means that he, being a stream-enterer, considering the anāgāmī noble female disciple his elder, said ‘sister’; then again, because she was in the first stage of life, considering her younger than himself, and considering himself to be much older on account of having a lifespan of nine million years, he said ‘brother.’ ‘Excellent, auspicious one!’ means: ‘Auspicious one, it is good, it is excellent; your coming is a welcome one. You have come to a fitting place.’ ‘Let this be your hospitality’ means: ‘Let this very recitation of the Dhamma be your guest-offering. Indeed, I see nothing more excellent than this to be given to you.’ This is the intention. ‘And so this will be my hospitality’ means that, having thus requested the sharing of merit for himself, and saying, ‘This is your honorarium as a Dhamma teacher,’ he filled twelve hundred and fifty granaries with red rice, made the resolution, ‘As long as this laywoman is about, may these not be depleted,’ and then departed. For as long as the laywoman lived, they were not able to see the bottom floor of the granaries. From that time onwards, the expression arose: ‘Like the granary of Nandamātā.’

Akatapātarāsoti abhuttapātarāso. Puññanti pubbacetanā ca muñcanacetanā ca. Puññamahīti aparacetanā. Sukhāya hotūti sukhatthāya hitatthāya hotu. Evaṃ attano dāne vessavaṇassa pattiṃ adāsi.

'Without having eaten the morning meal' means without having consumed the morning meal. 'Merit' means both the prior volition and the volition at the time of relinquishing. 'The ground of merit' means the subsequent volition. 'May it be for happiness' means may it be for the sake of happiness and for the sake of benefit. Thus, she gave a share of the merit from her gift to Vessavaṇa.

Pakaraṇeti kāraṇe. Okkassa pasayhāti ākaḍḍhitvā abhibhavitvā. Yakkhayoninti bhummadevatābhāvaṃ. Teneva purimena attabhāvena uddassetīti purimasarīrasadisameva sarīraṃ māpetvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatto sirigabbhasayanatale attānaṃ dasseti. Upāsikā paṭidesitāti upāsikā ahanti evaṃ upāsikābhāvaṃ desesiṃ. Yāvadeti yāvadeva. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Regarding the cause' means because of a reason. 'Having dragged down by force' means having dragged and having overwhelmed. 'The yakkha-womb' means the state of being a terrestrial deity. 'He displayed himself in that former existence' means, having created a body just like his former one, adorned and prepared, he showed himself on the glorious couch in the inner chamber. 'The laywoman devotee declared' means, 'I am a laywoman devotee,' thus she made known her state as a laywoman devotee. 'As long as' means just so long. The rest is clear throughout.

Mahāyaññavaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on the Great Sacrifice is the fifth.

Paṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is completed.

6. Abyākatavaggo

6. The Chapter on the Undeclared

1. Abyākatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on the Undeclared

54. Chaṭṭhavaggassa [M 3.0172][V 3.0173] paṭhame abyākatavatthūsūti ekaṃsādivasena akathitavatthūsu. Tathāgatoti satto. Diṭṭhigatametanti micchādiṭṭhimattakametaṃ, na tāya diṭṭhiyā gahitasatto nāma atthi. Paṭipadanti [P 4.0038] ariyamaggaṃ. Na chambhatīti diṭṭhivasena na kampati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Taṇhāgatanti diṭṭhitaṇhā. Saññāgatādīsupi eseva nayo. Diṭṭhisaññā eva hettha saññāgataṃ, diṭṭhinissitamānoyeva diṭṭhimaññitameva vā maññitaṃ, diṭṭhipapañcova papañcitaṃ, diṭṭhupādānameva upādānaṃ, diṭṭhiyā virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇabhāvoyeva vippaṭisāro nāmāti veditabbo. Ettha ca diṭṭhiggahaṇena dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo, diṭṭhinirodhagāminipaṭipadāgahaṇena sotāpattimaggo gahitoti.

54. In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, 'on the undeclared points' means on topics not spoken of by way of being one-sided, and so on. 'Tathāgata' means a being. 'This is a view-held thing' means this is merely a wrong view; there is no such thing as a being grasped by that view. 'The path' means the Noble Path. 'He does not waver' means he does not tremble due to view. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. 'Gone to craving' means craving associated with view. The same method applies to 'gone to perception' and so on. Here, 'gone to perception' is indeed perception associated with view; 'what is conceived' is either conceit dependent on view or what is conceived by view; 'what is proliferated' is the proliferation that is view; 'clinging' is the clinging to views; and remorse is to be understood as the state of perversely resorting to a view. Here, by the taking of 'view', the sixty-two views are taken, and by the taking of 'the path leading to the cessation of views', the path of stream-entry is taken.

2. Purisagatisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sutta on the Courses of a Person

55. Dutiye purisagatiyoti purisassa ñāṇagatiyo. Anupādāparinibbānanti apaccayanibbānaṃ. No cassāti atīte attabhāvanibbattakaṃ kammaṃ no ce abhavissa. No ca me siyāti etarahi me ayaṃ attabhāvo na siyā. Na bhavissatīti etarahi me anāgatattabhāvanibbattakaṃ kammaṃ na bhavissati. Na ca me bhavissatīti anāgate me attabhāvo na bhavissati. Yadatthi yaṃ bhūtanti yaṃ atthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ paccuppannakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Taṃ pajahāmīti upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatīti taṃ tattha chandarāgappahānena pajahāmīti vipassanupekkhaṃ paṭilabhati. Bhave na rajjatīti atīte khandhapañcake taṇhādiṭṭhīhi na rajjati. Sambhave na rajjatīti anāgatepi tatheva na rajjati. Atthuttari [P 4.0039] padaṃ santanti uttari santaṃ nibbānapadaṃ nāma atthi. Sammappaññāya passatīti taṃ sahavipassanāya maggapaññāya sammā passati. Na sabbena sabbanti ekaccānaṃ kilesānaṃ appahīnattā saccapaṭicchādakassa tamassa sabbaso aviddhaṃsitattā na sabbākārena sabbaṃ. Haññamāneti saṇḍāsena gahetvā muṭṭhikāya koṭṭiyamāne. Antarāparinibbāyīti upapattisamanantarato paṭṭhāya āyuno vemajjhaṃ anatikkamitvā etthantare kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto hoti. Anupahacca talanti ākāsatalaṃ anupahacca anatikkamitvā[M 3.0173], bhūmiṃ appatvā ākāseyeva nibbāyeyyāti [V 3.0174] imāhi tīhi upamāhi tayo antarāparinibbāyī dassitā.

55. In the second sutta, 'the courses of a person' means the courses of a person’s knowledge. 'Final Nibbāna without clinging' means Nibbāna without a cause. 'If it were not so' means: if in a past life the kamma that produces existence had not been. 'It would not be for me' means in this present time, this existence would not be for me. 'It will not be' means in this present time, the kamma that produces a future existence will not be. 'And it will not be for me' means in the future, there will be no existence for me. 'What is, what has come to be' means the present five aggregates that exist and have come to be. 'Thinking, "I will abandon that," he attains equanimity' means, regarding those aggregates, by abandoning passionate desire, he attains the equanimity of insight. 'He is not attached to existence' means he is not attached to the past five aggregates through craving and views. 'He is not attached to becoming' means in the same way, he is not attached to the future five aggregates either. 'There is a further, peaceful state' means there exists the state to be attained called Nibbāna, which is supremely peaceful. 'He sees with right wisdom' means he sees it well with the wisdom of the path together with the wisdom of insight. 'Not entirely everything' means because some defilements are not abandoned and because the delusion that conceals the truth is not entirely destroyed, the whole is not realized in every way. 'Being struck' means being seized with tongs and beaten with a hammer. 'One who attains final Nibbāna in the interval' means, starting from immediately after rebirth, without passing the middle of the lifespan, he is extinguished within that interval by the final extinguishing of defilements. 'Without striking the surface' means without passing the sky-surface and without reaching the ground, one would be extinguished in the sky itself. By these three similes, the three types of those who attain final Nibbāna in the interval are shown.

Upahaccaparinibbāyīti āyuvemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā pacchimakoṭiṃ appatvā parinibbuto hoti. Upahacca talanti jalamānā gantvā ākāsatalaṃ atikkamitvā pathavītalaṃ vā upahanitvā pathaviyaṃ patitamattāva nibbāyeyya. Asaṅkhārena appayogena kilese khepetvā parinibbāyīti asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilese khepetvā parinibbāyīti sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Gacchanti nirārakkhaṃ araññaṃ. Dāyanti sārakkhaṃ abhayatthāya dinnaṃ araññaṃ. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Imasmiṃ sutte ariyapuggalāva kathitāti.

'One who attains final Nibbāna upon reaching' means one who, having passed the middle of the lifespan but without reaching the final limit, is extinguished. 'Having struck a surface' means, going while blazing, having passed the sky-surface and having struck the earth-surface, it would be extinguished just upon falling to the earth. 'One who attains final Nibbāna without exertion' is so called because, having exhausted the defilements without exertion and without effort, one attains final Nibbāna. 'One who attains final Nibbāna with exertion' is so called because, having exhausted the defilements with exertion and with effort, one attains final Nibbāna. '`Gaccha`' means an unprotected wilderness. '`Dāya`' means a protected wilderness given for the sake of safety. The rest here has a clear meaning. In this sutta, only noble individuals are discussed.

3. Tissabrahmāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Tissa Brahmā Sutta

56. Tatiye [P 4.0040] bhikkhuniyoti mahāpajāpatiyā parivārā pañcasatā bhikkhuniyo. Vimuttāti pañcahi vimuttīhi vimuttā. Anupādisesāti upādānasesaṃ aṭṭhapetvā pañcahi vimuttīhi anavasesāhipi vimuttā. Saupādisese vā saupādisesoti saupādānasese puggale “saupādānaseso aya”nti. Itarasmimpi eseva nayo. Tissoti therassa saddhivihārikabrahmā. Anulomikānīti paṭipattiyā anulomāni vivittāni antimapariyantimāni. Indriyānīti saddhādīni vipassanindriyāni. Samannānayamānoti samannāhāre ṭhapayamāno. Na hi pana teti idaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Sattamassa puggalassa dassanatthaṃ. Sattamo hi saddhānusāripuggalo na dassito. Atha bhagavā balavavipassakavasena taṃ dassento evamāha. Tattha sabbanimittānanti sabbesaṃ niccanimittādīnaṃ. Animittanti balavavipassanāsamādhiṃ.

56. In the third sutta, 'bhikkhunīs' refers to the five hundred bhikkhunīs in Mahāpajāpatī's retinue. 'Liberated' means liberated by the five liberations. 'Without residue' means liberated by the five liberations without remainder, having not left a residue of clinging. 'With residue' means, regarding a person with a residue of clinging, it is the knowledge, 'This one has a residue of clinging.' The same method applies to the other case. 'Tissa' is the Brahmā who was the Elder's co-resident disciple. 'Conducive' means conducive to the practice, secluded, and ultimate. 'Faculties' refers to the insight faculties, beginning with faith. 'Applying' means placing them in a state of balance. Why was the passage beginning 'But not for you...' introduced? It was introduced to show the seventh person. For the seventh person, the faith-follower, had not been shown. Then the Blessed One, demonstrating him by way of strong insight, spoke thus. Therein, 'of all signs' refers to all signs of permanence and so on. 'The signless' refers to the concentration of strong insight.

4. Sīhasenāpatisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sīha the General Sutta

57. Catutthe maccharīti pañcamaccherayutto. Kadariyoti thaddhamacchariyo, paresaṃ diyyamānampi vāreti. Anuppadānaratoti punappunaṃ dānaṃ dadamānova ramati. Anukampantāti “ko ajja amhehi anuggahetabbo, kassa deyyadhammaṃ vā paṭiggaṇheyyāma, dhammaṃ vā deseyyāmā”ti evaṃ cittena anukampamānā.

57. In the fourth sutta, 'stingy' refers to one endowed with the five kinds of stinginess. 'Miserly' means obstinately stingy, preventing even what is being given to others. 'Delighting in giving' means one who delights in giving again and again. 'Compassionate' means being compassionate in mind, thinking: 'Who today should be helped by us? Whose suitable gift should we accept, or to whom should we teach the Dhamma?'

5. Arakkheyyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Arakkheyya Sutta

58. Pañcame [V 3.0175][M 3.0174][P 4.0041] nimittanti dhammanimittampi puggalanimittampi. Ayañhi attanā desitadhamme ekapadampi durakkhātaṃ aniyyānikaṃ apassanto dhammanimittaṃ na samanupassati, “durakkhāto tayā dhammo na svākkhāto”ti uṭṭhahitvā paṭippharantaṃ ekaṃ puggalampi apassanto puggalanimittaṃ na samanupassati nāma. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo. Chaṭṭhasattamāni uttānāneva.

58. In the fifth sutta, 'sign' refers to both the sign of the Dhamma and the sign of a person. For He, not seeing even a single word in the Dhamma taught by himself as poorly explained or not leading to deliverance, does not perceive the sign of the Dhamma. Not seeing even one person rising up and objecting, 'The Dhamma was poorly taught by you, not well-proclaimed,' He is said not to perceive the sign of a person. The same method applies to the remaining two cases. The sixth and seventh suttas are straightforward.

8. Pacalāyamānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Pacalāyamāna Sutta

61. Aṭṭhame pacalāyamānoti taṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya ekasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe samaṇadhammaṃ karonto sattāhaṃ caṅkamanavīriyena nimmathitattā kilantagatto caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pacalāyamāno nisinno hoti. Pacalāyasi noti niddāyasi nu. Anumajjitvāti parimajjitvā. Ālokasaññanti middhavinodanaālokasaññaṃ. Divāsaññanti divātisaññaṃ. Yathā divā tathā rattinti yathā divā ālokasaññā adhiṭṭhitā, tathā naṃ rattimpi adhiṭṭhaheyyāsi. Yathā rattiṃ tathā divāti yathā ca te rattiṃ ālokasaññā adhiṭṭhitā, tathā naṃ divāpi adhiṭṭhaheyyāsi. Sappabhāsanti dibbacakkhuñāṇatthāya sahobhāsaṃ. Pacchāpuresaññīti purato ca pacchato ca abhiharaṇasaññāya saññāvā. Antogatehi indriyehīti bahi avikkhittehi anto anupaviṭṭheheva pañcahi indriyehi. Middhasukhanti niddāsukhaṃ. Ettakena [P 4.0042] ṭhānena bhagavā therassa middhavinodanakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Soṇḍanti mānasoṇḍaṃ. Kiccakaraṇīyānīti ettha avassaṃ kattabbāni kiccāni, itarāni karaṇīyāni. Maṅkubhāvoti nittejatā domanassatā. Ettakena ṭhānena satthārā therassa bhikkhācāravattaṃ kathitaṃ.

61. In the eighth sutta, 'nodding off' means: relying on that village and practicing the ascetic's duties in a certain forest grove, for seven days, because of being worn out by the effort of walking meditation, with a weary body, he is seated at the end of the walking path, nodding off. 'Are you nodding off?' means 'Are you sleeping?' 'Having rubbed' means having stroked. 'Perception of light' means the perception of light for dispelling drowsiness. 'Perception of daytime' means the perception of day. 'As by day, so by night' means: just as the perception of light is established by day, so you should establish it at night. 'As by night, so by day' means: and just as the perception of light is established by you at night, so you should establish it by day. 'Radiant' means accompanied by brightness, for the purpose of the knowledge of the divine eye. 'Perceiving before and after' means one who has perception by means of the perception of attending forwards and backwards. 'With faculties gone within' means with the five faculties not scattered outside, but indeed having entered within. 'The pleasure of drowsiness' means the pleasure of sleep. By this much, the Blessed One taught the Elder the meditation subject for dispelling drowsiness. 'Trunk' means the trunk of conceit. 'Duties and obligations' means: herein, things that must certainly be done are 'duties' (kiccāni); the others are 'obligations' (karaṇīyāni). 'Dejection' means lack of energy and displeasure. By this much, the Teacher explained to the Elder the observances of the alms-round.

Idāni bhasse pariyantakāritāya samādapetuṃ tasmātihātiādimāha. Tattha viggāhikakathanti “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsī”tiādinayappavattā viggāhikakathā. Nāhaṃ moggallānātiādi pāpamittasaṃsaggavivajjanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Kittāvatā nu khoti kittakena nu kho. Taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hotīti taṇhāsaṅkhaye nibbāne taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vimuttacittatāya [M 3.0175] taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto nāma saṃkhittena kittāvatā hoti. Yāya paṭipattiyā taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutto hoti, tameva khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ saṃkhittena desethāti pucchati. Accantaniṭṭhoti [V 3.0176] khayavayasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ atītāti accantā, accantā niṭṭhā assāti accantaniṭṭho, ekantaniṭṭho satataniṭṭhoti attho. Accantayogakkhemīti accantaṃ yogakkhemī, niccayogakkhemīti attho. Accantabrahmacārīti accantaṃ brahmacārī, niccabrahmacārīti attho. Accantaṃ [P 4.0043] pariyosānamassāti purimanayeneva accantapariyosāno. Seṭṭho devamanussānanti devānañca manussānañca seṭṭho uttamo. Evarūpo bhikkhu kittāvatā hoti, saṅkhepeneva tassa paṭipattiṃ kathethāti yācati.

Now, to get him to undertake making a limit in speech, the passage beginning 'Therefore...' was spoken. Therein, 'contentious talk' refers to contentious talk that proceeds by way of statements like, 'You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya,' and so on. The passage beginning, 'I am not, Moggallāna...' was spoken for the purpose of avoiding association with bad friends. 'To what extent, pray?' means 'by what measure, pray?' The phrase 'is liberated by the destruction of craving' means: by what measure, in brief, is one called 'liberated by the destruction of craving' on account of a mind liberated by taking as its object Nibbāna, the destruction of craving? He asks: 'By what practice does one become liberated through the destruction of craving? Please explain to me in brief that preliminary practice of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.' 'Utterly perfected' means: 'utterly' (accanta) because it has gone beyond the end (anta) designated as destruction and passing away; one is 'utterly perfected' (accantaniṭṭho) because one has an utter perfection (accantā niṭṭhā); the meaning is completely perfected, perpetually perfected. 'Utterly secure from bondage' means utterly secure from bondage; the meaning is always secure from bondage. 'Utterly living the holy life' means utterly living the holy life; the meaning is always living the holy life. One is 'utterly consummated' (accantapariyosāno) by the same method as before, because one has an utter consummation (accantaṃ pariyosānaṃ). 'Foremost among devas and humans' means the best, the highest of devas and humans. He requests: 'By what measure does such a bhikkhu come to be? Please explain his practice to me in brief.'

Sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāyāti ettha sabbe dhammā nāma pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, te sabbepi taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinivesāya nālaṃ na pariyattā na samattā na yuttā. Kasmā? Gahitākārena atiṭṭhanato. Te hi niccā sukhā attāti gahitāpi aniccā dukkhā anattāva sampajjanti. Tasmā nālaṃ abhinivesāya. Abhijānātīti aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti ñātapariññāya abhijānāti. Parijānātīti tatheva tīraṇapariññāya parijānāti. Yaṃkiñci vedananti antamaso pañcaviññāṇasampayuttaṃ yaṃkiñci appamattakampi vedanaṃ anubhavati. Iminā bhagavā therassa vedanāvasena ca vinivaṭṭetvā arūpapariggahaṃ dassesi.

Regarding the phrase 'All phenomena are not fit for clinging': Here, 'all phenomena' means the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements. All of these are not fit, not sufficient, not complete, and not suitable for clinging by way of craving and wrong view. Why? Because they do not remain in the way they are grasped.
