For even when they are grasped as permanent, pleasant, and self, they turn out to be only impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Therefore, they are not fit for clinging. 'He knows directly' means he knows directly through the full understanding of what is known that 'it is impermanent, suffering, non-self'. 'He fully understands' means he fully understands in the same way through the full understanding by investigation. 'Whatever feeling' means he experiences whatever slight feeling, even down to that associated with the five sense-consciousnesses. By this, the Blessed One, having caused the Elder to turn away by way of feeling, showed the comprehension of immaterial phenomena.

Aniccānupassīti aniccato anupassanto. Virāgānupassīti ettha dve virāgā khayavirāgo ca accantavirāgo ca. Tattha saṅkhārānaṃ khayaṃ khayato passanā vipassanāpi, accantavirāgaṃ nibbānaṃ virāgato dassanamaggañāṇampi virāgānupassanā. Tadubhayasamaṅgipuggalo virāgānupassī nāma. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “virāgānupassī”ti, virāgato anupassantoti attho. Nirodhānupassimhipi eseva nayo. Nirodhopi hi khayanirodho accantanirodhoti duvidhoyeva. Paṭinissaggānupassīti ettha paṭinissaggo vuccati vossaggo. So [P 4.0044] ca pariccāgavossaggo pakkhandanavossaggoti duvidho hoti. Tattha pariccāgavossaggoti vipassanā. Sā hi tadaṅgavasena kilese ca khandhe ca vossajati. Pakkhandanavossaggoti maggo. So hi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇato pakkhandati. Dvīhipi vā kāraṇehi so vossaggoyeva, samucchedavasena khandhānaṃ kilesānañca vossajanato nibbāne ca pakkhandanato. Tasmā [M 3.0176] kilese ca khandhe ca pariccajatīti pariccāgavossaggo. Nirodhāya nibbānadhātuyā cittaṃ pakkhandatīti pakkhandanavossaggoti ubhayampetaṃ magge sameti. Tadubhayasamaṅgī puggalo imāya paṭinissaggānupassanāya samannāgatattā [V 3.0177] paṭinissaggānupassī nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Na kiñci loke upādiyatīti kiñci ekampi saṅkhāragataṃ taṇhāvasena na upādiyati na gaṇhāti na parāmasati. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassatīti aggaṇhanto taṇhāparitassanāya na paritassati. Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatīti sayameva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati. Khīṇā jātītiādinā panassa paccavekkhaṇā dassitā. Iti bhagavā saṃkhittena khīṇāsavassa pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ pucchito saṃkhitteneva kathesi. Idaṃ pana suttaṃ therassa ovādopi ahosi vipassanāpi. So imasmiṃyeva sutte vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pattoti.

‘Contemplating impermanence’ means one who contemplates as impermanent. Regarding ‘contemplating dispassion’: Here, there are two kinds of dispassion: dispassion as destruction and absolute dispassion. Therein, both the seeing, which is insight, of the destruction of formations as destruction, and the path-knowledge that sees Nibbāna, the absolute dispassion, as dispassion, is the contemplation of dispassion. A person endowed with both is called one who contemplates dispassion. With reference to this, it is said, ‘one who contemplates dispassion,’ meaning one who contemplates as dispassion. The same method applies to ‘one who contemplates cessation.’ For cessation is also twofold: cessation as destruction and absolute cessation. Regarding ‘one who contemplates relinquishment’: Here, relinquishment is called letting go (vossagga). And it is twofold: letting go by abandoning (pariccāgavossagga) and letting go by plunging into (pakkhandanavossagga). Herein, letting go by abandoning is insight (vipassanā). For it lets go of both defilements and aggregates by way of substitution. Letting go by plunging into is the path. For it plunges into Nibbāna as its object. Or, it is called letting go for two reasons: because of letting go of aggregates and defilements by way of cutting off, and because of plunging into Nibbāna. Therefore, because it abandons defilements and aggregates, it is letting go by abandoning. Because the mind plunges into the Nibbāna-element for the sake of cessation, it is letting go by plunging into. Both of these come together in the path. A person endowed with both, being furnished with this contemplation of relinquishment, is called one who contemplates relinquishment. With reference to this, it is said. ‘He does not cling to anything in the world’ means: he does not cling to, does not grasp, does not misapprehend even a single conditioned thing by way of craving. ‘Not clinging, he is not agitated’ means: not grasping, he is not agitated with the agitation of craving. ‘He is personally fully extinguished’ means: he himself is fully extinguished with the full extinguishment of defilements. By ‘Destroyed is birth,’ etc., his reviewing knowledge is shown. Thus, the Blessed One, having been asked in brief about the preliminary practice of one whose cankers are destroyed, spoke in brief. Moreover, this discourse was both an exhortation and insight for the Elder. He, having developed insight in this very discourse, attained Arahantship.

9. Mettasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Loving-Kindness

62. Navame mā, bhikkhave, puññānaṃ bhāyitthāti puññāni karontā tesaṃ mā bhāyittha. Mettacittaṃ bhāvesinti tikacatukkajjhānikāya mettāya sampayuttaṃ paṇītaṃ katvā cittaṃ bhāvesinti dasseti. Saṃvaṭṭamāne sudāhanti saṃvaṭṭamāne sudaṃ ahaṃ. Saṃvaṭṭamāneti [P 4.0045] jhāyamāne vipajjamāne. Dhammikoti dasakusaladhammasamannāgato. Dhammarājāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Dhammena vā laddharajjattā dhammarājā. Cāturantoti puratthimasamuddādīnaṃ catunnaṃ samuddānaṃ vasena cāturantāya pathaviyā issaro. Vijitāvīti vijitasaṅgāmo. Janapado tasmiṃ thāvariyaṃ thirabhāvaṃ pattoti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīruno. Vīraṅgarūpāti vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vīraṅgarūpametesanti vīraṅgarūpā. Vīriyajātikā vīriyasabhāvā vīriyamayā viya akilāsuno divasampi yujjhantā na kilamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāgarapariyantanti cakkavāḷapabbataṃ sīmaṃ katvā ṭhitasamuddapariyantaṃ. Adaṇḍenāti dhanadaṇḍenapi chejjabhejjānusāsanena satthadaṇḍenapi vināyeva. Asatthenāti ekatodhārādinā paraviheṭhanasatthenapi vināyeva. Dhammena abhivijiyāti ehi kho, mahārājāti evaṃ paṭirājūhi sampaṭicchitāgamano “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā dhammeneva vuttappakāraṃ pathaviṃ abhivijinitvā.

62. In the ninth sutta: ‘Monks, do not fear merit’ means: while making merit, do not fear it. ‘I developed a mind of loving-kindness’ shows: ‘I developed the mind, having made it refined and associated with the loving-kindness of the three-fold and four-fold jhānic systems.’ The phrase `Saṃvaṭṭamāne sudāhaṃ` should be parsed as `saṃvaṭṭamāne sudaṃ ahaṃ`. `Saṃvaṭṭamāne` means when it is burning up, when it is perishing. ‘Righteous’ means endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action. ‘King of Dhamma’ is a synonym for that very word. Or, because he obtained kingship by the Dhamma, he is a King of Dhamma. ‘Whose domain has four ends’ means ruler of the earth that has four ends, by way of the four oceans beginning with the eastern ocean. ‘Victorious’ means one who has won the battle. Because the country under him attained stability and firmness, he is called `janapadatthāvariyappatto`. ‘Over a thousand’ means more than a thousand. ‘Heroes’ means fearless ones. Regarding ‘of heroic form’: the limb (aṅga) of heroes is vīraṅga; this is a name for energy (vīriya). They have heroic form (vīraṅgarūpa), thus they are vīraṅgarūpā. It is said that they are of an energetic nature, have a nature of energy, are as if made of energy, are untiring, and do not become fatigued even when fighting for a whole day. ‘Ocean-bounded’ means bounded by the ocean which stands having the Cakkavāḷa mountain range as its boundary. ‘Without a rod’ means without the rod of wealth, and without the rod of weapons, which is an instruction involving cutting and breaking. ‘Without a sword’ means without even a weapon for harming others, such as a single-edged sword. ‘Having conquered by Dhamma’ means: having conquered the earth in the aforesaid manner only by the Dhamma beginning with ‘Living beings should not be killed,’ with his arrival accepted by rival kings saying, ‘Come, great king!’.

Sukhesinoti [M 3.0177] sukhapariyesake satte āmanteti. Suññabrahmūpagoti suññabrahmavimānūpago. Pathaviṃ imanti imaṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ mahāpathaviṃ. Asāhasenāti [P 4.0046] na sāhasikakammena. Samena manusāsitanti samena kammena anusāsiṃ. Tehi etaṃ sudesitanti tehi saṅgāhakehi mahākāruṇikehi buddhehi etaṃ ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ sudesitaṃ sukathitaṃ. Pathabyoti puthavisāmiko.

‘Seekers of happiness’ means: he addresses beings who are seekers of happiness. ‘Gone to the empty Brahma-world’ means one who has gone to the empty Brahma-mansion. ‘This earth’ means this great earth bounded by the ocean. ‘Without violence’ means not by a violent action. ‘I ruled with fairness’ means ‘I instructed with a fair action.’ ‘This was well-taught by them’ means: this much of a topic was well-taught, well-spoken by those Buddhas who are inclusive and greatly compassionate. ‘Of the earth’ means lord of the earth.

10. Bhariyāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bhariyā Sutta

63. Dasame [V 3.0178] kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilopeti kevaṭṭānaṃ macchapacchiṃ otāretvā ṭhitaṭṭhāne jāle vā udakato ukkhittamatte macchaggāhakānaṃ mahāsaddo hoti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sujātāti visākhāya kaniṭṭhā. Sā neva sassuṃ ādiyatīti sassuyā kattabbavattaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ na karoti, sassūtipi naṃ na gaṇeti. Na sasuraṃ ādiyatīti vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti. Evaṃ anādaratāyapi aggahaṇenapi na ādiyati nāma. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ anāthapiṇḍiko suṇisāya ācāraṃ gahetvā satthu purato nisīdi. Sāpi sujātā “kiṃ nu kho ayaṃ seṭṭhi dasabalassa santike mayhaṃ guṇaṃ kathessati udāhu aguṇa”nti gantvā avidūre saddaṃ suṇantī aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthā ehi sujāteti āmantesi.

63. In the tenth sutta, ‘Like fishermen, I think, at the plundering of fish,’ refers to the great noise made by those taking the fish, either in the place where the fishermen have set down their fish-baskets, or just as the net is lifted from the water; this was said in reference to that. Sujātā was Visākhā’s younger sister. ‘She does not heed her mother-in-law’ means that there is a duty to be performed towards the mother-in-law, but she does not do it, nor does she regard her as a mother-in-law. ‘She does not heed her father-in-law’ means she does not take his words. Thus, due to her disrespect and non-acceptance, she is called ‘not heeding’. The same principle applies to the rest. Thus Anāthapiṇḍika, having taken up his daughter-in-law’s conduct, sat before the Teacher. Sujātā, too, thinking, ‘I wonder, will this merchant speak of my virtues or faults in the presence of the Ten-Powered One?’ went and stood nearby, listening to the sound. Then the Teacher addressed her, ‘Come, Sujātā.’

Ahitānukampinīti na hitānukampinī. Aññesūti [P 4.0047] parapurisesu. Atimaññateti omānāti mānavasena atimaññati. Dhanena kītassāti dhanena kītā assa. Vadhāya ussukā vadhituṃ ussukkamāpannā. Yaṃ itthiyā vindati sāmiko dhananti itthiyā sāmiko yaṃ dhanaṃ labhati. Appampi tassa apahātumicchatīti thokatopi assa harituṃ icchati, uddhane āropitaukkhaliyaṃ pakkhipitabbataṇḍulatopi thokaṃ haritumeva vāyamati. Alasāti nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnāva ṭhitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāva hoti. Pharusāti kharā. Duruttavādinīti dubbhāsitabhāsinī, kakkhaḷaṃ vāḷakathameva katheti. Uṭṭhāyakānaṃ abhibhuyya vattatīti ettha uṭṭhāyakānanti bahuvacanavasena viriyuṭṭhānasampanno sāmiko vutto, tassa taṃ uṭṭhānasampattiṃ abhibhavitvā heṭṭhā katvā vattati. Pamodatīti āmoditapamoditā hoti[M 3.0178]. Koleyyakāti kulasampannā. Patibbatāti patidevatā. Vadhadaṇḍatajjitāti daṇḍakaṃ gahetvā vadhena tajjitā, “ghātessāmi na”nti vuttā. Dāsīsamanti sāmikassa vattapūrikā dāsīti maṃ bhagavā dhāretūti vatvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāsi.

‘Not compassionate towards what is beneficial’ means she is not compassionate towards what is beneficial. ‘Among others’ means among other men. ‘She looks down upon’ means she despises by way of contempt and conceit. ‘Bought with wealth’ means she was bought with wealth. ‘Eager for killing’ means she is intent on killing. ‘Whatever wealth the husband finds for the woman’ means whatever wealth the woman's husband obtains. ‘She wishes to take even a little from it’ means she desires to take even a small amount from it; she strives to take even a little, even from the rice to be put into a pot placed on a stove. ‘Lazy’ means she remains seated where she is seated and stands where she is standing. ‘Harsh’ means rough. ‘She speaks rude words’ means she speaks evil speech, uttering only harsh and cruel speech. ‘She acts by overpowering the industrious’—here, by ‘the industrious’ (in the plural form), the husband, who is endowed with energy and exertion, is meant; she acts by overpowering and subjugating his endowment with exertion. ‘She delights’ means she is joyful and exceedingly happy. ‘Of good lineage’ means endowed with good family. ‘A devoted wife’ means one for whom her husband is her deity. ‘Threatened with punishment and death’ means threatened with a stick and with killing, being told, ‘I will kill you.’ ‘Like a female slave’ means: ‘May the Blessed One regard me as a female slave who fulfills her husband’s duties.’ Having said this, she became established in the refuges.

11. Kodhanasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Kodhana Sutta.

64. Ekādasame sapattakantāti sapattānaṃ verīnaṃ kantā piyā tehi icchitapatthitā. Sapattakaraṇāti [V 3.0179][P 4.0048] sapattānaṃ verīnaṃ atthakaraṇā. Kodhaparetoti kodhānugato. Pacuratthatāyāti bahuatthatāya bahuhitatāya. Anatthampīti avuddhimpi. Attho me gahitoti vuḍḍhi me gahitā.

64. In the eleventh [sutta], ‘dear to rivals’ means dear and beloved to enemies, to rivals, desired and wished for by them. ‘Doing things for rivals’ means doing things for the benefit of enemies, of rivals. ‘Possessed by anger’ means followed by anger. ‘For the sake of abundance’ means for the sake of much benefit, for the sake of much welfare. ‘Even harm’ means even non-growth. ‘Benefit has been grasped by me’ means growth has been grasped by me.

Atho atthaṃ gahetvānāti atho vuddhiṃ gahetvā. Anatthaṃ adhipajjatīti anattho me gahitoti sallakkheti. Vadhaṃ katvānāti pāṇātipātakammaṃ katvā. Kodhasammadasammattoti kodhamadena matto, ādinnagahitaparāmaṭṭhoti attho. Āyasakyanti ayasabhāvaṃ, ayaso niyaso hotīti attho. Antarato jātanti abbhantare uppannaṃ. Atthaṃ na jānātīti vuddhiatthaṃ na jānāti. Dhammaṃ na passatīti samathavipassanādhammaṃ na passati. Andhatamanti andhabhāvakaraṃ tamaṃ bahalatamaṃ. Sahateti abhibhavati.

‘Then, having grasped benefit’ means then, having grasped growth. ‘He attains harm’ means he perceives, ‘Harm has been grasped by me.’ ‘Having done killing’ means having performed the act of destroying life. ‘Intoxicated by the intoxication of anger’ means intoxicated by the madness of anger; the meaning is ‘seized, grasped, and wrongly held’. ‘To disgrace’ means the state of disgrace; the meaning is: he becomes disgraced. ‘Born from within’ means arisen internally. ‘Does not know the benefit’ means does not know the benefit of growth. ‘Does not see the Dhamma’ means does not see the Dhamma of serenity and insight. ‘Blinding darkness’ means the thick darkness that causes the state of blindness. ‘It crushes’ means it overwhelms.

Dummaṅkuyanti dummaṅkubhāvaṃ nittejataṃ dubbaṇṇamukhataṃ. Yato patāyatīti yadā nibbattati. Na vāco hoti gāravoti vacanassapi garubhāvo na hoti. Na dīpaṃ hoti kiñcananti kāci patiṭṭhā nāma na hoti. Tapanīyānīti tāpajanakāni. Dhammehīti [P 4.0049] samathavipassanādhammehi. Ārakāti dūre. Brāhmaṇanti khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇaṃ. Yāya mātu bhatoti yāya mātarā bhato posito. Pāṇadadiṃ santinti jīvitadāyikaṃ samānaṃ. Hanti kuddho puthuttānanti kuddho puggalo puthu nānākāraṇehi attānaṃ hanti. Nānārūpesu mucchitoti nānārammaṇesu adhimucchito hutvā. Rajjuyā bajjha mīyantīti rajjuyā bandhitvā maranti. Pabbatāmapi kandareti pabbatakandarepi patitvā maranti.

‘Sullenness’ means the state of being sullen, without luster, with an ugly-colored face. ‘When it arises’ means when it is produced. ‘There is no respect for speech’ means there is no weightiness even of speech. ‘There is no island whatsoever’ means there is no support whatsoever. ‘Those that cause torment’ means those that generate torment. ‘From the dhammas’ means from the dhammas of serenity and insight. ‘Far away’ means far. ‘The Brahmin’ means the Brahmin whose cankers are destroyed. ‘He who was supported by his mother’ means he who was supported and nourished by his mother. ‘The one who gave life’ means being a giver of life. ‘The angry one harms oneself in many ways’ means an angry person harms themselves for various different reasons. ‘Infatuated with various forms’ means having become utterly infatuated with various sense-objects. ‘Being bound by a rope, they die’ means they die having been bound by a rope. ‘Even from a mountain into a chasm’ means they die having fallen even into a mountain chasm.

Bhūnahaccānīti [M 3.0179] hatavuddhīni. Itāyanti iti ayaṃ. Taṃ damena samucchindeti taṃ kodhaṃ damena chindeyya. Katarena damenāti? Paññāvīriyena diṭṭhiyāti vipassanāpaññāya ceva vipassanāsampayuttena kāyikacetasikavīriyena ca maggasammādiṭṭhiyā ca. Tatheva dhamme sikkhethāti yathā akusalaṃ samucchindeyya, samathavipassanādhammepi tatheva sikkheyya. Mā no dummaṅkuyaṃ ahūti mā amhākaṃ dummaṅkubhāvo ahosīti imamatthaṃ patthayamānā. Anāyāsāti anupāyāsā. Anussukāti katthaci ussukkaṃ anāpannā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

‘Destroyers of growth’ means those whose growth is destroyed. ‘Thus this’ is the word division of ‘itāyaṃ’. ‘One should cut it off with taming’ means one should cut off that anger with taming. With what taming? ‘With wisdom, energy, and view’ means with insight-wisdom, with bodily and mental energy associated with insight, and with the right view associated with the path. ‘Likewise, one should train in the Dhamma’ means just as one would cut off the unwholesome, so too should one train in the dhammas of serenity and insight. ‘May there not be sullenness for us’ means wishing for this meaning: ‘May the state of sullenness not be for us.’ ‘Without trouble’ means without distress. ‘Without anxiety’ means not having fallen into anxiety about anything. The rest is clear everywhere.

Abyākatavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Sixth Chapter: The Undeclared.

7. Mahāvaggo

7. The Great Chapter

1. Hiriottappasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Hiriottappa Sutta

65. Sattamassa [V 3.0180][P 4.0050] paṭhame hatūpanisoti hataupaniso chinnapaccayo. Yathābhūtañāṇadassananti taruṇavipassanā. Nibbidāvirāgoti balavavipassanā ceva maggo ca. Vimuttiñāṇadassananti arahattavimutti ca paccavekkhaṇā ca.

65. In the first [sutta] of the seventh [vagga], ‘with cause destroyed’ means having a destroyed cause, a cut-off condition. ‘The knowledge and vision of things as they really are’ is nascent insight. ‘Disenchantment and dispassion’ is both strong insight and the path. ‘The knowledge and vision of liberation’ is the liberation of Arahantship and reviewing knowledge.

2. Sattasūriyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Satta Sūriya Sutta

66. Dutiye yasmā ayaṃ sattasūriyadesanā tejosaṃvaṭṭadassanavasena pavattā, tasmā tayo saṃvaṭṭā, tisso saṃvaṭṭasīmā, tīṇi saṃvaṭṭamūlānī, tīṇi kolāhalānīti ayaṃ tāva āditova imassa suttassa purecārikakathā veditabbā. Sā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.403) pubbenivāsānussatiniddese vitthāritāva. Etadavocāti aniccakammaṭṭhānikānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ ajjhāsayena upādinnakānaṃ anupādinnakānaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vipattidassanatthaṃ etaṃ “aniccā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā”tiādisattasūriyopamasuttantaṃ avoca. Tattha aniccāti hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Saṅkhārāti upādinnakaanupādinnakā saṅkhāradhammā. Addhuvāti evaṃ aciraṭṭhena na dhuvā. Anassāsikāti [M 3.0180] asassatabhāvena assāsarahitā. Alamevāti yuttameva.

66. In the second [sutta], because this teaching of the seven suns proceeds by way of showing the destruction by fire, therefore [there are] three destructions, three boundaries of destruction, three roots of destruction, and three commotions. This much should be known from the very beginning as the preliminary discourse of this sutta. That [preliminary discourse] has been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition on the recollection of past lives. ‘He spoke this’ means: for the purpose of showing the destruction of conditioned things, whether appropriated or unappropriated, according to the disposition of the five hundred bhikkhus who had impermanence as their meditation subject, He spoke this Sutta of the Simile of the Seven Suns, beginning with, ‘Impermanent, O bhikkhus, are formations.’ Therein, ‘impermanent’ means they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. ‘Formations’ means conditioned phenomena, whether appropriated or unappropriated. ‘Not lasting’ means they are not lasting in the sense of being not for long. ‘Unreliable’ means they are devoid of solace due to being ungratifying. ‘It is indeed enough’ means it is indeed fitting.

Ajjhogāḷhoti udake anupaviṭṭho. Accuggatoti udakapiṭṭhito uggato. Devo na vassatīti paṭhamaṃ tāva upakappanamegho nāma koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷe ekamegho hutvā vassati, tadā [P 4.0051] nikkhantabījaṃ na puna gehaṃ pavisati. Tato paṭṭhāya dhamakaraṇe niruddhaṃ viya udakaṃ hoti, puna ekabindumpi devo na vassatīti upamānadhammakathāva pamāṇaṃ. Vinassante pana loke paṭhamaṃ avīcito paṭṭhāya tuccho hoti, tato uṭṭhahitvā sattā manussaloke ca tiracchānesu ca nibbattanti. Tiracchānesu nibbattāpi puttabhātikesu mettaṃ paṭilabhitvā kālakatā devamanussesu nibbattanti. Devatā ākāsena carantiyo ārocenti – “na idaṃ ṭhānaṃ [V 3.0181] sassataṃ na nibaddhaṃ, mettaṃ bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ, muditaṃ, upekkhaṃ bhāvethā”ti. Te mettādayo bhāvetvā tato cutā brahmaloke nibbattanti.

‘Submerged’ means entered into the water. ‘Emerged’ means risen from the surface of the water. Regarding the phrase ‘The deva does not rain’: first, a cloud called the world-ending cloud, having become a single cloud, rains over a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems. At that time, the scattered seed does not enter the house again. From then on, the water becomes as if stopped in a water-course, and again the deva does not rain even a single drop. This discourse on the simile is the authority. But when the world is perishing, it first becomes empty, starting from Avīci. Rising from there, beings are reborn in the human world and among animals. Even beings reborn among animals, having gained loving-kindness for their sons and brothers, when they die, are reborn among devas and humans. Deities traveling through the sky announce: ‘This place is not permanent, not fixed. Develop loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity!’ They, having developed loving-kindness and so on, pass away from there and are reborn in the Brahma-world.

Bījagāmāti ettha bījagāmo nāma pañca bījajātāni. Bhūtagāmo nāma yaṃkiñci nikkhantamūlapaṇṇaṃ haritakaṃ. Osadhitiṇavanappatayoti ettha osadhīti osadharukkhā. Tiṇāti bahisārā tālanāḷikerādayo. Vanappatayoti vanajeṭṭhakarukkhā. Kunnadiyoti ṭhapetvā pañca mahānadiyo avasesā ninnagā. Kusobbhāti ṭhapetvā satta mahāsare avasesā rahadādayo. Dutiyo sūriyotiādīsu dutiyasūriyakāle eko udeti, eko atthaṅgameti. Tatiyakāle eko udeti, eko atthaṅgameti, eko majjhe hoti. Catutthakāle catukulike gāme cattāro piṇḍacārikā dvārapaṭipāṭiyā ṭhitā viya honti. Pañcamādikālepi eseva nayo. Palujjantīti [P 4.0052] chijjitvā chijjitvā patanti. Neva chārikā paññāyati na masīti cakkavāḷamahāpathavī sinerupabbatarājā himavā cakkavāḷapabbato cha kāmasaggā paṭhamajjhānikabrahmalokāti ettake ṭhāne daḍḍhe accharāya gahetabbamattāpi chārikā vā aṅgāro vā na paññāyati. Ko mantā ko saddhātāti ko tassa saddhāpanatthāya samattho, ko vā tassa saddhātā. Aññatra diṭṭhapadehīti diṭṭhapade [M 3.0181] sotāpanne ariyasāvake ṭhapetvā ko añño saddahissatīti attho.

Here, `bījagāma` means the five kinds of seeds. `Bhūtagāma` means any green plant that has put forth roots and leaves. In `osadhitiṇavanappatayo`, `osadhi` means medicinal plants. `Tiṇā` means those with an outer core, such as palm and coconut trees. `Vanappatayo` means the chief trees in the forest. `Kunnadiyo` means the remaining small rivers, excluding the five great rivers. `Kusobbhā` means the remaining small lakes and so on, excluding the seven great lakes. In phrases such as ‘the second sun’: at the time of the second sun, one rises, and one sets. At the time of the third, one rises, one sets, and one is in the middle. At the time of the fourth, it is as if four alms-collecting bhikkhus were standing in order of the doors in a village of four families. At the time of the fifth and so on, this is the method. `Palujjanti` means they fall, having been broken again and again. `Neva chārikā paññāyati na masi` means: when these places are burned—namely, the great earth of the Cakkavāḷa, Sineru king of mountains, Himavā, the Cakkavāḷa mountain range, the six kāma heavens, and the first-jhāna brahma worlds—not even as much ash or charcoal as could be picked up with a finger-snap is apparent. `Ko mantā ko saddhātā` means: Who is able to consult whom for the purpose of inspiring faith? Or who would have faith in that person? `Aññatra diṭṭhapadehi` means: excluding the noble disciples, the stream-enterers, who have seen the state of Nibbāna, what other person would be able to believe? This is the meaning.

Vītarāgoti vikkhambhanavasena vītarāgo. Sāsanaṃ ājāniṃsūti anusiṭṭhiṃ jāniṃsu, brahmalokasahabyatāya maggaṃ paṭipajjiṃsu. Samasamagatiyoti dutiyattabhāve sabbākārena samagatiko ekagatiko. Uttari mettaṃ bhāveyyanti paṭhamajjhānato uttari yāva tikacatukkajjhānā paṇītaṃ katvā mettaṃ bhāveyyaṃ. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Parinibbutoti bodhipallaṅkeyeva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Evaṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ dīpetvā satthari desanaṃ vinivaṭṭente pañcasatāpi te aniccakammaṭṭhānikā bhikkhū desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā nisinnāsanesuyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

‘Free from lust’ means free from lust by means of suppression. ‘They understood the teaching’ means they knew the instruction; they practiced the path for the sake of co-existence in the Brahma-world. ‘Of equal, same destiny’ means in a second existence, having an equal state and a single destination in all respects. ‘One should develop loving-kindness further’ means: one should develop loving-kindness, making it sublime, beyond the first jhāna up to the three-fold and four-fold jhānas. ‘Possessing the eye’ means possessing the eye with the five kinds of eyes. ‘Fully extinguished’ means fully extinguished by the full extinguishing of the defilements right at the Bodhi-throne. Thus, having shown the characteristic of impermanence, while the Teacher was concluding the discourse, those five hundred bhikkhus who practiced the meditation on impermanence, having sent forth their knowledge in accordance with the discourse, attained Arahantship right on the seats where they were sitting.

3. Nagaropamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Simile of the City Sutta

67. Tatiye yatoti yadā. Paccantimanti raṭṭhapariyante raṭṭhāvasāne niviṭṭhaṃ. Majjhimadesanagarassa [V 3.0182][P 4.0053] pana rakkhākiccaṃ natthi, tena taṃ na gahitaṃ. Nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhatanti nagarālaṅkārehi alaṅkataṃ. Akaraṇīyanti akattabbaṃ ajiniyaṃ. Gambhīranemāti gambhīraāvāṭā. Sunikhātāti suṭṭhu sannisīdāpitā. Taṃ panetaṃ esikāthambhaṃ iṭṭhakāhi vā karonti silāhi vā khadirādīhi vā sārarukkhehi. Taṃ nagaraguttatthāya karontā bahinagare karonti, alaṅkāratthāya karontā antonagare. Taṃ iṭṭhakāmayaṃ karontā mahantaṃ āvāṭaṃ katvā cayaṃ cinitvā upari aṭṭhaṃsaṃ katvā sudhāya limpanti. Yadā hatthinā dantehi abhihato na calati, tadā sulitto nāma hoti. Silāthambhādayopi aṭṭhaṃsā eva honti. Te sace aṭṭha ratanā honti, caturatanamattaṃ āvāṭe pavisati, caturatanamattaṃ upari hoti. Soḷasaratanavīsatiratanesupi eseva nayo. Sabbesañhi upaḍḍhaṃ heṭṭhā hoti, upaḍḍhaṃ upari. Te gomuttavaṅkā honti, tena tesaṃ antare padaramayaṃ katvā kammaṃ kātuṃ sakkā hoti, te pana katacittakammā paggahitaddhajāva honti.

67. In the third Sutta. `Yato` means `yadā` (when). `Paccantimaṃ` means situated at the country's border, at the country's end. For a city in the middle country, however, there is no duty of guarding; therefore, that is not included. `Nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhataṃ` means adorned with the city's ornaments. `Akaraṇīyaṃ` means unassailable by enemies, unconquerable. `Gambhīranemā` means having deep ditches. `Sunikhātā` means well-embedded. Now, this city-pillar is made of bricks, or of stones, or of heartwood trees like khadira and so on. Those who make it for the city's protection make it outside the city; those who make it for decoration make it inside the city. When making it of bricks, they dig a large pit, build up a mound, make the top octagonal, and plaster it with lime. When it does not move even when struck by an elephant's tusks, it is called well-plastered. Stone pillars and the like are also octagonal. If they are eight ratanas, four ratanas enter the pit and four ratanas are above. This is also the method for those of sixteen or twenty ratanas. Indeed, for all of them, half is below and half is above. They are curved like the stream of a cow's urine; therefore, it is possible to do construction in the space between them by making a wooden platform. And they, with artistic work done upon them, are indeed like raised banners.

Parikhāti [M 3.0182] parikkhipitvā ṭhitamātikā. Anupariyāyapathoti anto pākārassa pākārena saddhiṃ gato mahāpatho, yattha ṭhitā bahipākāre ṭhitehi saddhiṃ yujjhanti. Salākanti [P 4.0054] saratomarādinissaggiyāvudhaṃ. Jevanikanti ekatodhārādisesāvudhaṃ.

`Parikhā` is a moat established, having surrounded the city. `Anupariyāyapatho` is the great road inside the wall that runs alongside the wall, where those stationed there fight with those stationed on the outer wall. `Salākaṃ` is a missile weapon such as an arrow or javelin. `Jevanikaṃ` is a single-edged weapon and other remaining weapons.

Hatthārohāti sabbepi hatthiācariyahatthivejjahatthibandhādayo. Assārohāti sabbepi assācariyaassavejjaassabandhādayo. Rathikāti sabbepi rathācariyarathayodharatharakkhādayo. Dhanuggahāti issāsā. Celakāti ye yuddhe jayaddhajaṃ gahetvā purato gacchanti. Calakāti “idha rañño ṭhānaṃ hotu, idha asukamahāmattassā”ti evaṃ senābyūhakārakā. Piṇḍadāyikāti sāhasikamahāyodhā. Te kira parasenaṃ pavisitvā piṇḍapiṇḍamiva chetvā chetvā dayanti, uppatitvā niggacchantīti attho. Ye vā saṅgāmamajjhe yodhānaṃ bhattapānīyaṃ gahetvā pavisanti, tesampetaṃ nāmaṃ. Uggā rājaputtāti uggatuggatā saṅgāmāvacarā rājaputtā. Pakkhandinoti ye “kassa sīsaṃ vā āvudhaṃ vā āharāmā”ti vatvā “asukassā”ti vuttā saṅgāmaṃ pakkhanditvā tadeva āharanti, ime pakkhandantīti pakkhandino. Mahānāgā viya mahānāgā, hatthiādīsupi abhimukhaṃ āgacchantesu anivattiyayodhānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sūrāti ekasūrā, ye sajālikāpi savammikāpi samuddaṃ tarituṃ sakkonti. Cammayodhinoti [P 4.0055] ye cammakañcukaṃ vā pavisitvā saraparittāṇacammaṃ vā gahetvā yujjhanti. Dāsakaputtāti balavasinehā gharadāsayodhā[V 3.0183]. Dovārikoti dvārapālako. Vāsanalepanasampannoti vāsanena sabbavivarapaṭicchādanena sudhālepena sampanno. Bahi vā khāṇupākārasaṅkhātena vāsanena ghanamaṭṭhena ca sudhālepena sampanno puṇṇaghaṭapantiṃ dassetvā katacittakammapaggahitaddhajo. Tiṇakaṭṭhodakanti hatthiassādīnaṃ ghāsatthāya gehānañca chādanatthāya āharitvā bahūsu ṭhānesu ṭhapitatiṇañca, gehakaraṇapacanādīnaṃ atthāya āharitvā ṭhapitakaṭṭhañca, yantehi pavesetvā pokkharaṇīsu ṭhapitaudakañca. Sannicitaṃ hotīti paṭikacceva anekesu ṭhānesu suṭṭhu nicitaṃ hoti. Abbhantarānaṃ ratiyāti antonagaravāsīnaṃ ratiatthāya. Aparitassāyāti [M 3.0183] tāsaṃ anāpajjanatthāya. Sāliyavakanti nānappakārā sāliyo ceva yavā ca. Tilamuggamāsāparaṇṇanti tilamuggamāsā ca sesāparaṇṇañca.

Hatthārohā means all elephant masters, elephant doctors, elephant keepers, and the like. Assārohā means all horse masters, horse doctors, horse keepers, and the like. Rathikā means all chariot masters, chariot warriors, chariot guards, and the like. Dhanuggahā means archers. Celakā means those who, in battle, carry the victory banner and go in front. Calakā means those who arrange the army formations, saying, 'Let the king’s position be here, let so-and-so's great minister’s position be there.' Piṇḍadāyikā means daring great warriors. It is said they enter the enemy army, and cutting off heads like clusters of fruit, they leap away; this is the meaning. Or, it is also the name for those who, in the midst of battle, take food and water and serve the warriors. Uggā rājaputtā means renowned princes who frequent the battlefield. Pakkhandino means those who, having said, 'Whose head or weapon shall we bring?' and having been told 'So-and-so's,' charge into battle and bring that very thing. Because they charge in, they are called pakkhandino. Mahānāgā means like great elephants; this is a designation for warriors who do not retreat even when elephants and others are coming towards them. Sūrā means singularly brave ones; those who are able to cross the ocean even with their chain mail and armor. Cammayodhino means those who fight having entered a leather tunic or holding a leather shield for protection from arrows. Dāsakaputtā means household slave warriors of strong loyalty. Dovāriko means a doorkeeper. Vāsanalepanasampanno means endowed with a covering for all crevices and with lime plaster. Or, endowed with an outer fence of stakes and with thick, smooth lime plaster, displaying rows of full water pots and having raised banners with artistic work done upon them. Tiṇakaṭṭhodakaṃ means grass brought and stored in many places for fodder for elephants, horses, and so on, and for thatching houses; and firewood brought and stored for the purpose of building houses, cooking, and so on; and water brought in by machines and stored in ponds. Sannicitaṃ hoti means it is well stored up in many places from the very beginning. Abbhantarānaṃ ratiyā means for the delight of the city-dwellers. Aparitassāya means for the purpose of their not falling into terror. Sāliyavakaṃ means various kinds of fine rice and barley. Tilamuggamāsāparaṇṇaṃ means sesame, green gram, black gram, and other pulses.

Idāni yasmā tathāgatassa nagare kammaṃ nāma natthi[P 4.0056], nagarasadisaṃ pana ariyasāvakaṃ, nagaraparikkhārasadise ca satta dhamme, catuāhārasadisāni ca cattāri jhānāni dassetvā ekādasasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ pakkhipitvā desanaṃ vinivaṭṭessāmīti ayaṃ upamā ābhatā. Tasmā taṃ desanaṃ pakāsetuṃ idaṃ evameva khotiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha saddhammehīti sudhammehi. Saddhoti okappanasaddhāya ceva paccakkhasaddhāya ca samannāgato. Tattha dānasīlādīnaṃ phalaṃ saddahitvā dānādipuññakaraṇe saddhā okappanasaddhā nāma. Maggena āgatasaddhā paccakkhasaddhā nāma. Pasādasaddhātipi esā eva. Tassā lakkhaṇādīhi vibhāgo veditabbo.

Now, since for the Tathāgata there is no so-called work to be done in a city, this simile has been brought forth with the thought: 'Having shown the noble disciple to be like a city, the seven good qualities to be like the city's equipment, and the four jhānas to be like the four kinds of food, I will conclude the teaching by placing it in Arahantship in eleven instances.' Therefore, to make that teaching clear, this discourse beginning with 'Evameva kho' was undertaken. Therein, 'saddho' (faithful) means endowed with both conviction-faith and direct-experience-faith. In this context, faith in performing meritorious deeds such as giving, by believing in the fruit of giving, virtue, and so on, is called conviction-faith. The faith that comes by way of the path is called direct-experience-faith. This itself is also called faith of serene clarity. Its analysis by way of characteristics and so on should be understood.

“Sampakkhandanalakkhaṇā ca, mahārāja, saddhā sampasādanalakkhaṇā cā”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.10) hi vacanato idaṃ saddhāya lakkhaṇaṃ nāma. “Tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi saddho pasanno veditabbo. Katamehi tīhi? Sīlavantānaṃ dassanakāmo hotī”tiādinā (a. ni. 3.42) nayena vuttaṃ pana saddhāya nimittaṃ nāma. “Ko cāhāro saddhāya, saddhammassavanantissa vacanīya”nti (a. ni. 10.61) ayaṃ panassā āhāro nāma. “Saddhāpabbajitassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno ayaṃ anudhammo hoti, yaṃ rūpe nibbidābahulo viharissatī”ti ayamassa [P 4.0057] anudhammo nāma. “Saddhā bandhati pātheyyaṃ, sirī bhogānamāsayo” (saṃ. ni. 1.79). “Saddhā dutiyā purisassa hoti” (saṃ. ni. 1.36). “Saddhāya tarati oghaṃ” (saṃ. ni. 1.246). “Saddhā bījaṃ tapo vuṭṭhi” (su. ni. 77; saṃ. ni. 1.197). “Saddhāhattho mahānāgo. Upekhāsetadantavā”tiādīsu pana suttesu [V 3.0184] etissā baddhabhattapuṭādisarikkhatāya anekasarasatā bhagavatā pakāsitā. Imasmiṃ pana nagaropamasuttante esā acalasuppatiṭṭhitatāya esikāthambhasadisā katvā dassitā.

“Faith, great king, is characterized by leaping forward and by serenity”; thus from this statement, this is called the characteristic of faith. “A faithful and devoted person, monks, is to be recognized by three things. Which three? He desires to see the virtuous,” and so on—by this method, what is spoken of is called the sign of faith. “And what is the nutriment for faith? It should be said: listening to the true Dhamma”; this is called its nutriment. “For a monk gone forth in faith, monks, this is the corresponding Dhamma: that he will dwell with much disenchantment towards form”; this is called its corresponding Dhamma. “Faith binds provisions for the journey; prosperity is the basis of enjoyments.” “Faith is a person’s companion.” “By faith, one crosses the flood.” “Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain.” “The great nāga has faith as its trunk, equanimity as its white tusks,” and so on—in these discourses, its manifold nature, similar to a bound bundle of food and the like, has been revealed by the Blessed One. But in this City-simile Discourse, it is shown as being like a gate-pillar, due to its nature of being unshakable and well-established.

Saddhesikoti saddhaṃ esikāthambhaṃ katvā ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahatīti iminā nayena sabbapadesu yojanā kātabbā. Apicettha hirottappehi tīsu dvāresu saṃvaro sampajjati, so catupārisuddhisīlaṃ hoti[M 3.0184]. Iti imasmiṃ sutte ekādasasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ pakkhipitvā desanāya kūṭaṃ gahitanti veditabbaṃ.

Faith as the gate-pillar: having made faith the gate-pillar, the noble disciple abandons the unwholesome. In this way, the application should be made in all passages. Moreover, here, restraint at the three doors is accomplished through moral shame and moral dread; this constitutes the fourfold purification virtue. Thus, it should be understood that in this sutta, by including Arahantship in eleven places, the pinnacle of the teaching has been grasped.

4. Dhammaññūsuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Dhammaññū Sutta

68. Catutthe kālaṃ jānātīti yuttappattakālaṃ jānāti. Ayaṃ kālo uddesassāti ayaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhanakālo. Paripucchāyāti atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ paripucchāya. Yogassāti yoge kammaṃ pakkhipanassa. Paṭisallānassāti nilīyanassa ekībhāvassa. Dhammānudhammappaṭipannoti navannaṃ lokuttaradhammānaṃ anurūpadhammaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu puggalaparoparaññū hotīti evaṃ [P 4.0058] bhikkhu puggalānaṃ paroparaṃ tikkhamudubhāvaṃ jānanasamattho nāma hoti.

68. In the fourth, “he knows the time”—he knows the appropriate and suitable time. “This is the time for learning”—this is the time for learning the Buddha’s words. “For questioning”—for inquiring into meaning and non-meaning, cause and non-cause. “For exertion”—for undertaking the work of the practice. “For seclusion”—for dwelling in solitude, for being alone. “Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma”—he has undertaken the preliminary path, the Dhamma that is in conformity with the nine supramundane Dhammas. “Thus, monks, a monk is one who knows the caliber of persons”—thus, a monk is said to be capable of knowing the sharp and dull nature of persons.

5. Pāricchattakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Pāricchattaka Sutta.

69. Pañcame pannapalāsoti patitapalāso. Jālakajātoti sañjātapattapupphajālo. Tassa hi pattajālañca pupphajālañca saheva nikkhamati. Khārakajātoti pāṭiyekkaṃ sañjātena suvibhattena pattajālakena ca pupphajālakena ca samannāgato. Kuṭumalakajātoti sañjātamakuḷo. Korakajātoti avikasitehi mahākucchīhi sambhinnamukhehi pupphehi samannāgato. Sabbapāliphulloti sabbākārena supupphito. Dibbe cattāro māseti dibbena āyunā cattāro māse. Manussagaṇanāya pana tāni dvādasa vassasahassāni honti. Paricārentīti ito cito ca indriyāni cārenti, kīḷanti ramantīti attho.

69. In the fifth, “fallen leaves”—leaves that have fallen. “Net-like”—having a network of leaves and flowers. For its network of leaves and network of flowers emerge together. “Having distinct clusters”—endowed with a distinct and well-divided network of leaves and network of flowers. “Budding”—having developed buds. “Having large buds”—endowed with flowers that have not yet opened, with large calyxes whose tips are splitting open. “In full bloom”—fully flowered in every way. “For four divine months”—four months by divine lifespan. But by human calculation, these amount to twelve thousand years. “They attend”—they direct their senses here and there, playing and delighting—this is the meaning.

Ābhāya phuṭaṃ hotīti tattakaṃ ṭhānaṃ obhāsena phuṭaṃ hoti. Tesañhi pupphānaṃ bālasūriyassa [V 3.0185] viya ābhā hoti, pattāni paṇṇacchattappamāṇāni, anto mahātumbamattā reṇu hoti. Pupphite pana pāricchattake ārohanakiccaṃ vā aṅkusakaṃ gahetvā namanakiccaṃ vā pupphāharaṇatthaṃ caṅgoṭakakiccaṃ vā natthi, kantanakavāto uṭṭhahitvā pupphāni vaṇṭato kantati, sampaṭicchanakavāto sampaṭicchati, pavesanakavāto sudhammaṃ devasabhaṃ paveseti, sammajjanakavāto purāṇapupphāni nīharati, santharaṇakavāto [P 4.0059] pattakaṇṇikakesarāni rañjento santharati. Majjhaṭṭhāne dhammāsanaṃ [M 3.0185] hoti yojanappamāṇo ratanapallaṅko upari tiyojanena setacchattena dhāriyamānena, tadanantaraṃ sakkassa devarañño āsanaṃ atthariyati, tato tettiṃsāya devaputtānaṃ, tato aññesaṃ mahesakkhānaṃ devānaṃ, aññataradevatānaṃ pupphakaṇṇikāva āsanaṃ hoti. Devā devasabhaṃ pavisitvā nisīdanti. Tato pupphehi reṇuvaṭṭi uggantvā uparikaṇṇikaṃ āhacca nipatamānā devatānaṃ tigāvutappamāṇaṃ attabhāvaṃ lākhārasaparikammasajjitaṃ viya suvaṇṇacuṇṇapiñjaraṃ viya karoti. Ekacce devā ekekaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā aññamaññaṃ paharantāpi kīḷantiyeva. Paharaṇakālepi mahātumbappamāṇā reṇu nikkhamitvā sarīraṃ pabhāsampannehi gandhacuṇṇehi sañjatamanosilārāgaṃ viya karoti. Evaṃ sā kīḷā catūhi māsehi pariyosānaṃ gacchati. Ayamānubhāvoti ayaṃ anupharituṃ ānubhāvo.

The light spreads—that is, that entire place is suffused with radiance. For those flowers have a glow like the rising sun, the leaves are the size of parasols, and inside, the pollen is as large as a large betel-box. When the coral tree is in bloom, there is no task of climbing, or taking a hook to bend it down, or using a basket for carrying the flowers. The wind that cuts arises and severs the flowers from their stems; the wind that receives gathers them; the wind that causes them to enter brings them into the Sudhammā divine assembly; the wind that sweeps removes the old flowers; and the wind that strews, arranging them in order, scatters the petals and pollen. In the central place, there is a Dhamma-seat, a jeweled couch a yojana in size, with a white parasol three yojanas in size held above it. Next to it, the seat of Sakka, king of the devas, is laid out; then those of the thirty-three devaputtas; then those of other powerful devas. For the devas of unknown lineage, the flower's corolla itself is the seat. The devas enter the divine assembly and sit down. Then, the wind, having taken up the pollen dust from the flowers, strikes the pinnacle above and falls, making the bodies of the devas, which are three gāvutas in size, as if smeared with lac-juice or smeared with gold dust. Some devas, taking one flower each, play by striking one another. Even when they strike, pollen the size of a large betel-box emerges and makes their bodies as if colored with well-prepared red arsenic and realgar by means of fragrant powders endowed with radiance. Thus, that play comes to an end in four months. This is the power to pervade.

Idāni yasmā na satthā pāricchattakena atthiko, tena pana saddhiṃ upametvā satta ariyasāvake dassetukāmo, tasmā te dassetuṃ evameva khotiādimāha. Tattha pabbajjāya cetetīti pabbajissāmīti cinteti. Devānaṃvāti devānaṃ viya. Yāva brahmalokā saddo abbhuggacchatīti pathavitalato yāva brahmalokā sādhukārasaddena sabbaṃ ekasaddameva hoti. Ayamānubhāvoti [P 4.0060] ayaṃ khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno anupharaṇānubhāvo. Imasmiṃ sutte catupārisuddhisīlaṃ pabbajjānissitaṃ hoti, kasiṇaparikammaṃ paṭhamajjhānasannissitaṃ, vipassanāya saddhiṃ tayo maggā tīṇi ca phalāni arahattamaggasannissitāni honti. Desanāya heṭṭhato vā uparito vā ubhayato vā paricchedo hoti, idha pana ubhayato paricchedo. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṅkhepato panettha vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, because the Teacher has no need for the coral tree, but rather, wishing to show the seven noble disciples by comparing them with it, he therefore spoke the words beginning with “Just so…”. Here, “one intends to go forth” means one thinks, “I will go forth.” `Devānaṃ vā` means: like that of the devas. “The sound of approval rises as far as the Brahmā world” means from the surface of the earth up to the Brahmā world, all becomes a single, simultaneous sound of approval. “This is the power” means this rising of the sound of fame up to the Brahmā world is the pervading power of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed. In this sutta, the fourfold purification virtue is dependent on the going forth, the preliminary kasina practice is dependent on the first jhāna, and together with insight, the three paths and the three fruits are dependent on the path of arahantship. The exposition has a delimitation either from below, by way of the fourfold purification virtue; or from above, by way of insight, paths, and fruits; or from both sides. But here, it is from both sides. Therefore, this was said. Furthermore, it should be understood that here, in brief, the round of existence and that which is free from the round are taught.

6. Sakkaccasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sakkacca Sutta.

70. Chaṭṭhe parisuddhā ca bhavissantīti bhiyyosomattāya parisuddhā bhavissanti nimmalā. Sakammāragatoti ettha sa-kāro nipātamattaṃ, kammāragato kammāruddhanagatoti attho.

70. In the sixth, they will be purified; indeed, they will be purified to a greater extent, they will be immaculate. Regarding 'sakammāragato,' here the 'sa-' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'gone to the smith's forge, gone to the smith's furnace.'

7. Bhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Bhāvanā Sutta.

71. Sattame [M 3.0186][V 3.0186] ananuyuttassāti na yuttappayuttassa hutvā viharato. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍānīti imā kaṇhapakkhasukkapakkhavasena dve upamā vuttā. Tāsu kaṇhapakkhūpamā atthassa asādhikā, itarā sādhikāti sukkapakkhūpamāya eva attho veditabbo. Seyyathāti opammatthe nipāto. Apīti sambhāvanatthe. Ubhayenāpi seyyathāpi nāma, bhikkhaveti dasseti. Kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vāti ettha pana kiñcāpi kukkuṭiyā vuttappakārato ūnādhikānipi aṇḍāni honti, vacanasiliṭṭhatāya panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañhi loke siliṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ hoti. Tānassūti tāni assu, bhaveyyunti attho. Kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitānīti tāya janettiyā kukkuṭiyā pakkhe pasāretvā tesaṃ upari sayantiyā sammā adhisayitāni. Sammā pariseditānīti kālena kālaṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpentiyā suṭṭhu samantato seditāni, usmīkatānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sammā [P 4.0061] paribhāvitānīti kālena kālaṃ suṭṭhu samantato bhāvitāni, kukkuṭagandhaṃ gāhāpitānīti attho.

71. In the seventh (sutta), 'not devoted' means living without being yoked and applied. Just as, bhikkhus, a hen's eggs—here two similes are stated, based on the dark fortnight and the bright fortnight. Among these, the simile of the dark fortnight does not accomplish the meaning, while the other does. Therefore, the meaning should be understood through the simile of the bright fortnight. 'Seyyathā' is a particle in the sense of comparison. 'Api' is in the sense of emphasis. Both together show, 'Just as, bhikkhus...' 'A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs'—here, although a hen may have fewer or more eggs than stated, this is spoken for the sake of idiomatic expression. For such an expression is idiomatic in the world. 'Tānassu' means 'those would be,' 'they would come to be.' 'Properly sat upon by the hen' means they are properly sat upon by that mother hen who, spreading her wings, lies over them. 'Properly incubated' means she warms them thoroughly all around from time to time, making them heated. 'Properly imbued' means they are thoroughly imbued from all around from time to time, being made to take on the hen's smell—this is the meaning.

Kiñcāpi tassā kukkuṭiyāti tassā kukkuṭiyā imaṃ tividhakiriyākaraṇena appamādaṃ katvā kiñcāpi na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya. Atha kho bhabbāva teti atha kho te kukkuṭapotakā vuttanayena sotthinā abhinibbhijjituṃ bhabbāva. Te hi yasmā tāya kukkuṭiyā evaṃ tīhākārehi tāni aṇḍāni paripāliyamānāni na pūtīni honti. Yopi nesaṃ allasineho, so pariyādānaṃ gacchati, kapālaṃ tanukaṃ hoti, pādanakhasikhā ca mukhatuṇḍakañca kharaṃ hoti, sayampi pariṇāmaṃ gacchati. Kapālassa tanuttā bahiddhā āloko anto paññāyati, tasmā “ciraṃ vata mayaṃ saṃkuṭitahatthapādā sambādhe sayimha, ayañca bahi āloko dissati, ettha dāni no sukhavihāro bhavissatī”ti nikkhamitukāmā hutvā kapālaṃ pādena paharanti, gīvaṃ pasārenti, tato taṃ kapālaṃ dvedhā bhijjati. Atha te pakkhe vidhunantā taṃkhaṇānurūpaṃ viravantā nikkhamantiyeva. Nikkhamantā ca gāmakkhettaṃ upasobhayamānā vicaranti.

'Even though that hen' means, even though for that hen, having acted diligently by performing these three actions, such a desire might not arise. 'Yet they are capable' means those chicks are indeed capable of breaking out safely in the manner described. For because those eggs were nurtured by that hen in these three ways, they did not rot. Whatever moisture was in them was used up, the shell became thin, their claws and beaks became hard, and they themselves matured. Due to the thinness of the shell, the light outside became visible inside. Therefore, desiring to break out, thinking, 'For so long we have lain with contracted limbs in this narrow space, and now light outside is visible; here now will be our pleasant abiding,' they strike the shell with their feet, stretch their necks, and then the shell splits in two. Then, shaking their wings, making sounds appropriate to the moment, they emerge. And having emerged, they roam about, adorning the village fields.

Evameva [M 3.0187] khoti idaṃ opammasampaṭipādanaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ atthena saṃsandetvā veditabbaṃ – tassā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍesu adhisayanāditividhakiriyākaraṇaṃ viya hi imassa bhikkhuno bhāvanaṃ anuyuttakālo[V 3.0187], kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyāsampādanena [P 4.0062] aṇḍānaṃ apūtibhāvo viya bhāvanaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇassa aparihāni. Tassā tividhakiriyākaraṇena aṇḍānaṃ allasinehapariyādānaṃ viya tassa bhikkhuno tividhānupassanāsampādanena bhavattayānugatanikantisinehapariyādānaṃ, aṇḍakapālānaṃ tanubhāvo viya bhikkhuno avijjaṇḍakosassa tanubhāvo, kukkuṭapotakānaṃ nakhatuṇḍakānaṃ thaddhabhāvo viya bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇassa tikkhakharavippasannasūrabhāvo, kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pariṇāmakālo viya bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇassa pariṇāmakālo vaḍḍhikālo gabbhaggahaṇakālo, kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā pakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā abhinibbhidākālo viya tassa bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā vicarantassa tajjātikaṃ utusappāyaṃ vā bhojanasappāyaṃ vā puggalasappāyaṃ vā dhammassavanasappāyaṃ vā labhitvā ekāsane nisinnasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa anupubbādhigatena arahattamaggena avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā abhiññāpakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā arahattappattakālo veditabbo.

Just so, this is the application of the simile. It should be understood by connecting the meaning in this way: just as there is that hen's performance of the three kinds of actions, such as sitting on the eggs, so too is the time when this bhikkhu is devoted to meditation. Just as through the hen's accomplishment of the three actions there is the non-rotting of the eggs, so too for the bhikkhu devoted to meditation, through the accomplishment of the three contemplations, there is the non-decline of insight-knowledge. Just as through her performance of the three actions there is the exhaustion of the eggs' moisture, so too through that bhikkhu's accomplishment of the three contemplations there is the exhaustion of the sticky craving that follows the three realms of existence. Just as there is the thinness of the eggshells, so too there is the thinness of the bhikkhu's eggshell of ignorance. Just as there is the hardness of the chicks' claws and beaks, so too there is the sharpness, firmness, special clarity, and courage of the bhikkhu's insight knowledge. Just as there is the time for the chicks to mature, so too there is the time for the bhikkhu's insight knowledge to mature, to grow, to grasp the embryo. Just as there is the time when the chicks, breaking the eggshell with the tip of their claws or with their beaks and flapping their wings, emerge safely, so too should be understood the time of safely attaining Arahantship for that bhikkhu who, having taken up the embryo of insight knowledge and living accordingly, having obtained suitable conditions—whether favorable weather, suitable food, a suitable person, or hearing the Dhamma suitably—and, while sitting in one place developing insight, breaks the eggshell of ignorance with the successively attained path of Arahantship and flaps the wings of higher knowledge.

Yathā pana kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā mātāpi aṇḍakosaṃ bhindati, evaṃ tathārūpassa bhikkhuno ñāṇaparipākaṃ ñatvā satthāpi –

Just as a mother hen, knowing the ripeness of her chicks, also breaks the eggshell, so too, the Teacher, knowing the maturity of such a bhikkhu's knowledge—

“Ucchinda [P 4.0063] sinehamattano, kumudaṃ sāradikaṃva pāṇinā;

Santimaggameva brūhaya, nibbānaṃ sugatena desita”nti. (dha. pa. 285) –

“Cut off your own sticky craving, as one plucks an autumn water lily with the hand; cultivate only the path to peace, Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.”

Ādinā nayena obhāsaṃ pharitvā gāthāya avijjaṇḍakosaṃ paharati. So gāthāpariyosāne avijjaṇḍakosaṃ bhinditvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tato paṭṭhāya yathā te kukkuṭapotakā gāmakkhettaṃ upasobhayamānā tattha vicaranti, evaṃ ayampi mahākhīṇāsavo nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā saṅghārāmaṃ upasobhayamāno vicarati.

With a verse in this way, having pervaded with radiance, he strikes the eggshell of ignorance. At the conclusion of the verse, having broken the eggshell of ignorance, he attains Arahantship. From then on, just as those chicks, adorning the village fields, wander there, so too does this great one, whose taints are destroyed, having entered the fruition attainment with Nibbāna as its object, wander, adorning the monastery.

Phalagaṇḍassāti [M 3.0188] vaḍḍhakissa. So hi olambakasaṅkhātaṃ phalaṃ cāretvā dārūnaṃ gaṇḍaṃ haratīti phalagaṇḍoti vuccati. Vāsijaṭeti vāsidaṇḍakassa gahaṇaṭṭhāne. Ettakaṃ me ajja āsavānaṃ khīṇanti pabbajitassa hi pabbajjāsaṅkhepena uddesena paripucchāya yonisomanasikārena vattapaṭipattiyā ca niccakālaṃ āsavā khīyanti. Evaṃ khīyamānānaṃ pana nesaṃ “ettakaṃ ajja [V 3.0188] khīṇaṃ ettakaṃ hiyyo”ti evamassa ñāṇaṃ na hotīti attho. Imāya upamāya vipassanānisaṃso dīpito.

'Phalagaṇḍassa' means 'of the carpenter.' For he is called 'phalagaṇḍa' because, by holding a marking string called 'olambaka,' he removes the knots from the wood. 'Vāsijaṭe' means 'at the gripping place of the adze handle.' Regarding 'So much of my taints are destroyed today': for a person who has gone forth, the taints are constantly destroyed by the state of monkhood, by learning the Pāḷi text, by learning the commentary, by appropriate attention, and by the fulfillment of major and minor duties. But as they are being destroyed, the knowledge does not arise in him, 'So much was destroyed today, so much yesterday'—this is the meaning. By this simile, the benefit of insight is shown.

Hemantikenāti hemantasamayena. Paṭippassambhantīti thirabhāvena parihāyanti. Evameva khoti ettha mahāsamuddo viya sāsanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nāvā viya yogāvacaro, nāvāya mahāsamudde pariyāyanaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno ūnapañcavassakāle ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike vicaraṇaṃ, nāvāya mahāsamuddaudakena [P 4.0064] khajjamānānaṃ bandhanānaṃ tanubhāvo viya bhikkhuno pabbajjāsaṅkhepena uddesaparipucchādīhiyeva saṃyojanānaṃ tanubhāvo, nāvāya thale ukkhittakālo viya bhikkhuno nissayamuttakassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññe vasanakālo, divā vātātapena saṃsussanaṃ viya vipassanāñāṇena taṇhāsinehassa saṃsussanaṃ, rattiṃ himodakena temanaṃ viya kammaṭṭhānaṃ nissāya uppannena pītipāmojjena cittatemanaṃ, rattindivaṃ vātātapehi ceva himodakena ca parisukkhaparitintānaṃ bandhanānaṃ dubbalabhāvo viya vipassanāñāṇapītipāmojjehi saṃyojanānaṃ bhiyyosomattāya dubbalabhāvo, pāvussakamegho viya arahattamaggañāṇaṃ, meghavuṭṭhiudakena nāvāya antopūtibhāvo viya āraddhavipassakassa rūpasattakādivasena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa okkhāyamāne pakkhāyamāne kammaṭṭhāne ekadivasaṃ utusappāyādīni laddhā ekapallaṅkena nisinnassa arahattaphalādhigamo. Pūtibandhanāya nāvāya kiñci kālaṃ ṭhānaṃ viya khīṇasaṃyojanassa arahato mahājanaṃ anuggaṇhantassa yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhānaṃ, pūtibandhanāya nāvāya anupubbena bhijjitvā apaṇṇattikabhāvūpagamo viya khīṇāsavassa upādinnakkhandhabhedena anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutassa apaṇṇattikabhāvūpagamoti imāya upamāya saṃyojanānaṃ dubbalatā dīpitā.

'In the winter season' means 'during the winter time.' 'They are allayed' means 'they diminish from a state of firmness.' Just so, here, the Dispensation should be seen like the great ocean, and the meditator like a boat. The boat's journey across the great ocean is like this bhikkhu's wandering near his teachers and preceptors during his less-than-five-year period. The attenuation of the boat's bonds worn by the ocean water is like the attenuation of the bhikkhu's fetters by the very fact of being a monk, by learning the Pāḷi text, learning the commentary, and so forth. The boat being hauled onto land is like the bhikkhu, freed from dependence, taking up a meditation subject and dwelling in the forest. The drying by day from wind and sun is like the drying up of the moisture of craving through insight-knowledge. The moistening at night by dew-water is like the moistening of the mind by joy and gladness arising in dependence on the meditation subject. The bonds becoming weak day and night from wind, sun, and dew-water is like the fetters becoming exceedingly weak through insight-knowledge, joy, and gladness. The rain cloud of the rainy season is like the knowledge of the path to Arahantship. The boat rotting internally from rainwater is like the attainment of the fruition of Arahantship for one who has aroused insight, who is developing insight by way of the sevenfold analysis of form, etc., and, while the meditation subject is becoming manifest, having obtained favorable conditions such as climate in a single day, sits in a single session. The boat with rotten bonds lasting for some time is like the Arahant, whose fetters are destroyed, abiding for his lifespan while assisting the great multitude. The boat with rotten bonds gradually breaking apart and reaching a state of non-designation is like the one whose taints are destroyed, through the breakup of the appropriated aggregates, attaining the state of non-designation by final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue. Thus, by this simile, the weakness of the fetters is shown.

8. Aggikkhandhopamasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta

72. Aṭṭhamaṃ [M 3.0189][P 4.0065] atthuppattiyaṃ kathitaṃ. Atthuppatti panassa heṭṭhā cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasuttavaṇṇanāya (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.51 ādayo) vitthāritā eva. Passatha noti passatha nu. Āliṅgitvāti upagūhitvā. Upanisīdeyyāti samīpe nissāya nisīdeyya. Upanipajjeyyāti upagantvā nipajjeyya. Ārocayāmīti ācikkhāmi. Paṭivedayāmīti paṭivedetvā jānāpetvā kathemi. Vālarajjuyāti assavālagovālehi vaṭṭitarajjuyā. Paccorasminti [V 3.0189] uramajjhe. Pheṇuddehakanti pheṇaṃ uddehitvā, ussādetvāti attho. Attatthanti attano diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikalokiyalokuttaraṃ atthaṃ. Paratthobhayatthesupi eseva nayo. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasuttassa (a. ni. 1.51 ādayo) atthuppattiyaṃ kathitameva. Idañca pana suttaṃ kathetvā satthā cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasuttaṃ kathesi. Navamaṃ uttānatthameva.

72. The eighth (sutta) was spoken in connection with its origination. Its origination, however, has already been detailed below in the commentary on the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta. 'Passatha no' means 'passatha nu' (do you see?). 'Āliṅgitvā' means 'having embraced.' 'Upanisīdeyya' means 'should sit down nearby.' 'Upanipajjeyya' means 'should lie down, approaching close.' 'Ārocayāmi' means 'I announce.' 'Paṭivedayāmi' means 'having informed and made known, I speak.' 'Vālarajjuyā' means 'with a rope twisted from the tail-hairs of horses and cows.' 'Paccorasmiṃ' means 'in the middle of the chest.' 'Pheṇuddehakaṃ' means 'having caused foam to arise and having raised it up'—this is the meaning. 'Attatthaṃ' means one's own benefit: the benefit pertaining to this life, to the next life, the worldly, and the supramundane. The same method applies to 'parattha' (the benefit of others) and 'ubhayattha' (the benefit of both). Whatever else should be said here, all that has been spoken in the origination story of the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta. And having spoken this sutta, the Teacher spoke the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta. The ninth has a plain meaning.

10. Arakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Araka Sutta

74. Dasame parittanti appaṃ thokaṃ. Tañhi sarasaparittatāyapi khaṇaparittatāyapi ṭhitiparittatāyapi parittameva. Lahuṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhanato lahukaṃ. Mantāyaṃ [P 4.0066] boddhabbanti mantāya boddhabbaṃ, paññāya jānitabbanti attho. Pabbateyyāti pabbatasambhavā. Hārahārinīti rukkhanaḷaveḷuādīni haritabbāni harituṃ samatthā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

74. In the tenth (sutta), 'parittaṃ' means little, small. Indeed, that life is short due to its short essence, short duration, and short stability. Because it arises and ceases quickly, it is called 'lahukaṃ' (quick). 'Mantāya boddhabbaṃ' means it should be known by wisdom; the meaning is that it should be known by wisdom. 'Pabbateyyā' means originating from a mountain. 'Hārahārinī' means capable of carrying things that are to be carried, such as trees, reeds, and bamboos. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Mahāvaggo sattamo.

The Great Chapter, the Seventh.

8. Vinayavaggo

8. The Vinaya Chapter

1. Paṭhamavinayadharasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Sutta on One Versed in the Vinaya

75. Aṭṭhamassa paṭhame āpattiṃ jānātīti āpattiṃyeva āpattīti jānāti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

75. In the first (sutta) of the eighth (vagga), 'āpattiṃ jānāti' means he knows an offense as 'an offense'. In the remaining phrases, too, this is the method.

2. Dutiyavinayadharasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Sutta on One Versed in the Vinaya

76. Dutiye [M 3.0190] svāgatānīti suāgatāni suppaguṇāni. Suvibhattānīti koṭṭhāsato suṭṭhu vibhattāni[V 3.0190]. Suppavattīnīti āvajjitāvajjitaṭṭhāne suṭṭhu pavattāni daḷhappaguṇāni. Suvinicchitānīti suṭṭhu vinicchitāni. Suttasoti vibhaṅgato. Anubyañjanasoti khandhakaparivārato.

76. In the second (sutta), 'svāgatāni' means well-mastered, well-practiced. 'Suvibhattāni' means well-divided by way of sections. 'Suppavattīni' means they proceed well in whatever place is adverted to, being firmly practiced. 'Suvinicchitāni' means well-adjudicated. 'Suttaso' means by way of the Vibhaṅga. 'Anubyañjanaso' means by way of the Khandhaka and Parivāra.

3. Tatiyavinayadharasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Third Sutta on One Versed in the Vinaya

77. Tatiye vinaye kho pana ṭhito hotīti vinayalakkhaṇe patiṭṭhito hoti. Asaṃhīroti na sakkā hoti gahitaggahaṇaṃ vissajjāpetuṃ.

77. In the third (sutta), 'vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti' means he is established in the characteristic of the Vinaya. 'Asaṃhīro' means it is not possible to make him abandon a view that has been grasped.

9. Satthusāsanasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Teacher's Dispensation

83. Navame ekoti adutiyo. Vūpakaṭṭhoti kāyena gaṇato, cittena kilesehi vūpakaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho dūrībhūto. Appamattoti [P 4.0067] satiavippavāse ṭhito. Pahitattoti pesitatto. Nibbidāyāti vaṭṭe ukkaṇṭhanatthāya. Virāgāyāti rāgādīnaṃ virajjanatthāya. Nirodhāyāti appavattikaraṇatthāya. Vūpasamāyāti kilesavūpasamāya appavattiyā. Abhiññāyāti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā abhijānanatthāya. Sambodhāyāti maggasaṅkhātassa sambodhassa atthāya. Nibbānāyāti nibbānassa sacchikaraṇatthāya.

83. In the ninth (sutta), 'eko' means without a companion. 'Vūpakaṭṭho' means withdrawn, secluded, and distant, with the body from the group and with the mind from the defilements. 'Appamatto' means established in the non-absence of mindfulness. 'Pahitatto' means having a mind dispatched towards Nibbāna. 'Nibbidāya' is for the purpose of weariness with the round of existence. 'Virāgāya' is for the purpose of dispassion towards lust and so on. 'Nirodhāya' is for the purpose of causing non-arising. 'Vūpasamāya' is for the calming of defilements, for non-arising. 'Abhiññāya' is for the purpose of knowing with higher knowledge, having applied the three characteristics. 'Sambodhāya' is for the purpose of the enlightenment designated as the path. 'Nibbānāya' is for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna.

10. Adhikaraṇasamathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sutta on the Settlement of Issues

84. Dasame adhikaraṇāni samenti vūpasamentīti adhikaraṇasamathā. Uppannuppannānanti uppannānaṃ uppannānaṃ. Adhikaraṇānanti vivādādhikaraṇaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇanti imesaṃ catunnaṃ. Samathāya vūpasamāyāti samathatthañceva vūpasamanatthañca. Sammukhāvinayo dātabbo…pe… tiṇavatthārakoti ime satta samathā dātabbā. Tesaṃ vinicchayo vinayasaṃvaṇṇanato (cūḷava. aṭṭha. 186-187 ādayo) gahetabbo. Apica dīghanikāye saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanāyampi [M 3.0191] (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.331 adhikaraṇasamathasattakavaṇṇanā) vitthāritoyeva, tathā majjhimanikāye sāmagāmasuttavaṇṇanāyāti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.46).

84. In the tenth sutta, because they settle and appease legal questions (adhikaraṇa), they are called settlements of legal questions (adhikaraṇasamathā). 'Uppannuppannānaṃ' means 'of those that have arisen and arisen.' 'Adhikaraṇānaṃ' means of these four legal questions: legal questions of dispute, legal questions of accusation, legal questions of offenses, and legal questions of procedure. 'Samathāya vūpasamāya' means for the purpose of settling and for the purpose of appeasing. 'Sammukhāvinayo dātabbo…pe… tiṇavatthārako'—these seven settlements should be applied. Their adjudication is to be understood from the commentary on the Vinaya. Moreover, it is explained in detail in the commentary on the Saṅgīti Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya, and likewise in the commentary on the Sāmagāma Sutta in the Majjhima Nikāya.

Vinayavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Vinaya Chapter, the Eighth.

Ito [V 3.0191] parāni satta suttāni uttānatthāneva. Na hettha kiñci heṭṭhā avuttanayaṃ nāma atthīti.

Henceforth, the seven suttas have an obvious meaning. There is nothing here whatsoever of a method not mentioned before.

Manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

In the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Sattakanipātassa saṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of the Sevens is concluded.
